name: Nevada Current
title: Reno Hawk Fire destroys 32 homes, crews make progress on containment
description: Firefighting crews have made progress containing the Hawk fire blazing near Reno that has destroyed more than 30 homes and placed tens of thousands under evacuation orders or warnings. The fast-moving Hawk fire began on Saturday to the north-west of Reno, Nevada’s second most populous city, and quickly spread across more than 15,000 acres by […]
text:
A firefighting aircraft drops fire retardant during the Hawk Fire on August 23, 2026 in Reno, (Photo by Trevor Bexon/Getty Images)Firefighting crews have made progress containing the Hawk fire blazing near Reno that has destroyed more than 30 homes and placed tens of thousands under evacuation orders or warnings.
The fast-moving Hawk fire began on Saturday to the north-west of Reno, Nevada’s second most populous city, and quickly spread across more than 15,000 acres by Monday afternoon. 
Richard Edwards, the chief of Truckee Meadows Fire Protection District said that first responders have identified 32 destroyed homes and six damaged homes as a result of the fire. 
“We expect those numbers to increase as damage assessment teams are still out in the field assessing other areas right now,” said Edwards during a fire briefing Monday afternoon. 
The fire has also resulted in four civilian injuries and three firefighter injuries, according to officials. Canine search teams have not detected any loss of life in the fire areas.
“The dogs have had no hits on that, so good news for us there as well,” Edwards said. 
As of Monday afternoon, about 23,000 people are under a “go-now” evacuation order and 40,000 people are under a “get-set” warning. 
Authorities said the fire reached 27% containment by Monday afternoon, including regions along the southern portion of Somerset and east of US Route 395, a major north-south highway that was shut down due to the fire. More than 900 personnel are currently assigned to the fire, according to officials. 
“We’ve got helicopters assigned. We’ve got scoopers available to us that have been scooping out of Stampede Reservoir, and we’re utilizing them as needed around the hotspots around the outside of the fire,” said Pete Bryant, the division chief with the Reno Fire Department.
Representatives for NV Energy said about 10,000 Northern Nevada customers are without power due to emergency measures related to the Hawk Fire. Another 250 gas customers in northern Nevada have been left without service. More than 100 power poles were damaged by the fire, and gas infrastructure in the area will require ongoing work.
Matt Zumstein, an agency administrator for the U.S Forest Service, urged residents to avoid flying drones in airspace where firefighting crews are still working.
“It shuts down our aviation assets and causes problems for the suppression side,” Zumstein said. 
Gov. Joe Lombardo declared a state of emergency in Washoe County, Sunday warning residents to follow local officials’ instructions and leave immediately if ordered.
On Monday, the FEMA Region 9 Regional Administrator authorized the use of federal funds to assist the state of Nevada in combating the Hawk Fire burning in Washoe County.
Washoe County said residents can get up to date information about the fire, resources and evacuations at EmergencyWashoe.com. 
Residents can also find the latest evacuation updates at the website Perimeter Map. Information on the current state of the fire can be found at either WatchDuty.com or InciWeb.Wildfire.gov. 
The Nevada Department of Transportation has listed all highway updates and closures at NVRoads.com.
Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program recipients who lost food due to the wildfires have until Aug. 28 to report the loss and request replacement benefits through the Nevada Division of Social Services.
Nevada Sen. Jacky Rosen called on affected areas to contact her office if they need assistance accessing resources by phone at 775-337-0110, or by email at nnv.cs@rosen.senate.gov.
“When disasters like these strike, it is critical that we come together as a community to support each other,” Rosen said in a press release listing various resources. 
Local Resources

For any other general questions such as emergency housing or animal services, please visit EmergencyWashoe.com.


All school closures in Washoe County will be at washoeschools.net

Federal Agencies

Veterans in need of assistance can call 1-800-698-2411 or visit www.va.gov/resources/disaster-help/ for specialized support. 


Those in need of housing assistance during disasters can apply for FEMA assistance www.hud.gov/disaster-resources


The State Department offers free passport replacements following a major disaster, with all application fees waived up to 18 months after the disaster.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Lawrence+Memorial Hospital staff seek better conditions, higher pay
description: Picketing workers said declining staff levels are compromising patient care but higher compensation would aid recruiting and retention.
text:
Healthcare workers rallied outside Lawrence + Memorial Hospital in New London on Monday, demanding higher compensation to help alleviate issues with staff recruitment and retention that they say are compromising patient care.
“Let’s be clear: in a hospital, working conditions are patient care conditions,” said Stuart Savelkoul, chief of staff for AFT CT, a union of healthcare and education workers. “When skilled professionals are assigned more patients than anyone can safely care for, the entire community is at risk.”
Hospital employees and union leaders who spoke to a crowd of roughly 100 attendees described unsafe staffing conditions, inadequate wages and worker burnout — all of which directly impacts the quality of care at the hospital, they said.
Katelynne Pluss, an emergency room nurse and vice president of the hospital’s nurses union, said that in the last few years resignations have plagued several departments, including nurses, techs and cleaning staff. 
Management has been slow to replace those workers, so if someone is out sick or on vacation, staffing can get tight, Pluss said.
“They’ve been cutting back, cutting back. They’re not replacing the people who are leaving,” said Pluss, who works at the Pequot Health Center, a satellite location of Lawrence + Memorial.
Lawrence + Memorial, which is owned by Yale New Haven Health, is currently in contract negotiations with three separate unions that together represent over 2,100 of the hospital’s employees, including nurses, techs, paramedics and other healthcare workers, like patient care assistants and warehouse workers.
On Monday afternoon, Fiona Phelan, a spokesperson with Yale New Haven Health, said management was aware of the gathering and that the hospital “deeply values” the workforce, whose “skill and compassion are integral to our vision of providing access to high value, patient-centered care.”
“Our leadership team continues to negotiate in good faith, and we are confident that we will reach an agreement that is fair, responsible and competitive within the broader healthcare marketplace,” Phelan said.
Healthcare staffing shortages came to light during the pandemic, but continue to pose a challenge years later.
For example, Connecticut needs roughly 3,000 new registered nurses a year to make up for retirements — without factoring in nurses who leave the profession for other reasons, like burn out, according to a Governor’s Workforce Council Strategic Plan published in 2020. At the time, the state’s nursing programs were only producing 1,900 graduates a year. 
Demonstrators on Monday were joined by a handful of state legislators, as well as Attorney General William Tong. 
Sen. Martha Marx, D-New London, who has worked for 40 years as a nurse, blamed hospital management and lobbyists for the challenging conditions healthcare workers face.
“There is no reason why we should not have safe staffing,” Marx told the crowd. “Don’t let them win.”
Pluss and several other speakers also discussed downgrades to certain hospital supplies, like tape and IVs. Pluss said the supply changes seemed like an attempt to cut costs.
In recent years, legislators have taken steps to improve staffing conditions in hospitals with mixed success.
In 2023, Connecticut passed a measure banning mandated overtime for registered nurses. The law prohibits a hospital from forcing a nurse to work 48 hours in a work week or 12 hours in a 24 hour period. But that same year, a bill to create mandatory nurse staffing ratios in Connecticut hospitals failed.  
John Brady, vice president of AFT CT, said he would like to see the mandated overtime ban expanded to other healthcare professionals as a recruitment tool, but also a safety tool for both staff and patients.

name: South Dakota Searchlight
title: State of South Dakota faces lawsuit over proof-of-citizenship voter registration law
description: A nonprofit organization and a Sioux Falls voter filed a lawsuit Monday in federal court over the implementation of South Dakota’s new proof-of-citizenship requirement for voter registration. Senate Bill 175, passed by lawmakers and signed into law by Republican Gov. Larry Rhoden in March, requires documentary proof of citizenship from people registering to[...]
text:
A voter fills out a ballot at a Brandon polling place during the runoff election for the South Dakota Republican nomination for governor on July 28, 2026. (Photo by Makenzie Huber/South Dakota Searchlight)A nonprofit organization and a Sioux Falls voter filed a lawsuit Monday in federal court over the implementation of South Dakota’s new proof-of-citizenship requirement for voter registration.
Senate Bill 175, passed by lawmakers and signed into law by Republican Gov. Larry Rhoden in March, requires documentary proof of citizenship from people registering to vote.
That proof can take forms including a birth certificate, passport, driver’s license, non-driver’s identification card or tribal identification card, or “any other type of acceptable documentary evidence of citizenship” under federal law. Photocopies are acceptable for any of the documents except driver’s licenses or state or tribal ID cards. 
People who don’t provide those documents are registered but receive a “federal-only” ballot, meaning one that lists only candidates for federal offices such as the president and Congress, but not state or local offices.
New laws result in 1,500 federal-only voter registrations ahead of South Dakota primary election

In addition to proof of citizenship, the new law requires a person to provide a physical address in South Dakota, other than a mail-forwarding service or post office box, to be registered for voting in state and local elections. That provision — enforceable at the time of registration or upon a request for an absentee ballot — targets people such as full-time recreational vehicle drivers who may receive forwarded mail and register their vehicles in the state but otherwise don’t live there.
An analysis of voter data by South Dakota Searchlight in May showed that about 1,500 people in South Dakota had been registered as “federal only” since the law took effect with the governor’s signature in March.
The lawsuit alleges that South Dakota’s rollout of the proof-of-citizenship requirement has disqualified eligible voters over erroneous minutiae and failed to offer them a realistic shot at fixing problems with their registration application.
The lawsuit asks a judge to force the state to: 

Accept photocopies of driver’s licenses, tribal IDs and nondriver IDs for voter registration.
Rescind guidance requiring in-person registration for people who use such IDs as proof of citizenship. 
Make sure registrants designated as federal-only are offered accurate explanations as to why they’ve been denied access to state and local ballots. 
Offer voters registered as federal-only an opportunity to challenge the designation. 

The lawsuit also seeks a ruling that the non-acceptance of photocopies for state and tribal IDs violates the U.S. Civil Rights Act, and asks the state to pay the plaintiffs’ attorney fees.
Group’s proposed rule changes previously rejected
The League of Women Voters is a nonpartisan, nonprofit group that holds registration drives, provides voter education and lobbies on voting rights issues.
Members of its South Dakota chapter argued before the state’s Board of Elections for rule changes earlier this summer that would have addressed the issues raised in their lawsuit. The board voted the changes down 5-2, ruling that the League lacked the legal standing to propose them.
Group wants help for voters affected by proof-of-citizenship law and federal-only designation

The League’s lawsuit, which also includes a Sioux Falls man named Jaysen Hill as a plaintiff, names South Dakota Secretary of State Monae Johnson, the state Board of Elections and each board member as defendants.
The lawsuit says the League’s representatives have tried to work with Johnson’s office to fix what they see as issues with the law’s administration, but that her office has been unwilling to do so.
The complaint says Minnehaha County registered Hill as federal-only after he applied to register by mail, sending a photocopy of his state identification card in May. 
The card showed his address, the lawsuit says, but the letter he received telling him he’d be registered federal-only said he’d failed to provide a physical address. Hill was “confused” about the letter, which the lawsuit says is a form letter sent to those registered as federal-only.
Hill “now believes he was registered as a federal-only voter because he submitted a photocopy of a state identification card,” the lawsuit says, running afoul of the requirement to present the actual ID card.
“It was never made clear to Plaintiff Hill by any state or local officials that he was registered as a federal-only voter because he failed to provide documentary proof of citizenship, nor is it clear to Plaintiff Hill how he should go about fixing his application.”
Hill “was unable to participate” in the June 2 primary election, the lawsuit says. 
State says it’s yet to see lawsuit
Hill and the League are represented by lawyers from the American Civil Liberties Union of South Dakota and the ACLU Foundation, a lawyer from the Sioux Falls law firm Heidepriem Purtell Siegel Hinrichs, and attorneys for the Campaign Legal Center, a nonpartisan legal aid organization in Washington, D.C., founded more than two decades ago by a former member of the Federal Election Commission. 
Kathryn Johnson, president of the League of Women Voters’ South Dakota chapter, said in a press release that the state’s approach to the proof-of-citizenship issue “has not only effectively shut down our League’s ability to register new voters, but it has pointlessly caused voter confusion and made voting harder.”
Andrew Malone, a lawyer with the ACLU of South Dakota, said in the release that the case is about making sure the state’s new law is administered “in compliance with federal mandates.”
“There is no proof of widespread voter fraud or evidence of non-citizens voting that justifies a law that imposes burdensome show-your-papers requirements for eligible voters to cast their ballots,” Malone said.
Tony Mangan, spokesman for South Dakota Attorney General Marty Jackley, told South Dakota Searchlight on Monday evening that the office had yet to be served with the lawsuit.
Secretary of State Monae Johnson and a spokesman for her office did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
LofWV complaint
 The complaint in a lawsuit filed against South Dakota state officials in August 2026.

name: WyoFile
title: Director Angi Bruce’s departure from Wyoming Game and Fish was likely involuntary, records suggest
description:
Details are still murky about what transpired before the department’s leader left her job after less than two years, but there are indications the job change wasn’t optional. 
The post Director Angi Bruce’s departure from Wyoming Game and Fish was likely involuntary, records suggest appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
A week before Gov. Mark Gordon announced Angi Bruce would trade in leading the Wyoming Game and Fish Department for a newly created policy job in his office, she was out checking Bighorn Basin anglers’ fishing licenses with game warden Jordan Winter. 
One goal of the ridealong was to “remain in touch with the department employees,” Bruce told the warden, according to a story in the Powell Tribune. Eight days after her rapport-building mission, Gordon released a short statement saying Bruce had resigned from Game and Fish’s top job “effective immediately” for a newly created position titled “director of special policy initiatives.”
That could be a temporary gig. Policy staffers working under Wyoming governors customarily cycle out with a change in administrations. Gordon’s term ends in less than five months, in January 2027.
Wyoming Gov. Mark Gordon and Wyoming Game and Fish Department Director Angi Bruce listen to remarks from Trapper’s Point at a June 26, 2026 celebration commemorating the designation of the Sublette Pronghorn Herd’s 150-mile-long migration corridor. (Mike Koshmrl/WyoFile)
Although it’s been suggested that Bruce quit on her own volition, information that WyoFile acquired through the Wyoming Public Records Act points toward an involuntary departure so sudden that it even caught Bruce off guard. 
Bruce’s calendar for the week of Aug. 10-14 — the week after her “effective immediately” job change — shows she had booked multiple meetings associated with her director role and even had Game and Fish obligations that following Monday. 
Bruce’s new position also came with a significant pay cut. As Wyoming Game and Fish Department director, Bruce’s salary in 2025 was $190,080, according to the government-transparency-focused nonprofit OpenTheBooks.com. With the governor’s office, she’ll be paid a monthly rate of $12,035 according to information provided by Betsy Anderson, Gordon’s general counsel and deputy chief of staff, in response to the records request. That pencils out to an annual paycheck of $144,420 — a $45,660 pay cut, roughly 24% less than what Bruce was making in 2025.
Bruce did not respond to interview requests on the day that her departure was announced and again on Monday. 
Emails acquired by WyoFile show that Gordon’s staff, the Game and Fish workforce and the public were all informed of Bruce’s departure within the span of 29 minutes on the afternoon of Friday, Aug. 7.























At 3:37 p.m., Sara DiRienzo informed her fellow governor’s office staffers that Bruce was coming aboard. Then 16 minutes later at 3:53 p.m., Game and Fish Deputy Director Eric Wiltanger informed his own staff of the transition. Some 13 minutes later, the general public was informed in a press release from the governor. 
None of roughly a half dozen Game and Fish employees whom WyoFile has spoken with were made aware of Bruce’s departure before that afternoon. 
Wiltanger was named interim director of the high-profile agency, which is charged with managing wildlife in a state where hunting and angling drive a significant segment of the economy and are interwoven into many residents’ everyday lives. 

Eric Wiltanger was named interim director of the Wyoming Game and Fish Department following the Aug. 7 resignation of the agency’s director, Angi Bruce. (Wyoming Game and Fish Department)

In a Monday press conference about Game and Fish leadership changes and priorities, Wiltanger told reporters that he would not be addressing the “transition that occurred a few weeks ago.” 
“I would say that in Angi’s time here at Game and Fish, she played a significant role in the great things [the agency did] for Wyoming’s wildlife,” Wiltanger said. 
Gordon’s press release also thanked Bruce for her time as director. In the new job, she will work on federal natural resources issues, including grizzly bears, sage grouse, shared stewardship agreements and the management of elk feedgrounds, according to the governor’s office.  
When she was tapped as director in 2024, Bruce became one of the few biologists and the first woman to ever rise to the top role at the agency. Her two-year tenure, however, was marked by several high-profile controversies.
At times, the tension broke out into the public. In February, retired longtime Game and Fish staffer Chris Madson wrote an opinion piece in WyoFile arguing that Bruce had made “several statements that should concern anyone with an interest in the state’s wildlife heritage.”
“First — and most alarming — was her contention that Game and Fish should not ‘advocate or speak for wildlife,’” Madson wrote. 
During Bruce’s tenure, Game and Fish commissioners took the rare step of twice reversing politically influenced proposals from the department. It happened with mountain lion hunting in the summer of 2025, and again when state wildlife managers sought to remove proposed protections for two segments of the Sublette Pronghorn Migration Corridor, which were overturned. (The migration was designated in June, and at Gordon’s direction it did not include the two contested segments recommended for protection by the commission.)
A dustup over Game and Fish’s handling of the Wyoming State Shooting Complex’s location in crucial mule deer habitat marked another controversy that preceded Bruce’s departure. Under her leadership, Game and Fish declined to conduct a formal environmental review of the site. In July, former Cody Region senior wildlife biologist Tony Mong told the Powell Tribune that the shooting complex was the final straw in his decision to resign from his job. 
Seventeen days after the Tribune’s story published, the announcement came that Bruce was changing jobs. 
During Monday’s press conference, Deputy Director Jeff Davis told reporters that Game and Fish is continuing its efforts to connect leadership with biologists, wardens and other staffers around the state. 
“The executive leadership team is really leaning in to spending more time outside of Cheyenne and in region offices and doing ride-alongs with folks,” he said. 
Chief Warden Dan Smith, who’s temporarily working as an interim deputy director, emphasized that the agency’s leadership is going to strive for an “open door policy.” Game and Fish staff “aren’t afraid to share their opinion,” he said. 
“We try to give the space to allow them to do that,” Smith said. “When we trip over something and don’t get it just right, people share with us — and we try to learn from that.” 
Wyoming Game and Fish Department Director Angi Bruce and Chief Warden Dan Smith attend a January 2025 meeting of the Wyoming Legislature’s House Travel, Recreation, Wildlife and Cultural Resources Committee. (Andrew Graham/WyoFile)
Wiltanger, Game and Fish’s temporary top employee, told reporters that the buck stops with him.  
“When we misstep or if we step in a hole, those [incidents] need to come to me and I’ve got to hear about them, because it’s my responsibility to address those appropriately,” Wiltanger said. “Whenever things don’t go right, I need to know.” 
Game and Fish’s next permanent director will be selected by Wyoming’s next governor. State Sen. Eric Barlow, who won the Republican nomination in last week’s primary election, will face Democrat Kenneth Casner and Rebecca Bextel. The Constitution Party candidate is the Teton County conservative activist at the center of the Checkgate controversy that dominated the 2026 legislative session. 
The state’s next chief executive will be able to choose from three candidates selected by the Wyoming Game and Fish Commission. That selection should be made by March, Wiltanger said.
The post Director Angi Bruce’s departure from Wyoming Game and Fish was likely involuntary, records suggest appeared first on WyoFile .

name: Daily Montanan
title: CBP agent ‘told me that he wanted me to run so that he could use his gun on me,’ imprisoned man says
description: Irving Alonso Acosta wants to become a barber to support his family, but he was arrested in Sidney, kicked while in custody, and threatened with staying in jail if he talked to an attorney, according to a court filing. Acosta, held at the Cascade County Detention Center, is a possible class member in a lawsuit […]
text:
Photo illustration by Getty Images.Irving Alonso Acosta wants to become a barber to support his family, but he was arrested in Sidney, kicked while in custody, and threatened with staying in jail if he talked to an attorney, according to a court filing.
Acosta, held at the Cascade County Detention Center, is a possible class member in a lawsuit filed against Cascade County, the U.S. Department of Homeland Security and other federal officials by Upper Seven Law.
In signed declarations, a couple of other potential class members said they passed out while in custody, including one who was held in the back of a hot truck.
One said he was threatened by a Customs and Border Patrol agent.
“A CBP agent put me in his car and told me that he wanted me to run so that he could use his gun on me,” said Jonny Hernandez Antunez in court records. “ … I was terrified.”
The lawsuit alleges U.S. Customs and Border Patrol and Immigration and Customs Enforcement officials are arresting people without warrants and detaining them without evidence they are a flight risk or danger to their communities, contrary to the U.S. Constitution or laws of the country.
The U.S. Attorney’s Office acknowledges government agents made arrests without warrants, but it argues the government issued warrants after the arrests, and in one court filing, it argues the plaintiffs are in the United States without legal permission.
The press team for the U.S. Department of Homeland Security did not respond Monday to an email with questions about the circumstances outlined in the declarations which were filed in federal court.
A federal judge earlier ordered the release of Jesus Verde Hernandez from the Cascade County Detention Center, and last week he ordered the release of Adrián Espinoza De La Cruz and his 9-year-old child from a facility in Havre.
In both cases, U.S. District Court of Montana Judge Brian Morris found federal authorities violated the constitutional rights of the petitioners, including by not having warrants ahead of time.
The judge said he found the “lack of regard” for the parent and child “particularly disturbing.”
Cascade County Sheriff Jesse Slaughter earlier said the county detention center is simply the contract facility for the detainees.
Monday, Upper Seven senior staff attorney Andres Haladay said the firm has identified at least 41 members of the potential class, and at least 38 remain in custody. A hearing on the petition to release the others is scheduled to take place this week.
In the meantime, Upper Seven filed declarations of three people who are possible class members in the case. Here are two summaries of the experiences described in the declarations.
From the declaration of Acosta:

        Acosta, 26, lives in Phoenix, Arizona, with his wife and child, who are U.S. citizens. He hasn’t been convicted of any crimes. The family was headed home after a vacation in North Dakota and stopped at a gas station in Sidney. They were looking for the clinic because his wife, who is diabetic, didn’t feel well. Acosta went into the gas station to buy food for his son, and a local sheriff’s officer showed up and said CBP would arrive. But CBP didn’t, and the sheriff’s officer handcuffed him and took him to jail. Acosta passed out in a cell and believes he hit his head after experiencing a panic attack. He was taken to a medical center, a CBP agent was there, and his wife tried to explain they were getting papers completed because they are married. The CBP agent arrested him without a warrant, the affidavit says. Later at a CBP station in a different town, another CBP agent kicked him to get his attention, and he still has pain in his back. The CBP agent said if Acosta talked to anyone, including an attorney, he would have to stay in jail. The CBP agent also said Acosta needed to sign documents to either voluntarily depart or stay and see a judge. The agent told Acosta, “If you don’t sign, I’m going to sign it for you.” Acosta said he didn’t know if the agent actually signed, and if he did, which option he chose for Acosta. He said he was never presented with a warrant or given the chance to call a lawyer. Eventually, he was taken to the Cascade County Detention Center, where he faced threats from other inmates and feared for his life and the life of an 18-year-old who was also detained and smaller than others being held. “There are a lot of people in Cascade who pick on the weak and pound on their cell windows.”    
 
From the declaration of Antunez:

        Antunez is 26 and has lived in the United States for seven years. He lives in Butte with his fiance and six-month-old son. His fiance has postpartum depression, and he cares for her and their son. He and his brother were passengers in a car with his friend, and CBP pulled them over, and three other trucks surrounded them. The CBP agent who came to the car didn’t tell them why they were pulled over. Thirteen or 14 agents were on the scene and put waist shackles and handcuffs on them. Antunez asked to take his gastritis medication with him but agents refused. A CBP agent told him he wanted him to run so that he could use his gun on Antunez, and the agent said the same thing to the others. “My wife knows people who have been killed by CBP. I was terrified,” Antunez said. He said agents never showed him a warrant or asked questions about his ties to the community. He was asked to sign a document he couldn’t read and was later told it was a voluntary departure form. Antunez and the others were held at a weigh station for three or four hours without being allowed to go to the bathroom. They were put in the back of a truck that was like a box and “very hot.” “I began hitting the wall of the box, asking for more air. At some point, my heart began to beat really fast. I felt the guy sitting next to me pour water on my head. … I believe that I passed out from the heat.” Later at a CBP station, he again was denied his medication. Agents asked him to sign more documents, but they only showed him the signature portion of the documents. After agents talked to him, they gave him a card with his rights written in Spanish. “There was only one rights card for all of us being held there.” He was transported to the Cascade County Detention Center, where he shares a cell with a couple of people who have criminal charges. He asked a third time for his medication but did not receive it.    
 
The press team for the Department of Homeland Security did not respond Monday to the experiences described in the declarations, but in an earlier email from DHS, a spokesperson for Customs and Border Patrol said Espinoza De La Cruz admitted to illegal immigration and “accepted voluntary return for himself and his minor child.”
The email said Espinoza De La Cruz was “placed into supervised release” with ICE, Immigration and Customs Enforcement.
“We encourage all illegal aliens to take control of their departure by utilizing the CBP Home app to receive a free flight home and $2,600,” the CBP spokesperson said in the email.
In January 2026, the Department of Homeland Security announced President Donald Trump was starting his second year of “making America safe again and continuing mass deportations.” A news release said “illegal aliens” who signed up to self deport through the CBP Home application would receive the flight and $2,600 “exit bonus.”
“More than 2 million illegal aliens have made the decision to self-deport,” the news release said.
The press team did not respond to a follow-up question Friday about how many people in Montana have received $2,600 checks.

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: NC State offers an out of-this-world homecoming for astronaut alum Christina Koch
description: It has been four-and-a-half months since the Artemis II splashed down in the Pacific Ocean on April 10, but the enthusiasm and pride for what the four-member crew accomplished has not diminished one iota at one astronaut’s alma mater. On Monday, students, faculty, and top elected officials gathered on North Carolina State University’s campus to […]
text:
Students walk past a freshly painted mural  honoring NASA astronaut and alum Christina Koch at NC State University's free-expression tunnel on August 24, 2026. (Photo: Clayton Henkel/NC Newsline)It has been four-and-a-half months since the Artemis II splashed down in the Pacific Ocean on April 10, but the enthusiasm and pride for what the four-member crew accomplished has not diminished one iota at one astronaut’s alma mater.
On Monday, students, faculty, and top elected officials gathered on North Carolina State University’s campus to welcome home NASA astronaut and NC State graduate Christina Hammock Koch. Koch became the first woman to travel beyond low Earth orbit, and with her crew broke the record for the farthest distance humans have ever traveled in space.
Governor Josh Stein told those who were there to celebrate Koch’s achievements that North Carolina has a long and remarkable connection to space exploration, starting with the Wright brothers first sustained flight in Kitty Hawk.
“It is also a reminder that extraordinary achievements do not happen overnight. They require ambitious vision,” said Stein. “They require sustained investment and they require special talent, which is why commitment to cultivating the next generation of engineers, scientists, explorers and dreamers is so important.”
NC State Chancellor Kevin Howell applauds after announcing a building on Centennial Campus would be named in Koch’s honor. (Photo: NC State livestream)
Koch graduated from the North Carolina School of Science and Mathematics in Durham in 1997 and went on to North Carolina State University to earn Bachelor of Science degrees in electrical engineering and physics, followed by a Master of Science degree in electrical engineering.
Stein told the audience that anything is possible with a public school education.
“The ideas and the people that spring from North Carolina public schools and public universities have taken humankind farther than they have ever gone before,” Stein said. “If North Carolina’s history is any indication, they will take us even farther still.”
Chancellor Kevin Howell said it was only appropriate to rename the Engineering Building II on Centennial Campus as Koch Hall in her honor.
“This three-time NC State graduate has broken barriers, set astounding records, and with her Artemis crewmates, traveled farther from Earth than any other humans in history. That, ladies and gentlemen, is how NC State defines a trailblazer,” said Howell.
Koch was also honored with a special campus mural at the free-expression tunnel and a limited-edition ice cream made by the university’s Howling Cow dairy.
Koch reminded the students that long before she was a NASA astronaut, she was just a quiet college student with ripped jeans, pink hair, and “an inexplicable love of rockets.”
She said her accomplishments would not have been possible if not for those who came before her.
Such as Mary Yarborough, who fought to be admitted, and in 1927 earned her Master of Chemistry, becoming the first woman to attain a graduate degree from NC State.
Or Augustus Witherspoon, who was the first African American professor at NC State.
Katharine Stinson was the first woman to graduate from NC State’s School of Engineering.
It’s not rocket science: UNC System leaders make the case for increased funding

“What I will ask of you is this — never underestimate any student here,” Koch told the faculty. “Validate their dreams and hold them accountable to see their unfinished stories through. Guide them through the good chapters and the bad.”
Koch said her 328 days in orbit and nearly 700,000 miles around the moon did not begin at a launch pad. They began on Stinson Drive at NC State University.
“It’s not the record for miles you travel away that really matters. It’s the impact you make right here at home.”

title: Washington’s newest Fish and Wildlife commissioner dies
description: Victor Garcia, an educator, hunter and fisherman appointed to the Washington Fish and Wildlife Commission last year, has died.   The Department of Fish and Wildlife announced his death Monday. No cause was provided. “Commissioner Garcia loved this state, and cared deeply for fish and wildlife,” said Commission Chair Jim Anderson. “He was ready to do […]
text:
Victor Garcia, a hunter, fisherman and retired teacher who was appointed to the Washington Fish and Wildlife Commission in April 2025, has died . (Photo courtesy of Department of Fish and Wildlife)Victor Garcia, an educator, hunter and fisherman appointed to the Washington Fish and Wildlife Commission last year, has died.  
The Department of Fish and Wildlife announced his death Monday. No cause was provided.
“Commissioner Garcia loved this state, and cared deeply for fish and wildlife,” said Commission Chair Jim Anderson. “He was ready to do the hard work, and he will be missed.”
Kelly Susewind, director of the Department of Fish and Wildlife, said in a statement that Garcia “leaves a lasting legacy from his work on the commission to care for the fish, wildlife, and wild spaces that he was so passionate about.”
Garcia, of Skagit County, was named to the commission in April 2025 amid ongoing tensions pitting conservationists and environmentalists against hunting and fishing groups over membership of the nine-member citizen panel.
Gov. Bob Ferguson appointed Garcia at the same time that he reappointed Anderson and Commissioner Molly Linville. He acted months after rejecting two nominees of his predecessor, Jay Inslee, who some environmental groups had embraced.
Hunters and fishers endorsed Anderson and Linville and appreciated the selection of Garcia.
“Incredibly sad news. Commissioner Garcia was a steady presence in the Washington Fish and Wildlife Commission,” the Sportsmen’s Alliance, a national voice for the hunting community, said in a statement.
Garcia, a native of Grays Harbor County, taught math, biology and other science courses in Washington schools before retiring. He earned a bachelor’s degree in marine zoology from the University of Washington and a master’s in science education from Vanderbilt University in Tennessee.
In an interview with the Standard last year, he described himself as having a wide variety of interests in the outdoors and suggested it would give him a unique perspective as a commissioner. 
“I’m a hunter, but I’m also in Audubon,” he said at the time. “I’ve gone all over the world to view specific birds. But, every now and then, I do hunt some of them.”
Before becoming an educator, Garcia was a commercial fisherman in the Bering Sea region and worked as a biologist for the National Marine Fisheries Service.
Garcia’s term runs through December 2030. He held one of the panel’s western Washington seats. It will be up to Ferguson to name a replacement.

title: Political complaints pointing to new AI law dropped
description: Three Commissioner of Political Practices complaints filed against Accountability in State Government, a conservative political action committee, over mailers that used generative artificial intelligence will be dismissed, according to court records from an accompanying lawsuit in federal district court. Rep. Eric Albus, a Hi-Line Republican, former legislat[...]
text:
A server room in a data center. (Photo by Getty Images)Three Commissioner of Political Practices complaints filed against Accountability in State Government, a conservative political action committee, over mailers that used generative artificial intelligence will be dismissed, according to court records from an accompanying lawsuit in federal district court.
Rep. Eric Albus, a Hi-Line Republican, former legislator Jennifer Carlson, running for a state House seat in the Bozeman area, and Rep. Llew Jones, running for state senate, filed the complaints earlier this year. 
The PAC, which lists Dan Bartel, a former Republican legislator, as its treasurer, ran mailers depicting those candidates with Pride flags and buttons. It accused Albus and Carlson of using taxpayer money for a “woke agenda.”
The COPP complaint is not yet published on the office’s website, but Commissioner of Political Practices Chris Gallus, in court documents, said the mailers were protected under satire laws. Montana does not require satire be marked on political mailers.
“I do find dismissal at this stage appropriate because further factual development is not necessary to determine that the election materials provided fall under the exemption for satire or parody,” Gallus wrote in court documents, adding those complaints were filed under the new deepfake law, Senate Bill 25. Photos, videos and soundbites can all be faked using AI-assisted technology, and the law sought to prohibit that being done to represent candidates during the 60 days leading up to an election.
Following the COPP complaints, Bartel filed a lawsuit in federal court over SB 25, which established the deepfake law, alleging it violates free speech protections in the U.S. Constitution.
“So far, three legislators have filed campaign complaints under a new Montana statute that patently violates the First Amendment and includes penalties of civil fines and potential prosecution with up to two years in state prison,” the lawsuit says.
The complaint says the law serves to “chill, suppress, and punish protected political speech,” and that his rights have been violated because of the law.
That bill added definitions surrounding deepfakes to state law and disallows deepfakes of candidates within 60 days of an election. Sen. Janet Ellis, a Helena Democrat, ran the bill, and Gov. Greg Gianforte, a Republican, signed it. The bill was not particularly controversial, passing by wide margins in both legislative bodies.
Ellis on Monday said the law is about fairness for voters. 
“AI is becoming more and more realistic, and it’s harder and harder for people to determine what is real and what is not,” she said.
There was a workaround built into the bill — campaigns and organizations that support their candidates can use AI generated content, but have to disclose it.
Even so, the suit takes issue with that part of the law as well.
“This compelled-speech remedy is itself constitutionally infirm, as it forces political speakers to brand their own constitutionally protected communications as false and deceptive as the price of speaking at all,” the suit reads.
The impact of AI-generated content before voters has become a growing concern in the state and around the country. Montana lawmakers worried that voters may not be able to distinguish between actual images and those created by AI.
Initial arguments challenging SB 25 were heard in Helena Federal District Court before Judge Susan Watters on Aug. 21. Hamilton Lincoln Law Institute attorney Adam Schulman, who along with Montana attorney Matthew Monforton are representing Bartel in the case, said they felt confident following those proceedings.
A decision hasn’t been made yet, Schulman said, but said the judge indicated she’ll have a ruling in September.
“At the hearing, the judge asked incisive questions and was clearly engaged with the case,” Schulman said in an email. “We’re optimistic about seeing a good result.”

name: Wisconsin Examiner
title: Wisconsin joins lawsuit against Trump threatening safety grants over immigration compliance
description: The Wisconsin Department of Justice (DOJ) has joined 19 other states, including the commonwealths of Massachusetts and Virginia, in a lawsuit pushing back against the Trump administration’s attempts to attach immigration enforcement requirements to federal grants supporting state and local public safety efforts. “Threatening to cut funding that supports law[...]
text:
Protesters march in Milwaukee following a surge in ICE arrests in early July 2026. (Photo by Isiah Holmes/Wisconsin Examiner)The Wisconsin Department of Justice (DOJ) has joined 19 other states, including the commonwealths of Massachusetts and Virginia, in a lawsuit pushing back against the Trump administration’s attempts to attach immigration enforcement requirements to federal grants supporting state and local public safety efforts.
“Threatening to cut funding that supports law enforcement if states don’t agree to unlawful conditions is an abuse of the Trump administration’s authority,” Attorney General Josh Kaul said in a statement. “This funding should be distributed to the states, not improperly used as a bargaining chip.”
The lawsuit states that the grant programs, which have been active for decades, “provide more than a billion dollars to States annually to address some of the most serious threats to the safety of their residents: from gang violence to drug trafficking to sexual assault to all kinds of violent crimes.” The funds, which are enacted by Congress, are used “to assist more than 8.5 million crime victims; pay more than 200,000 claims for losses suffered by crime victims; and fund ongoing criminal justice and public safety operations, such as drug task forces, crisis intervention programs, and youth recidivism reduction efforts, in all 50 states and over 1,000 local government units nationwide,” the lawsuit states.
Under President Donald Trump, states which depend on these funds have been advised to either cooperate with Trump’s immigration priorities or face losing access to those funds. Calling this a “brazen attempt to manipulate critical funding for law enforcement and crime victims to strong-arm States into supporting the Administration’s civil immigration policies,” the lawsuit asserts that the Trump administration is running afoul with governing principles of the United States: that a federal agency “has no power to act … unless and until Congress confers power upon it.” Since Congress has the power of the purse, it decides what criteria executive branch agencies — like the Justice Department — must use when awarding grants, the suit argues. 
The lawsuit also accuses the Trump administration of not considering how denying these grants would undermine public safety across the country. “Action by this Court is urgently needed,” the lawsuit states, asserting  that it is illegal for the administration to impose these conditions on the public safety grants. 
In a press release, the Wisconsin DOJ said Monday that last year the Trump administration declared that states wouldn’t be able to access Victims Crime Act funds unless they cooperated with the administration’s hardline deportation agenda, affecting $1.3 billion in grants.. A coalition of states sued and the administration reversed its action and released the money. 
This year, however, the immigration conditions have been applied funding for  juvenile justice and law enforcement, and amount to over $6 million in Wisconsin alone —  a loss of $3.2 million in grant assistance, $2.1 million for  a crisis intervention program, and  $800,000 for  juvenile justice and delinquency prevention, according to DOJ. 
Although 20 sheriff offices across Wisconsin partner with Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) through the 287(g) program, many communities have mixed relationships with the controversial federal agency. Some police departments may still cooperate with immigration enforcement even without an official 287(g) program. Others have policies prohibiting officers and jails from participating in immigration enforcement. 
Despite public pushback, immigration agents have conducted surges and arrests in neighborhoods, courthouses, and elsewhere since Trump returned to office. In Milwaukee County, where some of these enforcement efforts have played out, local elected officials have enacted  local ordinances and policies to curb the effect ICE operations have on public safety in the city. These, however, have invited further confrontation with the Trump administration.

name: Utah News Dispatch
title: New nuclear research and training hub may come to Brigham City
description: A new nuclear research and training campus may be coming to Brigham City as the state advances its effort to build out an “energy ecosystem” in northern Utah.  Hi Tech Solutions, a nuclear power and energy services company that’s sponsoring a nuclear campus in Brigham City, signed a memorandum of understanding with the municipality and […]
text:
Brigham City is pictured on Thursday, May 28, 2026. (Photo by Spenser Heaps for Utah News Dispatch)A new nuclear research and training campus may be coming to Brigham City as the state advances its effort to build out an “energy ecosystem” in northern Utah. 
Hi Tech Solutions, a nuclear power and energy services company that’s sponsoring a nuclear campus in Brigham City, signed a memorandum of understanding with the municipality and Utah State University to evaluate and plan a proposal for a “Center for Energy Research and Technology Campus,” or CERT, the company announced Monday. 
The proposed center would be located adjacent to the Utah State University Brigham City campus, according to a news release, and it is anticipated to offer “technical training, certification, and research and development center focused on nuclear energy, advanced energy systems, defense-related technologies, and associated supply chains.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“This partnership brings industry, education and local leaders together to give Utahns the hands-on training and skills they need for good-paying careers in a growing field,” Utah House Speaker Mike Schultz, R-Hooper, said in a statement. “It’s exactly the kind of collaboration that turns opportunity into a stronger workforce and a stronger economy, and we’re excited to see what this can mean for Northern Utah and the entire state.”
Nuclear ‘energy ecosystem’ and, eventually, Utah’s first reactor will live in Brigham City

The first phase of the development, which is planned to start construction by 2028, is expected to include an about 20,000-square-foot facility, pending funding and permit approvals, according to the release. 
By 2029, the facility is planning to employ approximately 20 full-time employees. But that number is expected to grow as the campus expands, the release says.
Initial construction may have a $100 million price tag. And the university “is participating through a favorable land arrangement, with additional financial commitments and partnerships to be explored as planning advances,” the release says.  
The project comes as Utah Republican leaders have been betting on nuclear development in the state, in line with the Trump administration’s ambitions to propel the technology. The state has signed agreements to support other nuclear operations and research and has even made the shortlist to host a “nuclear lifecycle innovation campus” after campaigning hard for one in response to a call for proposals from the Department of Energy. 
The state’s nuclear-positive position, specifically a taxpayer-funded ad campaign promoting nuclear energy development, has faced opposition from health advocates and downwinders.
“Meeting America’s growing energy demands and competing on the world stage will require bold investments in innovation, infrastructure and a highly skilled workforce,” Utah Senate President Stuart Adams, R-Layton, said in the release. “By bringing together higher education, industry and local communities, Utah can strengthen our national security, advance American energy independence and create high-paying opportunities for Utahns for generations to come.”



Let us know what you think...


 


The university’s role in the partnership would include participating in research, testing, training and academic programming, while Hi Tech Solutions and other affiliates would operate “commercial-facing portions” of the planned multiple facilities making up the campus.
And Brigham City is committing to supporting site planning, infrastructure coordination, local permitting and regional economic development projects.
“The CERT Campus would expand hands-on training, certification, and applied research in nuclear operations, maintenance, safety, engineering, and advanced manufacturing,” Chris Hayter, co-founder and Chief Operations Officer of Hi Tech Solutions said in the release. “We are proud to bring together industry, higher education, and local government to strengthen Utah’s energy capabilities, increase economic growth, and help power America’s nuclear renaissance.”
Ultimately, the hope for the new campus is to create educational, and credentialing opportunities in nuclear operations engineering support, safety, maintenance, advanced manufacturing, fuel handling, commercial nuclear services, among others, for students, skilled technicians and transitioning military service members.  
“This partnership reflects Utah State’s land-grant mission and our responsibility to help meet the evolving needs of our state,” Brad Mortensen, Utah State University president said in a statement. “Working alongside Brigham City and Hi Tech Solutions, we have an opportunity to explore new approaches to technical training and research that prepare students for high-demand careers, support economic growth, and strengthen Utah’s leadership in energy and national defense.”

name: South Dakota Searchlight
title: Federal government funds conservation in South Dakota while cutting the people who do the work
description: The federal government has found a strange way to practice conservation: put billions of dollars on the table, then cut many of the people needed to turn that money into work on the ground. That is the disconnect South Dakota’s congressional delegation should be concerned about, because right now the two policies are moving in […]
text:
The U.S. Department of Agriculture's Jamie L. Whitten Federal Building in Washington, D.C., pictured on Dec. 18, 2017. (USDA photo by Preston Keres)The federal government has found a strange way to practice conservation: put billions of dollars on the table, then cut many of the people needed to turn that money into work on the ground.
That is the disconnect South Dakota’s congressional delegation should be concerned about, because right now the two policies are moving in opposite directions.
The latest example is the America the Beautiful Act. Sen. Mike Rounds cosponsors the Senate bill, and Rep. Dusty Johnson cosponsors the House effort. It would renew the Legacy Restoration Fund and provide nearly $2 billion a year to repair deteriorating infrastructure in national parks, wildlife refuges and on other federal lands.
There is good reason to support it. South Dakota has Badlands and Wind Cave national parks, Mount Rushmore National Memorial, Jewel Cave National Monument, Minuteman Missile National Historic Site, five national wildlife refuges and hundreds of waterfowl production areas.
If the federal government owns these places, it ought to maintain them. But Congress cannot keep applauding the money while ignoring the missing people.
The urgent need for Congress to renew critical funding for South Dakota’s national parks 

The National Park Service lost about 24% of its permanent workforce last year. The Trump administration’s fiscal 2027 proposal would take staffing from about 16,000 full-time-equivalent positions to roughly 13,100 — about 20% lower. Fish and Wildlife Service staffing would fall about 25%.
So, Congress may spend billions repairing yesterday’s backlog while shrinking the workforce needed to prevent tomorrow’s.
A big appropriation can rebuild a park road. It cannot inspect the culvert next spring. Congress has not yet figured out how to issue a press release that clears a clogged drainageway.
The disconnect is even larger on farms and ranches.
Congress has pushed conservation spending to historic highs. The Inflation Reduction Act added $19.5 billion over five years for programs administered largely by the Natural Resources Conservation Service. The One Big Beautiful Bill Act signed by Trump last year repealed the remaining IRA conservation funding but shifted much of that investment into the regular farm bill baseline, boosting major conservation programs through 2031.
A Democratic administration sharply increased conservation funding. A Republican Congress and Trump kept much of it going while cutting the workforce needed to deliver it.
Between January 2025 and January 2026, NRCS lost about 23% of its workforce. USDA’s own budget documents brought the issue home. They projected NRCS technical-assistance staffing in South Dakota falling from 113 full-time-equivalent positions to 40.
Those were projections, not evidence that 73 positions disappeared. But a nearly two-thirds reduction needs explaining. At some point, calling that efficiency starts to resemble admiring the emperor’s new suit.
The South Dakota Farmers Union warned U.S. Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins that NRCS staffing losses were increasing workloads and reducing the agency’s ability to process applications.
NRCS work does not happen by mailing a check. Someone has to walk the land, examine soils, design the grazing or water system, complete engineering, prepare contracts and inspect finished work.
Cut enough people, and historic conservation funding can produce a historic waiting list.
That is where Senate Majority Leader John Thune, Rounds and Johnson could speak up.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Johnson said early in 2025 that USDA cuts and layoffs would not affect farmers. Given what has happened since, he should say whether he still believes that. Rounds supports nearly $2 billion a year for public-land repairs. Good. Then he should explain how cutting Park Service and Fish and Wildlife staffing protects that investment.
And Thune is not a spectator. As Senate majority leader, he helped Congress maintain historically high agricultural conservation funding. Now he should insist that enough people remain to put it to work.
The administration says fewer employees, more contractors and greater efficiency can make this work. Fine. South Dakota’s delegation should ask for the proof: How many NRCS field employees remain in the state? Are producers waiting longer? How many Park Service and Fish and Wildlife positions have been lost here?
Those answers would tell us whether Washington is becoming more efficient or simply creating the next backlog.
These are not partisan questions. They are basic management questions anyone running a farm, ranch or business would ask before putting more money into an operation after sharply reducing its workforce.
What Washington has created is not a temporary mismatch. It is a structural contradiction.
Congress can appropriate billions. But somewhere between the press release and the finished project, somebody still has to show up and do the work.

name: Idaho Capital Sun
title: Idaho Tax Commission won’t release private school tax-credit data despite public records requests
description: This story was originally posted on IdahoEdNews.org on Aug. 24, 2026. This month, taxpayers in Texas found out how many students receiving $1 billion in private education subsidies were already homeschooled or enrolled in a private school: 70%.  Taxpayers in Idaho are still waiting to get that number from a similar private school choice program […]
text:
House Bill 93 didn’t require the Idaho State Tax Commission to compile income data beyond the number of recipients who qualified for priority access by earning 300% or below the federal poverty level. (Photo illustration by Getty Images)This story was originally posted on IdahoEdNews.org on Aug. 24, 2026.
This month, taxpayers in Texas found out how many students receiving $1 billion in private education subsidies were already homeschooled or enrolled in a private school: 70%. 
Taxpayers in Idaho are still waiting to get that number from a similar private school choice program that serves nearly nine and a half times fewer students, costs $950 million less and was enacted two months earlier. 
And it’s not for lack of trying. 
Between February and July, the Idaho State Tax Commission received seven public records requests related to the Parental Choice Tax Credit. A college faculty member, a hobbyist data analyst, a homeschool advocate, a former public school superintendent and two journalists filed requests seeking data that would shed light on who’s benefitting from the $50 million-a-year taxpayer-funded program. 
Four of those requests — including two from Idaho Education News — sought the number of tax-credit recipients who previously attended a public school. This data would test a selling point of the program: that it helps students who couldn’t otherwise afford a private education. 
That tally doesn’t include unofficial requests. Democratic lawmakers, who asked for data in March, weren’t included in a tracking sheet of records requests obtained by EdNews. 
Nearly all of the requests were denied.
The State of Idaho Chinden Campus in Boise, where the Idaho State Tax Commission is housed, as seen on May 7, 2026. (Photo by Kaeden Lincoln/IdahoEdNews)
 What has the commission released?

It’s been almost a year and a half since the Idaho Legislature and Gov. Brad Little enacted House Bill 93, creating the Parental Choice Tax Credit and directing the Tax Commission to administer the program. 
It’s been four months since the commission closed the first round of applications and issued more than $42 million in awards. The second round closed last month. 
So far, the Tax Commission has released two data points on the program’s rollout: the total dollar amount that’s been awarded and the percentage of recipients whose income was above or below 300% of the federal poverty level. 
Meanwhile, officials at the commission have cited privacy laws to deny requests for additional data. The information that can be released to the public isn’t ready yet because computer systems haven’t been programmed to generate reports, they say, and applications are still being processed.
“It’s not like an Excel spreadsheet where you can just go and gather the data and hit print,” Julie Eavenson, public information director for the Tax Commission, told EdNews by phone last month. “We don’t have a lot of resources to devote to this.”
But some of the data that Idahoans requested in recent months isn’t being collected at all, according to commission responses to records requests.
Here’s who has asked for data, what they asked for and how the commission responded: 
 Previous enrollment status

Stuart Anderson, an education faculty member at Brigham Young University-Idaho, was preparing for a campus debate on school choice when he asked the Tax Commission for the number of tax-credit recipients who were previously enrolled in private school. 
Anderson — who stressed that he was not speaking on behalf of BYU-Idaho — told EdNews that about 140 students attended the debate, which featured two professors on each side of the argument for spending public funds on private education.
“We showed our students, who are mainly in education, that this is a complex issue,” he said. “Here are the challenges. Here are the pros. Here are the cons to this.”
The Tax Commission denied Anderson’s records request. “The information you’re requesting is not being collected or reported on through the Idaho Parental Tax Credit Program,” Eavenson wrote to Anderson on April 13.
Anderson’s request sought to shed light on who was benefitting from the program. HB 93 supporters argued that it would open doors for students who couldn’t otherwise afford an education outside the public school system.
Don Coberly, former Boise School District superintendent. (Photo by Kyle Pfannenstiel/Idaho EdNews)
But in other states with similar private school choice programs, most recipients weren’t attending public schools before applying for state subsidies. In Arizona, nearly 70% of education savings account recipients in the first year were already in a private setting. 
Don Coberly, the former superintendent of the Boise School District, got a similar response from the Tax Commission when he asked for the same figures. A critic of private school choice, Coberly said he planned to write an article about what the data showed. 
“One of the things that’s always been said about the voucher movement is it’s kids escaping failing schools,” he said. “I kind of wanted to know, are they really coming from public schools, or are they already enrolled (in private schools)?” 
Coberly said this data could be useful to public school leaders, if it showed that large numbers of students are fleeing public schools for private options. “That’s good information for the folks who are running those schools to know.” 
 Geographic information

Tucker Anderson — no relation to Stuart — is a hobbyist researcher who creates data visualizations and often shares his work in social media discussions about Idaho politics. 
Anderson asked the Tax Commission for aggregate geographic data, like the home ZIP codes that tax-credit recipients listed on their applications. He wanted to see whether recipients were primarily in urban or rural areas. Anderson previously made an illustration that showed private schools are concentrated in larger cities and rural towns have few choices outside the public system. 
A 2024 EdNews analysis of private school enrollment showed private schools are concentrated in urban areas.
“It’s public information that we should be able to pull,” he said of the geographic information on the tax-credit applications. 
The commission also denied Anderson’s request. “The information you’re requesting is not being aggregated or produced in any form at this time,” Eavenson told him. 
Eavenson noted that the Tax Commission will provide a report “containing geographic information” to Gov. Brad Little and the Legislature in 2027. 
HB 93 directed the commission to compile a report with eight data points on the program’s rollout, including the “geographic area” of recipients. But the legislation wasn’t specific about how detailed the information should be.
 Income data

HB 93 didn’t require the commission to compile income data beyond the number of recipients who qualified for priority access by earning 300% or below the federal poverty level. 
During the first application period, 55% of applicants were above the poverty threshold, while 45% were below it.
Melissa Nash, a member of Homeschool Idaho’s board of directors, asked the commission for additional income data, expecting it would show that wealthier families were the primary beneficiaries. Her request sought aggregate data on tax credit recipients broken down by income tax bracket, among other variables. 
While homeschoolers are eligible for the tax credit, Homeschool Idaho staunchly opposed HB 93. “We feel like partnerships between public and private entities result in private entities being regulated more by the government,” Nash told EdNews. “We wanted to discourage that public-private partnership.”
The commission also denied Nash’s request. 
“This program is being implemented through the income tax system, which means we must follow strict state and federal confidentiality laws,” Eavenson wrote in response to Nash’s request. “We are still in the application phase and actively developing the program, so not all data has been compiled into reportable formats.”
The Tax Commission fulfilled one records request related to the tax credit. Audrey Dutton, a reporter at ProPublica, asked for all statistics and reports related to the tax credit as of March 19. The commission handed over the number of applications and dollar amounts — data the agency later published online. 
Eavenson told EdNews last week that the commission’s focus is on processing applications. “We’re still working on that,” she said by email. 
As of Aug. 17, the commission has received 7,055 applications covering 12,561 students.

name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: O’Brien revives Goldberg feud with whistleblower claim
authors: Katie Castellani | State House News Service
description: O'Brien's lawsuit, filed Thursday in Suffolk County Superior Court, rehashes a two-year-long legal battle between her and Goldberg that highlighted internal strife within the CCC.
text:
FORMER CANNABIS CONTROL COMMISSION Chairwoman Shannon O’Brien is suing both the commission and Treasurer Deb Goldberg seeking compensation for alleged retaliation she faced during her time leading the agency and for damages she incurred throughout the legal battle to get her job back. Meanwhile, Goldberg’s office said O’Brien is dredging up old issues that have already been litigated to generate attention.
O’Brien’s lawsuit, filed Thursday in Suffolk County Superior Court, rehashes a two-year-long legal battle between her and Goldberg that highlighted internal strife within the CCC. It also comes months after Gov. Maura Healey appointed an entirely new commission under a recent law that reformed the marijuana industry and its oversight body while removing Goldberg’s authority to appoint commissioners to the agency. That law terminated O’Brien’s tenure and she was not reappointed.
O’Brien’s complaint, filed by Needham attorney Timothy Burke, includes three separate claims against Goldberg: retaliation in violation of the Massachusetts Whistleblower Act, a charge also brought against the CCC; violation of the Massachusetts Civil Rights Act; and that Goldberg invaded her privacy.
The lawsuit alleges that CCC personnel and Goldberg retaliated against O’Brien because she reported and opposed actions she believed violated the law or regulations and that posed risks to the public. 
Burke said O’Brien disclosed or “threatened to disclose” information to public bodies about “conflicts corrupting enforcement; obstruction and delay of investigations; preferential treatment of licensees; concealment of regulatory and public-safety information; data-security failures; testing fraud; contaminated and unregulated cannabis; misuse or loss of public funds; and retaliation against persons who reported such matters.”
In response to O’Brien’s actions, Burke alleged the CCC and Goldberg’s office subjected her to “threats and pressure to resign; manipulation of workplace complaints; unauthorized disclosure of confidential allegations; suspension; exclusion from her office and agency resources; removal; resistance to reinstatement; impairment of her statutory authority; withholding of information; obstruction of investigations and reforms; and other actions that would deter a reasonable public employee from reporting misconduct.”
And as a result of the alleged retaliation, Burke said O’Brien suffered “economic loss, professional and reputational injury, emotional distress, physical symptoms, litigation expenses, and other compensable damages.”
A CCC spokesperson declined to comment on the complaint, saying the commission can’t comment on pending litigation. 
Andrew Napolitano, spokesperson for Goldberg, said the treasurer has not been served with the complaint and that he can’t comment on the specifics of pending litigation. Napolitano said the treasurer’s office received a “purported ‘whistleblower’ notice” from O’Brien and “based on the baseless allegations set out in that notice, we are confident that our office has not violated the Whistleblower Protection Act or any other laws.” 
A six-page whistleblower notice sent Aug. 3, which the News Service obtained from Burke, includes similar allegations of retaliation against O’Brien to the ones presented in her complaint. It asks the treasurer’s office and CCC to provide O’Brien with her complete personnel file. O’Brien also requested that the agencies preserve evidence going back to January 1, 2023 concerning issues of regulatory compliance and misconduct O’Brien included in the complaint, and that those issues are investigated by an “independent decision-maker” designated by Goldberg’s office and the CCC.
Burke also said in the complaint that Goldberg violated O’Brien’s civil rights through using “threats, intimidation, and coercion.” Burke said Goldberg used those tactics to prevent O’Brien from exercising her right to communicate with public bodies, seek judicial relief, and “oppose unlawful government without retaliation.”
Burke argued Goldberg invaded O’Brien’s privacy by disclosing “the existence and substance of racial insensitivity” to Edward Farley, a political consultant and former Lottery official, during an investigation into allegations that O’Brien made racially insensitive comments, which she denied. Farley had no official role in the investigation or “governmental need” to receive them, Burke said. 
“Shannon O’Brien is once again attempting to rehash issues that have already been investigated or litigated, further wasting taxpayer dollars,” Napolitano said in a statement to the News Service. “This latest complaint is about generating headlines, not presenting the facts. We are focused on the work of our office. It is time to move on.”
O’Brien’s latest suit also turns on allegations of misconduct involving a commission licensee, Greatest Hits, and the alleged conflicts that existed between the company and former Executive Director Shawn Collins. A CCC spokesperson said the agency provided an investigative file related to the issues surrounding Greatest Hits to the attorney’s general’s office, which did not pursue any prosecution. In June, commissioners ratified a stipulated agreement on enforcement against Greatest Hits and the CCC considers the matter closed, according to the spokesperson.
In September 2023, O’Brien sued Goldberg over her suspension as CCC chair. Goldberg then fired O’Brien in September 2024, saying O’Brien “committed gross misconduct and demonstrated she is unable to discharge the powers and duties of a CCC commissioner” and that O’Brien made racially insensitive comments and contributed to a “hostile work environment.”
Last year, a judge cleared O’Brien to return to her post as CCC chair. That ruling came after a Superior Court judge found Goldberg unlawfully fired O’Brien, and granted her back pay and benefits from the start of her termination.
In the latest suit, O’Brien is seeking damages, in an amount to be determined by a jury, for reputational, professional, emotional, physical, and economic injuries that weren’t previously compensated. Along with that, the former CCC chair is seeking compensation equal to three times the lost wages, benefits, and other remuneration under the state’s Whistleblower Act.
The lawsuit comes as Goldberg is seeking reelection this fall and is expected to face Republican Elizabeth Dionne in November. Farley has since done work for Dionne’s campaign and was paid $1,500 last month for communications consulting, according to campaign finance records.
