name: Alaska Beacon
title: Gasoline hits $26 per gallon in the northwest Alaska village of Shungnak
description: It’s not a typo. The price of a gallon of gasoline in the northwest Alaska village of Shungnak was $26.82 on Friday, local residents and regional officials said, likely giving the community the dubious honor of having the most expensive gasoline in the United States. “It is very much real,” said Glenda Douglas, who manages […]
text:
Glenda Douglas of Shungnak, in the Northwest Arctic Borough, shared this photo on social media of a gasoline purchase she made on Friday, Aug. 21, 2026. (Glenda Douglas photo)It’s not a typo. The price of a gallon of gasoline in the northwest Alaska village of Shungnak was $26.82 on Friday, local residents and regional officials said, likely giving the community the dubious honor of having the most expensive gasoline in the United States.
“It is very much real,” said Glenda Douglas, who manages the store in Shungnak and posted a picture of the price on Facebook. 
Across the United States, the average price of a gallon of regular unleaded gasoline was $4.10 on Thursday.
Shungnak is about 280 river miles east of Kotzebue, up the Kobuk River, or 150 miles as the airplane flies. Air travel is the only reliable, year-round form of transportation. 
In summer, the river is usually navigable by boat. In winter, residents travel by snowmachine. Last fall and for parts of this summer, water levels on the Kobuk were low enough to interrupt barge traffic, which contributed to the high price of gasoline. 
“We sell groceries, diesel and gas,” Douglas said via Facebook message. “We had to get gas flown in twice this summer since (the) barge isn’t able to make it this way because the river water levels (are) too low. Just yesterday, the price was 13.99, but now it is 26.82.”
Shareholders in NANA Regional Corp. are eligible for a discount — they can buy gas for $21.46 per gallon. 
Albie Dallemolle is NANA’s vice president of economic development and sustainability.
“Confirmed, Shungnak gasoline price is $26.82 per gallon, which had to be flown into the community,” she said by text message. “This price does reflect the highest cost for gasoline in the region … for now. Unfortunately, prices for gasoline and diesel are expected to increase once communities receive their fall barge deliveries.” 
That’s because the current price is based in part on an average of the air-delivered fuel and cheaper barge-delivered fuel. New barge-delivered fuel, bought after the Iran War began, is expected to be more expensive than fuel bought before the war. 
Shungnak frequently endures some of the highest fuel prices in Alaska. 
In 2007, a gallon of regular unleaded was already $8.11 per gallon, so costly that the Wall Street Journal used the village as an example of what rural Alaska was experiencing that year. By 2022, the price was $14.03 per gallon, according to figures from the Northwest Arctic Borough.
In a message, Douglas said one thing that particularly concerns her is the fact that hunting season has arrived in the region.
Many people in the region practice a subsistence lifestyle, hunting and fishing for food they use to survive. 
“(That price) is really going to hurt our hunters that pay for gas to hunt,” she said.

name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: Northwest Indiana residents sue NIPSCO after storms leave thousands in the dark
description: Nearly two weeks after severe storms knocked out power across northwest Indiana, thousands of homes and businesses remain in the dark — and Northern Indiana Public Service Co. now faces a proposed class action lawsuit over its tree-trimming practices. NIPSCO reported about 10,000 customers without power as of Monday morning, including about 4,300 whose outag[...]
text:
Storm damage in Lake County, Indiana, on Wednesday, Aug. 12, 2026. (Photo courtesy Indiana Governor Flickr)Nearly two weeks after severe storms knocked out power across northwest Indiana, thousands of homes and businesses remain in the dark — and Northern Indiana Public Service Co. now faces a proposed class action lawsuit over its tree-trimming practices.
NIPSCO reported about 10,000 customers without power as of Monday morning, including about 4,300 whose outages were tied to the Aug. 11 storm and subsequent severe weather.
The utility expected restoration work to be substantially complete in Munster and Lake Station by Monday night and in Gary and Portage by Tuesday night, although it cautioned that some individual outages could last longer.
Smaller numbers of customers in Munster, Portage, Hammond, Lake Station and Merrillville were also without power. NIPSCO predicted most customers would be restored by Tuesday night. The utility said it had more than 350,000 outages after the storm hit.
Gary Common Council member Darren Washington told the Indiana Capital Chronicle that the outages require scrutiny beyond the immediate response.
“Northwest Indiana needs more than restored electricity,” Washington said. “It needs a serious public conversation about whether our infrastructure is adequate for the future and whether our elected and regulatory leaders are prepared to demand the accountability residents deserve.”
Gov. Mike Braun has sought an expedited federal major disaster declaration for 54 counties, citing winds of up to 99 mph near Gary and a near-total loss of power across Lake County.
The lawsuit filed in Porter County Superior Court, names Valparaiso resident Jack Tipold and 16 other northwest Indiana residents as plaintiffs. They allege the Northern Indiana Public Service Co. failed to adequately manage trees and other vegetation near its power lines, contributing to repeated outages since August 2024.
Story continues below.
First Amended Complaint.pdf
 
The case has not been certified as a class action. As of Monday morning, no hearings had been scheduled and NIPSCO had not filed a response in court.
The complaint says the Aug. 11 outage affected 317,000 customers, or nearly 60% of NIPSCO’s electric customers. It accuses the utility of ignoring public requests to address hazardous conditions, inadequately inspecting lines and poles, failing to identify hazard trees and not maintaining a sufficient workforce for vegetation management.
Tipold alleges he was undergoing oral surgery when the power failed, forcing the procedure to end before he had adequate pain control. The complaint says he also lost perishable household goods. Other plaintiffs allege economic losses and physical or emotional harm.
The plaintiffs are asking the court to certify a class of Indiana residents who suffered personal injury or financial harm because of what they describe as negligent vegetation management. They seek compensatory and punitive damages in an amount to be determined.
NIPSCO has disputed the allegations.
Indiana damages from flooding, high winds could exceed $5B, Braun tells feds

“We strongly disagree with the characterization of NIPSCO’s vegetation management practices,” utility officials said in a statement. “We will vigorously defend the company through the legal process. NIPSCO’s electric operations, including its active vegetation management program, are overseen by the Indiana Utility Regulatory Commission. NIPSCO’s vegetation management spend has more than doubled since 2016, demonstrating our commitment and focus on maintaining a safe and reliable electric system.”
The company said its immediate priority was restoring service safely and quickly after severe weather caused what it called unprecedented damage to its electric system.
The governor on Sunday said he mobilized the Indiana National Guard and sent personnel from several state agencies to help clear debris for utility crews.
“There is no excuse for these delays,” Braun said in a statement on X.

name: Nevada Current
title: Washoe County asking voters to signal support for higher fees on electric vehicles
description: Washoe County voters this November will have the opportunity to weigh in on whether electric vehicle owners are “paying their fair share” toward filling potholes and adding new streetlights. The Regional Transportation Commission of Northern Nevada, which pushed for the non-binding advisory question, is hoping voters will say “yes” and signal support for cha[...]
text:
(Photo: iStock / Getty Images Plus)Washoe County voters this November will have the opportunity to weigh in on whether electric vehicle owners are “paying their fair share” toward filling potholes and adding new streetlights.
The Regional Transportation Commission of Northern Nevada, which pushed for the non-binding advisory question, is hoping voters will say “yes” and signal support for charging electric and hybrid vehicles an annual road use fee on top of the registration fees they already pay.
 
Here’s what will appear on the ballot.
THIS QUESTION IS ADVISORY AND NON-BINDING: Do you support an annual road use fee on all electric and hybrid passenger vehicles registered in Washoe County, which would be adjusted annually for inflation? These fees are intended to approximate the annual contribution that owners of gasoline powered vehicles pay per year in local fuel taxes to support local transportation infrastructure. The revenue from these fees would be dedicated to the Regional Transportation Commission of Washoe County subject to annual audits and public disclosure of spending, and the revenue would be used solely for the funding of transportation projects that will reduce traffic congestion, repair and maintain roads, improve air quality, and increase safety.


“Probably nobody wants to pay” for road maintenance and improvement, conceded RTC Executive Director Bill Thomas during a presentation to the Washoe County Commission in June. “But it’s about fairness. Is there a subset of people who shouldn’t be paying their fair share?”
The primary funding source for the county’s road projects is the voter-approved fuel tax, known as RTC-5. Voters approved that tax in 2008, and it automatically adjusts for inflation each year.
Washoe County’s fuel tax brought in $110 million in 2025. It funded major roadway improvement and maintenance projects.
Thomas told commissioners conversations about how to reconcile the increase in roadway maintenance needs with the reality of declines in taxable gallons of fuel has been going on for “many years.”
Electric vehicle registrations in Washoe County increased 562% between 2020 and 2025, according to Thomas. Hybrid vehicle registrations increased 159%. 
If those EVs and hybrids had paid an equivalent in county fuel tax, it would have brought in $15.5 million over the past five years, according to Thomas.
EVs and hybrids still make up a small fraction of vehicle registrations in Washoe County — 5.3% as of June 2024, according to the Guinn Center. But their adoption, combined with better fuel efficiency in gas cars, has created funding challenges that need to be addressed.
The Guinn Center in an August 2025 report commissioned by Washoe County recommended an enhanced registration fee.
Nevada is currently 1 of 10 states that do not have one.
Other options making EVs contribute to roadway projects were seen as less ideal for the county.
A vehicle miles traveled tax is seen by many as the most equitable because it considers road use rather than power source. But getting such a system in place would be complicated and costly.
It is “not a near-term solution,” said Thomas.
Similarly, charging EVs per kilowatt would also be difficult to implement.
Drivers pay county fuel tax incrementally — each time they fill up at the pump.
According to Thomas, RTC of Northern Nevada commissioned two polls of registered voters in Washoe County — first in December 2025, then in June 2026. The results suggested a majority — 6 in 10 — support an additional fee on EVs and hybrids. Their survey asked about a potential $250 annual fee on EVs and $125 on hybrid vehicles.
Washoe County Commission and RTC do not have the authority to implement a new EV fee or tax. If the advisory question passes this November, lobbyists for the agency and county will take the results to the Nevada State Legislature along with a bill to allow the county to take action.
“We’ll have the sentiment of the public and a specific bill on what our needs are,” Thomas said.
The RTC’s board in February unanimously supported putting the advisory question on the ballot. Washoe County commissioners in late June voted 4-1 in support, with Commissioner Jeanne Herman casting the sole vote in opposition.
Commissioner Alexis Hill, who on the gubernatorial campaign trail earlier this year said she wanted commercial electric vehicles to contribute to highway and roadway maintenance, said she would be voting yes on the advisory question.
“We have been waiting for action from the Legislature on this issue,” she said, “and due to inaction we have got to advocate for our community. We have studies … that show that we need to invest in our infrastructure.”
Commission Chair Clara Andriola also supports the advisory question and noted that she is an EV owner.
“My vehicle is heavier than most other vehicles that are comparable to its size,” she said. “Everyday I’m going around and traveling, I am not paying my fair share.”

name: Delaware
title: Close and candid: two young Democrats competing for votes in Hockessin, Pike Creek, Yorklyn, North Star and Newark
description: Republican Councilwoman Kilpatrick has decided to retire, and her seat is up for grabs   For 16 years, Councilwoman Janet Kilpatrick has represented Hockessin, Yorklyn, North Star, Pike Creek and part of Newark which makes up New Castle County “District 3.” Councilwoman Kilpatrick is not seeking reelection, one of two decades-long tenures ending this year. D[...]
text:
Republican Councilwoman Kilpatrick has decided to retire, and her seat is up for grabs
 
For 16 years, Councilwoman Janet Kilpatrick has represented Hockessin, Yorklyn, North Star, Pike Creek and part of Newark which makes up New Castle County “District 3.”
Councilwoman Kilpatrick is not seeking reelection, one of two decades-long tenures ending this year. Democrats Kira Alejandro and Kyle Grantham are competing for her seat in the Sept. 15 primary; the winner faces Republican Melissa Brayman, a Delaware State Chamber of Commerce office administrator with no primary of her own. Both Alejandro and Grantham sat down for interviews about who they are and what they’d do if elected.
Kira Alejandro: A musician and community advocate
Growing up…
Alejandro, 30, grew up in Hockessin-off Brackenville Road-and still lives in the district, in Yorklyn. She plays piano and baritone ukulele, plays some guitar and bass, and grew up playing flute. She said she also grew up going to Ashland Nature Center, which she called “a focal point” in her life and where her love of the natural world began. Her favorite spot there is a boardwalk over a marsh, where she said watching frog eggs and cattails appear every year still feels peaceful. “I feel really lucky to live so close to it,” she said.
A formative influence…
She credits both parents with shaping how she sees public life: her father, “a very staunch environmental advocate” and believer in public education from his own years in New York’s public schools, and her mother, who volunteered on the spot to keep a Girl Scout camp on Sharpless Road running rather than let it close, and ran it for years afterward.
Making it personal…
Alejandro said she has personally helped save nearly 30 acres of land in Yorklyn from development, and pledged never to take donations from developers, land-use attorneys, corporations or corporate PACs. “I think you can’t be neutral if you’re funded by special interests,” she said.
On electric bills and data centers…
“The problem that we’re seeing with the delivery fees is partly because Delmarva is allowed to do non-mandatory construction of infrastructure,” Alejandro said, pointing to a pending Delaware Public Service Commission case in which Delmarva is seeking a $68 million rate increase.
“Adding poles, adding substations, building things for anticipated use… that is the only way that Delmarva can potentially profit, because they’re not supposed to be profiting off of the sale or delivery fees.” She said “part of the reason that the energy bills are continuing to increase is because data centers are getting built on our grid,” adding, “whether or not we have any data centers in Delaware, if data centers are being built on this larger grid, our energy bills are going to go up.”
“I believe the number one thing we can do at a county level to get a handle on these increasing rates is call for a data center moratorium,” she said. “We’ve seen precedent for this. Maryland has five different counties now that have enacted a moratorium. They have a county that has outright banned data centers.”
What’s been the hardest part of running?
“Running a campaign is grueling. I’m very fortunate to have a lot of people who are very invested in this campaign,” Alejandro said. “I would say overall I think the most challenging thing has just been that no one knows what the county council is. So often I find people asking me, ‘Are you running against Mike Smith? Are you running against Frank Burns?'”
Why do you think you’re the right fit for the job?
“I’m the only candidate that has any kind of concrete experience standing up for our communities and actually achieving results,” Alejandro said. “That’s why I’m running. I want to keep putting our communities first as a council member.”
Kyle Grantham: A photojournalist turned public servant
Growing up…
Grantham, 38, grew up in Cecil County, Maryland, and moved to Delaware in 2013. He considered the Naval Academy in high school before choosing journalism, as he learned more about the Iraq War, working through Ohio, Indiana, Wyoming, and California before landing at The News Journal full-time in 2013.
A formative influence…
Grantham said the person who shaped his approach to public service most was Rob Carr, an Associated Press photographer he met at 19 covering a bowl game in Mobile, Alabama. Carr later got him assignments at the Senior British Open and an Ireland-Scotland rugby match, then brought him along to shoot Orioles and Ravens games for his first national byline. “No one gets anywhere in this industry by themselves,” Grantham said Carr told him, a lesson he’s carried into politics.
Making it personal…
He left journalism after being assaulted by a Trump supporter about two weeks before the 2016 election, then spent nearly a decade in the county executive’s office after Gov. Matt Meyer, then county executive, brought him on. Grantham lives in Newark with his wife and 2-year-old son, still coaches the county’s adult co-ed soccer league at Banning Park.
On electric bills and data centers…
Grantham explains, “I think we need to work with the state to get power bills under control. I’m not convinced we can unilaterally impose a moratorium on data center construction without backing from the state legislature.
The companies building these things have more money than God and armies of lawyers. If we go it alone against them, I don’t think we can win. If we work with the state to take a comprehensive approach to fighting them – whether it be zoning, tax reform, or hopefully an outright ban – we have a better shot of making Delaware look less attractive and keeping them out of the state altogether.
But simply hitting ‘pause’ for a year or two with a moratorium isn’t going to be enough. The energy and environmental impacts from these facilities are never going to be solved, and even if they somehow were, these facilities are being built to power AI technology designed to replace workers and produce a product 40% the quality for 10% the cost. I’m never going to support that.
At the same time, the County can be bringing new clean power projects online to introduce power locally at cost and start curving bills down.”
What’s been the hardest part of running?
“This is easily the hardest thing I’ve ever done in my life,” Grantham said. “I think the one thing I wasn’t necessarily prepared for was the guilt, having a two-year-old and needing to spend so much time out putting the hard groundwork in. When I’m out 20, 30 hours a week knocking doors, I just feel guilty that I’m not at home with him. And then on the flip side, when I’m at home and I am enjoying myself, then I feel guilty that I’m not working hard enough.”
Why do you think you’re the right fit for the job?
“What I want people to see in those endorsements is that these people are recognizing the fact that I understand what this job is about and what it’s not about, and the way that it can have an impact on lives in a real way, and that they see in me the experience and qualifications to do it well,” Grantham said.
Where the two candidates’ money and endorsements stand
Grantham raised roughly $25,900 through Aug. 16, per the State’s Campaign Filing Report System, and have some noteworthy endorsements from six NCC council members, including Councilwoman Kilpatrick and Councilman Hollins, plus Gov. Matt Meyer.
Alejandro raised nearly $44,700 over the same period, almost $18,850 more than Grantham, with some notable endorsements from one council member, two state officials and the Sierra Club.
Both candidates agree Delaware’s electric bills are a real burden, and that data centers are part of the story. They disagree on whether the fix is a moratorium or a zoning overhaul. On Sept. 15, District 3’s Democrats decide which approach, and which candidate, gets the chance to prove it right.
How to vote
Only registered Democrats can vote in the Sept. 15 primary. The deadline to register was Saturday, Aug. 22; early voting runs Sept. 2-13. Check your registration or district at the state’s voter portal, ivote.de.gov/VoterView.

name: South Carolina Daily Gazette
title: SC estate with ties to slavery, circus and governors could next become a state preserve
description: The state is considering buying the Goodwill Plantation, where more than a dozen restored buildings tell the land's storied history.
text:
Goodwill Plantation includes a 35-acre lake, which attracts many migrating birds, according to The Conservation Fund. (Photo courtesy of Premier Sotheby’s International Realty)EASTOVER — In its past lifetimes, the Goodwill Plantation was a vast farm worked by slaves, a winter home for circus animals and a family hunting retreat.
In its next life, the estate located just south of Columbia could become a state preserve.
The Conservation Fund closed a deal on the property for $13.8 million earlier this month, primarily using a state-funded grant. The nonprofit plans to donate the land back to the state Department of Natural Resources to expand the nearby Wateree River Heritage Preserve.
The Faulkenberrys’ home sits on a 32-acre lake on the Goodwill Plantation, which recently sold to a conservation nonprofit. (Photo courtesy of Premier Sotheby’s International Realty)
The 736 acres include more than a dozen historic buildings dating to 1857, which the owners restored over the years. Fish swim in a 35-acre lake, and birds nest in a large rookery. Deer and turkey roam through hardwood forests, and water drains into the nearby Wateree River.
Saving a piece of land with so much historical significance along with ecological importance is rare, said Jason Johnson, director of South Carolina projects for the nonprofit.
“It’s not often that I work on a property that has that combination of, we’re conserving habitat and conserving history,” he said.
The property is also a donut hole of sorts, Johnson said. Thousands of acres surrounding it, including a previous portion of the plantation, are already protected. Any sort of major development on the land could disrupt the surrounding natural beauty, he said.
“It was important to fill in this last piece, because this is a very attractive property from a development standpoint,” Johnson said.
The owners, Larry and Jerry Faulkenberry, sold close to 4,500 acres over a decade ago to a company looking to offset the impacts of a gold mine. That land became the state-owned Wateree River Heritage Preserve.
What’s left is “the historical core, really,” Larry Faulkenberry said.
The Goodwill Plantation, a 736-acre estate just south of Columbia, could become a state preserve. (Photo courtesy of Premier Sotheby’s International Realty)
The couple put the estate on the market in 2024, including the home they built. The land already had approval for up to 22 separate lots, which realtors advertised as perfect for a prospective subdivision.
Looking back on the land’s storied history, and with urging from community members and the local state senator, the Faulkenberrys instead decided to sell their beloved property to a nonprofit, with the hopes that one day the state will open it for anyone interested in stopping by.
“We wanted to make sure it stayed intact and people could enjoy it for generations to come,” Faulkenberry said.
A plantation
In 1795, Daniel Huger, one of South Carolina’s first congressmen, established the Goodwill Plantation on 3,500 acres of land. A mill pond and canal system built on the property suggest Huger made one of the first attempts to farm on low-lying land in the state, according to the National Register of Historic Places. (The property’s been listed in the National Register since 1986.)
His son, Daniel Elliott Huger, took over the plantation after he died. While the state legislator, judge and U.S. senator lived most of his life in the Lowcountry, he more than doubled Goodwill’s acreage and improved the irrigation system to farm cotton and other crops. The “elaborate and successful irrigation system” brought a financial boon to the plantation, according to the application for national recognition.
Children learn how corn was milled in the 19th century at a restored mill house dating back to the 1850s on the Goodwill Plantation property in Eastover, S.C. (Photo courtesy of Premier Sotheby’s International Realty)
An overseer’s house built in 1857 remains on the property as a remnant of the Hugers’ ownership.
The property changed families for the first time in 1858, when Edward Barnwell “Barney” Heyward bought the land. Grandson of Nathaniel Heyward, South Carolina’s wealthiest rice planter, Barney Heyward may have continued to grow rice at his new plantation, along with other crops, according to the National Register.
Heyward’s son, Duncan Clinch Heyward, went on to be the state’s governor. Although records conflict on whether he was born on the property, records suggest he at least spent much of his childhood there, according to a compiled history of the property.
Although the Midlands region wasn’t as friendly for rice as the Lowcountry, the former governor recounted his father growing rice there, using a millpond on a hill to flood the fields and the Wateree River to drain them. Historians petitioning for a place on the National Register couldn’t find any evidence to back up his memory, but the estate’s owners believe it to be true.
After the Civil War broke out, Heyward and his family moved close to 900 slaves from their Lowcountry plantations to the Goodwill Plantation, where he had another 82 people enslaved, to “wait out the war.” After taking a train most of the way there, Heyward’s slaves had to walk the final 11 miles to the plantation, according to a compiled history.
After the war ended, Heyward employed at least some former slaves as day laborers, according to the National Register documentation, which doesn’t give specifics. Without slave labor, and facing the fallout of the war, Heyward sold the land to a New Yorker named George Wickes in 1869.
The Faulkenberrys restored a water wheel for the former grist mill at the Goodwill Plantation in Eastover, S.C. (Photo courtesy of Premier Sotheby’s International Realty)
However, reminders of Heyward’s ownership remain as well. Two slave cabins from that time still stand, along with the mill building, which the Faulkenberrys restored using a water wheel from the Hugers’ time.
The Heywards’ house, believed to be built in 1858, is now a small museum, where the Faulkenberrys showcase some of the artifacts and antiques collected on the property, according to the realty company that sold it.
A circus owner’s family retreat
Wickes didn’t keep the land long, either. After running a grist mill and sawmill for five years, he sold the plantation. The land changed hands seven times over the following 15 years.
The next major owner was famed showman P.T. Barnum. Recently retired from running the Barnum and Bailey circus, he bought the property in 1888, at a cost of $100,000 — about $3.5 million today.
Barnum gifted the land to his granddaughter, Julia Clarke. Some accounts say he sent his circus animals there for the winters.
“‘Goodwill’ is one of the finest estates in the South, containing upward of 7,000 acres, including a magnificent water power,” The New York Times wrote of Barnum’s purchase.
A restored blacksmith shop, believed to date back to 1865, is included on the Goodwill Plantation property in Eastover, S.C. (Photo courtesy of Premier Sotheby’s International Realty)
Clarke used prison labor to fix up the property, and a filled-in well still stands where historians believe Clarke housed convicts, according to the National Register documents.
The Clarkes built several still-standing structures, including the main house.
In 1910, Samuel McMaster, a distant relative of Gov. Henry McMaster, bought the land. The governor believes the buyer was a cousin of his grandfather. But he doesn’t recall spending any time on the land, his office told the SC Daily Gazette.
The McMasters opened the grist mill and hunting lodge that remain on the property. Some farming continued until the 1950s, according to National Register documents.
A family home
When Larry and Jerry Faulkenberry bought Goodwill Plantation in 1995, they didn’t plan to stay for long. The couple regularly bought and flipped massive properties, and the property had a lot of potential, Larry Faulkenberry said.
“The thing you don’t do in the land business is fall in love with a piece of land,” he said. “That’s what I did with Goodwill.”
Walking past the dikes, the ditches, the buildings and the millpond built in the 1800s, Faulkenberry didn’t want to leave. He learned the place’s history and realized he and his wife had something special, he said.
The McMaster family turned the Goodwill Plantation into a hunting retreat, complete with a hunting lodge, in the early 20th century. (Photo courtesy of Premier Sotheby’s International Realty)
“When I first started bringing Goodwill back to life 25 years ago, it dawned on me that Goodwill was much, much, much larger than one person — me,” Faulkenberry said.
So, the couple started to fix up the land.
The Faulkenberrys poured years of work and more than $1 million into the property, though Faulkenberry added he didn’t know precisely how much. (His wife keeps the books.)
They replaced roofs and restored buildings left to decay over more than a century and those damaged by Hurricane Hugo in 1989.
Faced with the option of living in the hunting lodge or the historic house the Heywards built, both far offset from the road, the Faulkenberrys opted to build their own home. Spanning 8,400 square feet, the house included four bedrooms, five bathrooms and a porch overlooking the 35-acre lake.
Although by far the most modern, that home has historical roots, too. The Faulkenberrys wanted their house to match the spirit of the rest of the property, so they had it designed in old Charleston style, including antique light fixtures and furniture.
Even the color of the walls is based in history, Faulkenberry said. The tan and pastel-colored paint are true to what might have existed in houses built in the 1800s, he said.
The Faulkenberrys tried to make their 2010 home look as authentic to the property as possible, using antiques and historic paint, owner Larry Faulkenberry said. (Photo courtesy of Premier Sotheby’s International Realty)
In 2010, the couple moved in.
“We’ve loved it ever since,” Faulkenberry said.
But the Faulkenberrys are in their 70s, and they have other land to tend, he said. Keeping more than 700 acres in good shape, along with multiple properties dating back decades, requires a lot of time and effort.
The couple wants to build a new home, which Faulkenberry called a “sister house,” next to one for their daughter in Columbia. They decided it was time to sell the land they loved.
Originally listed at $17.5 million, the former plantation could have attracted high-dollar developers. A brochure extolling the area’s virtues highlighted the benefits of building a subdivision in the secluded area just half an hour from the state capital.
The Faulkenberrys have long flirted with the idea of protecting their property. In 2005, Faulkenberry told a reporter he wanted most of the property to become a nature preserve, with 30 lots shaved off for high-end homes.
The couple had already sold most of the land — nearly 4,500 acres — to Haile Gold Mine in 2015. The company was looking to save wetlands to offset the impacts of the mining operation in Kershaw.
Thinking back on the history of the place, Faulkenberry couldn’t bear the idea of splitting off pieces of land.
A porch on the back of the Faulkenberrys’ home at the Goodwill Plantation overlooks a 35-acre lake. (Photo courtesy of Premier Sotheby’s International Realty)
“It survived all of them,” he said of the former owners. “It sure could survive me.”
The Faulkenberrys plan to donate an undisclosed portion of the money they receive from selling the land to Connie Maxwell Children’s Ministries to help build a new “healing center” for children who have experienced trauma.
A state preserve
The state Department of Natural Resources received initial approval Aug. 18 to start evaluating the property to make sure it’s a good fit to join the nature preserve. It’s unclear how the agency would use the Faulkenberrys’ home. It has not yet answered questions from the Gazette about it.
Talks about saving the property started years ago.
Conservationists and state officials have had the property on their minds for a long time, said Johnson, with The Conservation Fund. But the real push began when the Faulkenberrys started to talk about selling.

“You can just feel the history here,” Johnson said. “And it’s just a gorgeous spot.”
Earlier this year, The Conservation Fund got approved for a $12.6 million grant through the state’s Conservation Bank. Richland County chipped in an additional $600,000.
And the U.S. military paid another $600,000 through a grant to conserve land around military bases, Johnson said. (Goodwill is near both Fort Jackson and McEntyre Joint National Guard Base.)
Recognizing the significance of their property, the Faulkenberrys host tours and meet-ups for people interested in seeing the old buildings and learning about the history. They’ve had hundreds of people over the years, of all ages, Faulkenberry said.
A lot of schools like to bring their fifth grade classes, because that’s when students are learning about the 19th century, when much of the plantation was built. Many have only a vague understanding of what people did to survive back then, Faulkenberry said.
Once, a visiting student told Faulkenberry she loved cornbread but didn’t realize it was actually made from corn. Plenty of students don’t know how their morning grits are made. Before they visit, they haven’t seen how a grist mill works to get that context, he said.
‘What people overcame’
Among the visitors was Sen. Darrell Jackson, who lives only a few miles down the road but had no clue the property existed until a friend called him a few years ago.
Sen. Darrell Jackson asks questions during a Senate Finance subcommittee meeting in Columbia, S.C. on Wednesday, Feb. 18, 2025. (Photo by Travis Bell/STATEHOUSE CAROLINA/Special to the SC Daily Gazette)
The Hopkins Democrat came out for a tour and left very impressed at what he saw. Since then, he’s brought back other groups, including the men’s ministry at Bible Way Church of Atlas Road, where he’s the pastor.
“The last thing that any of us would have wanted is to see this precious land fall into the hands of some private developer,” Jackson said.
The Faulkenberrys also make a point of bringing descendants of the people enslaved on the property to see it.
Families want to come see where their ancestors lived, said Titus Duren, a local history teacher who has helped organize events for descendants and researched genealogy.
Acknowledging the property’s difficult history is important, Jackson said. Seeing the slave cabins in person gives people a better idea of what the hundreds of enslaved people there went through than simply hearing about it, he said.
As the country celebrates its 250th birthday, the property stands as a reminder that the Declaration of Independence didn’t guarantee freedom to every American, Jackson said.
“I still believe a picture is worth a thousand words,” Jackson said. “Goodwill Plantation will be a wonderful picture of the goodness of people and the endurance of people.”
It’s a reminder “not just of the atrocities of slavery but what people overcame and how far the country has come,” he continued.
When Jackson walked through the property with his church’s men’s ministry a few months ago, he watched the way members’ faces lit up at seeing a piece of their history preserved. Though painful and difficult, slavery remains a piece of the African American story, he said.
“To preserve that, our history, and to share it with not only other South Carolinians but with the world would be such a gift and such a wonderful thing,” he said.
Faulkenberry has noticed the same sorts of reactions from his tour groups.
“When white elderly people come out, they like it,” Faulkenberry said of the property. “When Black elderly people come out, they love it, because they can relate to it.”
If the state takes over the land, officials plan to make few changes to the existing buildings or the land, according to DNR documents. Those involved with the property hope to see tours taking people through the buildings, with signs explaining their significance.
When Faulkenberry was first researching the property’s history, a historian told him he’d bought “the most historic tract of land” in at least Richland County, “and no one knows about it.”
“That’s what I want to change,” Faulkenberry said. “I want the public to get involved in it.”

text:
The Ohio burgee. (Getty images file photo.)Every morning in the Ohio Capital Journal’s free newsletter, The Eye-Opener, we round up the news and commentary from across Ohio and around the country and world that is catching our attention. We call this feature Catching Our Eye, republished here.
Please subscribe to our free daily newsletter to get all the Ohio news you need to know right to your inbox every weekday morning.
If you already subscribe, please share with your family and friends so they know about the Ohio Capital Journal too: https://ohiocapitaljournal.com/subscribe/

 Catching Our Eye

• The Ohio Supreme Court and abortion rights decisions. The Statehouse News Bureau’s Jo Ingles and Karen Kasler report, “Both sides of abortion debate say latest Ohio Supreme Court action on amendment won’t be the last.”
The Ohio Supreme Court declined to take up a case that challenged the state’s new reproductive rights constitutional amendment. But supporters and opponents of the amendment agree on one thing; it’s not the end for lawsuits related to the 2023 voter-approved constitutional change.
• Wexner. WOSU’s Allie Vugrincic reports, “Les Wexner steps down as chair of namesake Ohio State Wexner Medical Center, remains on board.”
New Albany billionaire Les Wexner will step down as chair of his namesake Ohio State Wexner Medical Center, but will remain a member of the board. An Ohio State University Board of Trustees committee approved the change Thursday morning. The full board will vote in September.
Wexner has faced scrutiny for his relationship with convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein, though Wexner has denied any wrongdoing. Calls to remove Wexner’s name from Ohio State campus buildings have been piling up for months. Meanwhile, 88-year-old Wexner last attended a board meeting in May 2025.
• Ohio earthworks. The Ohio Newsroom’s Kaitlin Thorne reports, “Inspired by European guidebooks, this author created a tour book of Ohio’s historic earthworks.”
Ohio is home to an estimated 500 earthworks, created by Native American groups like the Hopewell over 2,000 years ago. Often large in scale, the architectural structures are made of mounded dirt, clay and other raw materials.
“They were built for ceremonial purposes,” John Hancock, professor emeritus of architecture at the University of Cincinnati said. “They were not forts, they were not cities. They were built as sacred spaces for these American Indian ancestors.” …
Hancock published two books on Ohio earthworks this spring: “Traveler’s Guide to Ancient Ohio,” and “Hopewell Ceremonial Earthworks: Landscape Monuments of the Ancient Ohio Valley.”

title: The Trump administration upended how we fight wildfires. Then came the West’s worst fire season in years.
authors: By Amy Alonzo, Rachel Becker, Robert Chaney, Mike Koshmrl, Brooke Larsen, Joseph T. O'Connor, Olivia Prentzel
description:
WyoFile joined a coalition of nonprofit newsrooms in six Western states to examine how the changes are impacting our ability to fight fires amid increasingly destructive conditions. 
The post The Trump administration upended how we fight wildfires. Then came the West’s worst fire season in years. appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
Four firefighters, two helicopter pilots and a contractor bulldozing a fireline have died in Colorado, Utah and Oregon this year.
Fast-moving fires have burned millions of acres and destroyed hundreds of homes and buildings in the West. California, which is having an unusually quiet fire summer, has deployed engines and crews to fight fires raging in Colorado and the Pacific Northwest — but even this well-resourced state continues to feel vulnerable.
The U.S. has been at Preparedness Level 5 since July 18, a status that means the federal government is committing the highest possible level of crews, aircraft and firefighting resources to wildfires across the country. And yet requests for help or equipment are going unanswered.

People gather along Highway 78 after having been forced to evacuate Beulah as the Aspen Acres fire raced toward the small town June 29, 2026. (Mike Sweeney/ Special to The Colorado Sun)

This dangerous fire season hit as the Trump administration has reshaped how America fights wildfire — consolidating crews from across Interior Department agencies into a new U.S. Wildland Fire Service. The new agency and the U.S. Forest Service are pursuing “full suppression” of every new blaze.
Administration officials say the aggressive approach is essential to protect firefighters and communities during a hazardous summer in an abnormally hot and dry West. Critics, though, worry it could worsen a long-standing problem: Decades of extinguishing wildfires and climate change-induced drought have left Western forests full of dry fuels, contributing to conditions that can produce catastrophic fires. Making full suppression the default response, they argue, could perpetuate that problem while demanding more firefighting resources than the government has available.
A coalition of nonprofit newsrooms in six Western states conducted roughly two dozen interviews with federal and state officials, former agency leaders and firefighters, experts and advocates. Reporting from CalMatters, The Colorado Sun, Montana Free Press, the Mountain Journal, the Nevada Independent, The Salt Lake Tribune, and WyoFile shows how on-the-ground changes made by the Trump administration have affected our ability to fight fires amid increasingly destructive conditions. 
Federal officials dispute that the reorganization played any role in the deaths of firefighters this year. And while officials in several Western states say the new fire service has so far caused few disruptions on the ground, interviews with former government officials, firefighters and researchers show there are concerns about what the administration’s broader changes could mean for how the country lives with fire over the long term.
A plane drops fire retardants on the Widemouth 2 Fire, on Monday, Aug. 3, 2026. (Rick Egan/The Salt Lake Tribune) 
The 10 a.m. rule
Some see the full suppression strategy as the return of a discredited 1930s-era “10 a.m. rule,” a former Forest Service directive to put out new fires by the next morning. Today, that strategy demands vast resources, critics point out, while removing the option used by the agency in more recent years to allow carefully chosen fires to burn naturally for the benefit of forests. They argue that will leave forests more vulnerable to catastrophic fires in the future.



Planned burning, or “prescribed fire is never even going to scratch the surface of the number of acres that need to burn every year,” said Johanna Nosal, a professional forester who worked for the U.S. Forest Service in California, Colorado and Montana for 15 years before accepting a federal buyout in 2025.
“We’re putting these fires out, and sometimes we’re successful at it … but it’s just a year-to-year Band-Aid,” Nosal told The Nevada Independent, “and what eventually happens is you have a lack of resources and these weather periods that will create these huge blazes that no matter what you will do will keep spreading.”
U.S. Forest Service Chief Tom Schultz argues full suppression is essential for this hazardous summer. And Brian Fennessy, director of the new U.S. Wildland Fire Service, defends a policy shift it’s made: Federal officials who want to promote forest health can no longer make the final call about whether to let a fire burn.Previously at the Interior Department, “when it was a fire for resource benefit, fire [officials] may have had a say, but they did not hold the final decision,” which was made by agency land managers, he told The Colorado Sun. “Now, we hold, on the fire side, that final decision.”At the Forest Service, underlying policies still provide the authority to manage wildfire to benefit forests. But a proposal to move the Forest Service (USDA) firefighting program into the U.S. Wildland Fire Service is stoking fears that could change.This summer, Schultz said, the Forest Service has not revived the 10 a.m. rule: “We aren’t making any commitment to that time frame.”

U.S. Forest Service Chief Tom Schultz speaks during a media tour at the fire camp for the Widemouth 2 Fire in Kanosh on Thursday, Aug. 6, 2026. (Bethany Baker/The Salt Lake Tribune) 

Instead, he told The Salt Lake Tribune, its full suppression strategy includes two approaches: Direct and indirect.“Direct is when you go right at it. Indirect is when you look at the topography,” he said. “The tactics will be different. Firefighter safety is critical, but also looking at the values at risk. We’re looking at structures. We’re looking at timber. We’re looking at grass. We’re looking at fencing. All of those things go into how we prioritize,” he said.Utah supports the full suppression policy, “mainly because of where we’re at condition-wise, the historical drought, the dry fuels, and the intensity of these fires,” to protect firefighters and communities, said Jamie Barnes, recently appointed as director of the Department of Natural Resources.
“We will never put people in an area that is unsafe for firefighters. We will always take an indirect approach from that if we have to,” she said.With the country at its highest level of preparedness, resource allocation will vary by fire, Schultz acknowledged.“But in terms of this time of the year, right now, we are not going to just sit back and let fire go and achieve other objectives,” Schultz said. “We’re going to be aggressively suppressing.”  
‘Fear of fire’
Bobbie Scopa is a 45-year firefighting veteran who worked for local, state and federal agencies, primarily in Western states. When she began in 1974, blazes were smaller, she said. “They weren’t ripping like they do now.”
The Forest Service shifted away from the 10 a.m. policy and began allowing some fires to burn for landscape health in 1971. But pressure from states has sometimes discouraged that federal policy, said Nosal, who now lives in Butte, Mont.
“Pretty much every administration I worked under,” she said, “there’s been at least one year when they’re like, ‘We’re not gonna let managed fires happen, we want to get everything under control as soon as possible.’”

Hand crews continue to work on the Bonneville Fire in Salt Lake City, Monday, June 22, 2026. (Chris Samuels/The Salt Lake Tribune) 

Nosal spent her 15 years with the Forest Service removing and thinning trees and other vegetation that would have been cleared out by smaller fires, she said. In the sagebrush ecosystems that cover the Great Basin, suppression has led to encroachment by pinyon-juniper woodlands and other trees. 
“Even in those really dry forest types, you’re seeing denser forests and more continuous forests than would have been there,” she said. “That means when a fire does roll through … you just get these really intense fires that burn everything, which historically isn’t the natural fire regime.”
In other areas, such as the Sierra Nevada, the forests are just too dense, she said. 
The spread of homes and other development into the wildland-urban interface (WUI) also has changed firefighting, Scopa said. “If a fire starts before there are houses, and firefighters show up, the Hot Shots cut lines, firefighters lay lines along the edge of the fire, they have a simple fire,” she said. “They’re going to come up with a strategy to anchor and flank the fire while it’s small.”Add just a few houses, and “some of the firefighters are going to go to the houses and start prepping to protect the properties,” she said. “Now, you have fewer firefighters on the fire. It totally complicates work for the firefighters. And it requires more people.”
Scopa estimated federal agencies would need another 30,000 to 40,000 firefighters to be able to implement full suppression, “and you still wouldn’t be successful.”
Multiple requests for hand crews and engines went unfilled on the Widemouth 2 Fire, Tony DeMasters, incident commander of Great Basin Team 2, told The Tribune. The fire has burned nearly 130,000 acres in western Utah. 
“We’re getting international help,” he continued. “That’s just how severe the fire season is, and we’re only in August. We got another 8, 10, maybe 12 weeks to go.”  
It’s common for resources to be this scarce, DeMasters added, when the Great Basin region and nation are at Preparedness Level 5. “When we go to those planning levels, that means everything is strapped.”The Forest Service has roughly 14,000 employees who manage and respond to fires, including around 11,800 firefighters.
The Wildland Fire Service employs fewer than 6,000 federal personnel and supports around 900 tribal personnel to cover more than 500 million acres of public and tribal lands across the country.
A new fire service 
To create the new U.S. Wildland Fire Service, the Trump administration combined firefighters from four Department of the Interior agencies: Bureau of Land Management, National Park Service, U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and the Bureau of Indian Affairs.“The goal of this is to reduce internal redundancy,” Brock Uhlig, a chief at the new service, told Nevada lawmakers at a May interim committee meeting. “Members of the public will see the exact same product.”By July in Nevada, it was “kind of business as usual and everyone’s still collaborating and responding to fires,” said Ryan Shane, State Forester Firewarden. But, he acknowledged, it was early in the season. “Time is going to tell what improvements we are going to see … or if there are any gaps.”
Utah officials have seen the transition go “very smoothly,” Barnes said. “We haven’t seen any issues with firefighters on the ground or financial resources.”
In Wyoming, the migration of Interior firefighting crews and resources into the new federal agency hasn’t altered what goes down when a wildfire is sparked, said state Fire Management Officer Jarod DeLay, who works closely with the regional chief for the U.S. Wildland Fire Service. They share a goal, he said, of ensuring the transition does not impact on-the-ground firefighting operations.
“They’re working through everything,” DeLay told WyoFile, “but there really hasn’t been any real hiccups.”The “field-level folks” who have spoken with Grassroots Wildland Firefighters, a nonprofit based in Sparks, Nevada, haven’t seen any negative impact, president Riva Duncan told Montana’s Mountain Journal.“But speaking to fire managers, they said it was pretty clunky for them,” Duncan said. “They’ve restructured decision-making authority, so there’s a lot of ‘Where do I go to now if I need something approved?’ There’s not as much communication as folks had hoped for.”
“Clunky” communication may be occurring at times, Fennessy said. “I mean, we’re talking about thousands of people. I’m sure that probably occurs. But that’s not the feedback I’m getting and it’s not from my people.”Officials are still investigating whether the transition played any role in the late June deaths of three federal firefighters who were killed while battling the Knowles Fire in Colorado and a fourth who died later from his injuries. Fennessy said he finds the suggestion that there may be a connection “offensive. It is absolutely wrong. … It’s just ludicrous.”
There is “absolutely zero connection between the rollout, the unification and these fatalities,” he said. “I am close enough to the investigation that is still ongoing, to certainly say that.”The firefighters were part of a helitack crew that got trapped near the Colorado-Utah border when high winds drove small, lightning-started wildfires in Utah. Sydney Watson, 27, of Warrior, Alabama, worked for the Wildland Fire Service, as did a fourth firefighter, Nathan Matthews, 43, of Lincoln, Nebraska, who was injured in the burnover and died later.Emily Barker, 38, of Clinton Township, Michigan, and Nick Hutcherson, 27, of Glendale, Arizona, worked for the Forest Service.

Clockwise from left: wildland firefighters Emily Barker; Nick Hutcherson; Sydney Watson; and Nathan Matthews were killed while working on the Knowles Fire in western Colorado in June. (U.S. Forest Service) 

Duncan stressed that investigations remain ongoing and no conclusions are available. “But fatalities really affect the workforce,” Duncan said. “There’s a lot of fire season left and people are fearful. The investigations take a long time to come out, and it’s frustrating if there are important lessons to learn.”
Fears for the future 
Rep. Andrea Salinas, an Oregon Democrat, pointed out to Schultz in July that removing fire personnel from the four Interior agencies separates them from former colleagues who are responsible for restoring forests and reducing fuels.“This proposal would fracture the critical communications link between land management and fire management,” Salinas said at a July 22 House Agriculture Committee hearing.The disconnect could mean that decisions once made between colleagues will have to be negotiated among agencies, said Brad Washa, an assistant professor of Wildland Fire Science at Utah State University.“Down the road, will [fire personnel] be sitting in a different office and not next to the folks that are managing the natural resource?” asked Washa, a former BLM firefighter.“And that can become an impact when making decisions on how to manage a fire, to what they’re doing fuels work wise … it could also impact just recruiting people from outside a fire to help support the fire effort,” he said.When working together, for example, a land manager could easily alert firefighters to not bulldoze lines in areas that could affect endangered species or cultural resources, he said. That may become more difficult now. “The land management agency might lose some of its ability to exert its authority in managing the natural resource,” Washa said.Professor Larissa Yocom, director of USU’s Utah Forest Restoration Institute, said she also wonders how much input land managers will be able to provide during an active fire — particularly in providing guidance about future times when it would benefit an ecosystem to let a fire burn.
“We do have a lot of science showing that fire is beneficial in a lot of our ecosystems,” she said. “For example, aspen is a tree that a lot of people love, and it thrives after fire. And the lack of fire during the 20th century may be part of the reason that we have been seeing a decline in aspen cover across the West.”These issues are why the National Association of Forest Service Retirees opposes the creation of the new fire agency, president Bill Avey said.“We don’t think wildfire should be divorced from the land — that’s been a policy failure,” he said. “We continue to stand on the fact that this national wildland fire service is the wrong solution.”
But Fennessy argues there is no disconnect. 
“We’ve not moved anybody on the Interior side out of where they are stationed. Offices that hold both land managers and executive firefighters, those offices haven’t changed,” he said. “They talk to each other every day. … I question the motive or intent of those that want to make that argument.” 
Fennessy said his agency recognizes that “land managers are the resource experts” and that they are “intimately involved and engaged.” Fire officials and land managers “need to be in lockstep,” he said, “when we’re doing prescribed fire or preparing for whatever treatment it may be.” 
The Forest Service is undergoing its own reform right now. Its headquarters are moving west from Washington, D.C., to Salt Lake City and regional centers will be closed, with research consolidated in Fort Collins, Colorado. The Forest Service has lost 16% of its workforce since 2024, Salinas noted.“This sweeping reorganization creates more questions than answers and the fact that it’s being implemented right as wildfire season is upon us is alarming,” Salinas told Schultz. “Doing so threatens the Forest Service overall — the loss of staff, and the institutional knowledge they have, should not be casualties in the Trump administration’s reorganization of the Forest Service. Each is too valuable to be lost.”
Few states are better equipped to weather the federal firefighting changes than California. 
California has invested billions in firefighting, a strategy that has carried through multiple administrations, with different emphases at different times. But it all amounts to this: California has its own people and equipment to rely on, including the world’s largest aerial firefighting fleet.
Cal Fire — officially the California Department of Forestry and Fire Protection — is the largest state-run fire department. As California experienced some of its most destructive wildfires on record, Cal Fire’s staffing skyrocketed — climbing past more than 12,000 employees, according to the agency.
It now employs more wildland firefighters than any agency in the world besides the U.S. Forest Service, according to a 2025 white paper led by researchers with Stanford University’s Climate & Energy Policy Program.
CalFire firefighters carry a fire hose up a hillside during the Sandy Fire in Simi Valley on May 18, 2026. (Zin Chiang/For CalMatters)
The department is primarily responsible for rural, mostly privately owned wildlands that make up about one-third of the state’s acreage. 
But federal agencies are tasked with protecting about half of the state, and California’s leadership is concerned about the Trump administration’s reorganization of the Forest Service, its staff cuts and its closure of research facilities.
“While I understand the intention to operate a more efficient federal agency, many of these changes could impact our state’s wildfire readiness and create added public safety risks,” California Secretary of Natural Resources Wade Crowfoot said in a May letter to U.S. Secretary of Agriculture Brook Rollins.Adequate investment and attention to federal lands in California, along with “strong collaboration” with state agencies, “is critical to protect California’s communities, economies, and natural resources from catastrophic fire,” Crowfoot wrote. 
No simple answer
The Department of Agriculture’s 2027 budget proposes transferring the departments, which includes the Forest Service, wildland firefighting resources and responsibilities into the new Wildland Fire Service.
The department awarded a $1.16 million contract to study consolidating all federal wildland fire operations into the new agency, according to a statement on Aug. 4. The department expects the report to be complete by Feb. 15, 2027, which means its results won’t be available for the fiscal 2027 budgeting that begins in September.The idea of unifying the Forest Service with other agencies would challenge the “cultural difference in how we approach fires,” said Andy Norman, who retired from firefighting for the Bridger-Teton National Forest in 2023 after a 37-year career.“Fire is considered a land management activity. It’s addressed in the forest plans,” he said, which call for occasionally managing wildfires rather than immediately extinguishing them in designated wilderness and in some backcountry settings.The Forest Service extinguishes more than 95% of the fires on its forests, Scopa said, but pursuing full suppression permanently wouldn’t be realistic.
“There’s no simple answer. We’re not gonna put [out] all the fires,” she said. “We’re never going to be successful. … The environment is not conducive to that, the fuels are not conducive to that, the staffing is not conducive to that.”
— Amy Alonzo, The Nevada Independent, Rachel Becker, CalMatters, Robert Chaney, Montana Free Press / Mountain Journal, Mike Koshmrl, WyoFile, Brooke Larsen, The Salt Lake Tribune, Joseph T. O’Connor,  Montana Free Press / Mountain Journal, Olivia Prentzel, The Colorado Sun

The post The Trump administration upended how we fight wildfires. Then came the West’s worst fire season in years. appeared first on WyoFile .

name: WyoFile
title: What is the ‘10 a.m. Rule?’ Controversial firefighting strategy could be back
authors: Robert Chaney, Montana Free Press / Mountain Journal
description:
As ‘10 a.m. Rule’ resurfaces, Forest Service chief says ‘every fire has a full-suppression strategy.’ 
The post What is the ‘10 a.m. Rule?’ Controversial firefighting strategy could be back appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
Wildfires once ran on deadlines.
After a series of catastrophic blazes in the early 20th century, the U.S. Forest Service sought to show it was able to control and protect forests under its care. In 1933, the agency mandated the “10 a.m. Rule,” declaring that any wildland fire should be extinguished by 10 a.m. the day after it was reported.
Snuffing all fires quickly, the agency reasoned, would prevent disasters like the Big Burn of 1910. That incident scorched more than 3 million acres along the Montana-Idaho border during a 36-hour rampage, killing at least 85 people and destroying five towns.
Unlike earthquakes or tornadoes, wildfires have weaknesses. We can suppress flames with water or retardant chemicals. Wildland fire crews remove fuels with hand tools and bulldozers. Sometimes they use tactical burnouts — literally fighting fire with fire.
These tools can obscure crucial facts about wildfire and reinforce strategies that can backfire.
Tales of heroism following the Big Burn established the Forest Service as a necessary government service. As New York Times reporter Tim Egan put it, “To this day, I think that agency owes its existence to this fire.” 
But Egan also described the consequences of that successful effort to control wildfire: “Actively trying to put out every fire left a lot of standing dead timber. So some of the big fires we had in the latter 20th century, including the Yellowstone fires of 1988 and some of the Idaho fires of the late 1990s, and fires still to come, are the result of having timber that probably should have burned every now and then during the seasonal fires.”
Rocky Mountain Research Station scientist David Calkin described the phenomenon as the “Wildfire Paradox” in a 2013 article published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. “Using wildfire suppression to eliminate large and damaging wildfires ensures the inevitable occurrence of these fires,” Calkin wrote. “Wildfire suppression, effective 95% to 98% of the time, inevitably leads to ecologically significant wildfires with higher intensities and rapid growth that are unable to be suppressed.”
Fire researchers began to notice the paradox in the 1960s, and began implementing “let burn” strategies in remote forests to reduce those fuel loads. The Forest Service modified the “10 a.m. Rule” in 1971 to allow some fires to burn, and officially abandoned the policy in 1978.
Over the following decades, wildfire managers adapted to a changing climate, shifting public opinion and funding challenges. A mid-century moist period began drying out toward the tail of the 20th century. The 1988 fires in and around Yellowstone National Park burned 1.4 million acres in one of America’s best-known landscapes. Colorado’s South Canyon fire in 1994 killed 14 wildland firefighters and prompted major federal fire policy reviews. One of the most consequential shifts was the growing focus on the wildland-urban interface, or WUI — the increasing overlap between private homes and fire-prone landscapes.
Several record-breaking fire seasons in the early 2000s made federal budget watchers aware that the Forest Service was spending more to fight fire than almost anything else in its mission, and frequently didn’t have enough funding to do so. In 2017, federal wildfire suppression costs topped $2 billion  — six times as much as was spent in the 1990s. 
The year 2018 produced one of the worst wildfire seasons in history and included the Camp Fire, which killed more than 80 people in and around Paradise, California.
More recently, political pressure for a more aggressive response to wildfire has renewed fire suppression. 
Last June, President Donald Trump issued an executive order “Empowering Commonsense Wildfire Prevention and Response,” which in its first sentence declared “The devastation of the January 2025 Los Angeles wildfires shocked the American people and highlighted the catastrophic consequences when State and local governments are unable to quickly respond to such disasters.” 
Draft versions of the policy included a return to the 10 a.m. Rule, according to numerous sources in the wildfire community.
“No one was dumb enough to use 10 a.m. policy language, but there was fear of a fire getting away,” said Bobbie Scopa, a 45-year firefighting veteran who worked at the local, state and federal levels and now is vice president of the advocacy group Grassroots Wildland Firefighters. “Anytime you light a fire or purposefully don’t put out a fire, you own it and you own every bad thing that can happen. You’re taking a risk when you do that.”
Draft versions of the Fix Our Forests Act also included a call for full suppression of all wildfires.
Matt Weiner, CEO of the advocacy group Megafire Action, said putting that into law would have had dangerous consequences.
“We were able to get that out of it,” Weiner said. “And long-term, we will push aggressively against the 10 a.m. Rule being included in statute anywhere. We don’t want to just create a suppression super-agency. We want a system that recognizes the need for a lot more beneficial fire on the landscape.”
Nevertheless, at a July 22 hearing before the House Subcommittee on Forestry and Horticulture, Forest Service Chief Tom Schultz told members of Congress his agency remained committed to prioritizing aggressive initial attack on wildfire this year.
“Keeping fire small protects firefighters, communities and also saves funding,” Schultz said. “I assure you every fire has a full-suppression strategy.”
