name: Ohio Capital Journal
title: Ohio high school sports on the installment plan
description: Youth sports have been in the spotlight recently, with even U.S. Senators talking about the high costs and the strain they put on families. While much of the conversation has focused on expensive travel teams and club sports, a growing financial barrier to participation exists within public schools. High school students who want to represent […]
text:
Getty Images photo of high school athletes.Youth sports have been in the spotlight recently, with even U.S. Senators talking about the high costs and the strain they put on families. While much of the conversation has focused on expensive travel teams and club sports, a growing financial barrier to participation exists within public schools.
High school students who want to represent their school are increasingly required to pay to play, with multiple Ohio districts charging fees that reach $500 for each sport a student pursues. According to the Ohio High School Athletic Association, the majority of high schools in Ohio now impose sports participation fees.
More schools are charging higher fees as districts grapple with inadequate state funding and rising costs.
Ohio’s approach to athletic participation fees is essentially the Wild West. There are no applicable state laws or limits on what school districts can charge student athletes and their families. While some districts offer fee waivers, there are no requirements that schools consider a family’s income or their ability to pay.
In the span of a few miles there is a staggering difference in costs and opportunity.
Columbus City Schools, the largest district in the state, does not charge a pay to play fee. But neighboring district Pickerington charges students $345 if they want to represent their community on the playing field.
Next door in Reynoldsburg, students and families are on the hook for a $500 fee per child, per season in order to participate in school sports.
Despite Ohio’s long standing embrace of high school sports, there is no cap across the state on what a large, athletic family might be required to pay.
Affirming a commitment to scholastic sports, state Rep. Gary Click has said that “No student athlete should be limited by their zip code.” But the reality is your zip code and the size of your wallet determine if you can play high school sports in Ohio.
For families in the Reynoldsburg school district, Click’s lofty words are overshadowed by a harsh reality. The $500 fee puts sports out of reach for many students. The district’s only publicized assistance is a payment plan; parents can pay the fee in two installments of $250. This in a school where the state labels more than 65% of the students economically disadvantaged.
Ohio is putting fees in the way of educational opportunity. Research studies have found students who participate in high school sports get better grades, are more likely to graduate high school and more likely to pursue education after high school.
Parents recognize the benefits sports provide. In a recent nationwide survey, 84% of parents in the U.S. agreed that participation in sports positively affects students’ performance in school.
Not only do parents see sports as beneficial, but so do the very school officials raising the cost to play. The entire school board in Mentor signed onto a statement declaring access to extracurriculars including athletics “another necessary component to producing well-rounded, successful young people, who are prepared for life after graduation.” Necessary or not, the Mentor school board raised their sports participation fee by 20% this year.
The survey of parents shows their support for their children participating in high school sports is nearly unanimous when there is no fee. When fees reach the levels charged by Reynoldsburg, however, most parents say they would discourage their children from pursuing a sport.
In fact, only in households making over $100,000 per year was there still a majority willing to encourage sports participation. Notable too, 87% of all parents said school-sponsored athletics should be funded through a district’s general budget rather than through imposing participation fees.
Ohio has a law requiring financial literacy be taught to every high school student, and a new law requires teaching something called the “success steps.” It is long past time for Ohio lawmakers to recognize that the financially sound path to student success is to fund scholastic athletics and put an end to pay to play.
Katie Niven is a Benton Scholar and Division 1 student athlete (softball) at Colgate University and is a 2025 graduate of Thomas Worthington High School.

name: Florida Phoenix
title: For two years, Florida Juvenile Justice department ducked records request
description: Nearly two years since the Department of Juvenile Justice received a records request from the Florida Phoenix, it remains unfulfilled.  Despite fulfilling a nearly identical request in 2024 within three months, the department has not provided a reason for the nearly two-year delay on the follow-up request, or an estimated time it may be completed. […]
text:
Florida Department of Juvenile Justice HQ in Tallahassee. (Photo by Michael Moline/Florida Phoenix)Nearly two years since the Department of Juvenile Justice received a records request from the Florida Phoenix, it remains unfulfilled. 
Despite fulfilling a nearly identical request in 2024 within three months, the department has not provided a reason for the nearly two-year delay on the follow-up request, or an estimated time it may be completed.
According to Bobby Block, executive director of the First Amendment Foundation, not returning public records requests is increasingly common, and is “not good for democracy.”
“The whole point of transparent government is to basically allow the public to participate and to see what decisions are being made in people’s names. And if you don’t, then this is no longer government of the people, by the people, and for the people,” Block told the Phoenix. 
“It’s government for, of, and by politicians who act behind closed doors, and that’s not how it’s supposed to be.”
The department fulfilled the Phoenix’s August 2024 records request for anonymized behavior reports. In a two-part series, drawing upon those records and interviews, the Phoenix reported that the department’s new school program enabled children in juvenile detention to watch porn on state-issued laptops and was running over budget by $10 million.
New school model enables incarcerated kids to watch porn, public records show

In October 2024, a month before the 2024 two-part series was published, the Phoenix requested behavior reports for August through October of that year.
The department acknowledged the request 12 minutes after receiving it. As of Friday, the request remained unfulfilled.
Another request made in February 2025, for behavior reports between October 2024 and February 2025, remains unfulfilled.
A March 23, 2026, Phoenix request for a statutorily mandated annual financial report also has not been returned.
Numerous follow-ups to the department’s communications director and general counsel seeking the status of the requests either went unanswered or yielded answers from the communications director such as, “Your request is still in process,” and, “I have no updates at this time.”
The department has not provided a reason for the nearly two-year delay.
Eric Hall, then-secretary of the Department of Juvenile Justice, told the Legislature in March 2025 that the access to porn, among other technical problems, were “growing pains” for the department’s then year-old unified education delivery method.
In November 2025, the new secretary, Matt Walsh, told the Legislature the students’ access to porn on state-funded devices had been addressed with “immediate” attention and intervention from the department and the Florida Virtual School, a legislatively authorized online teaching center under contract to run education programs for DJJ centers statewide. 
However, the department has yet to provide public records verifying those claims.
DJJ did not respond to requests for comment on this article.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
 ’Once upon a time’

State law requires agencies to make records “open for personal inspection and copying by any person,” calling it a “duty” of agencies. The Florida Constitution gives “every person” the right to “inspect or copy any public record.”
“It doesn’t matter what purposes you want them for, it doesn’t matter what party you belong to, it doesn’t matter whether you believe in democracy or you believe in something else, you are entitled to public information, to public records in the state of Florida. And it’s just unfortunately not something that is being universally respected right now,” Block said.
“Once upon a time, the default setting was disclosure; the default setting now is to delay, to deny, or ignore.”
A Tampa Bay Times editor laid out that publication’s public records hang-ups, including exorbitant charges for records requests, writing that “hefty invoices and delays are also tactical, designed to dissuade citizens (and reporters in cash-strapped, busy newsrooms) from sticking with it and getting access to documents.” 
A Tampa Bay Times story about insurance company profits sent a buzz around the Florida Capitol in 2025. The story focused on records that the state took two years to return to the Times reporter, delaying any chance of legislative action for at least that long.
In the “last decade, and definitely particularly under the DeSantis administration, they treat public records requests as an option — as not a right but a privilege they feel that they get to decide who gets,” Block said.
Government transparency “serves everybody,” Block said.
“I think politicians whose actions are open have a greater level of trust, and I think open government serves everybody, and I think access to public records is something that politicians should instinctively want to see,” he added.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: A legacy behind the heels: My 38 years with Nancy Wyman
description: Nancy Wyman was a gift to the State of Connecticut, a trailblazer who proved that one could be both a fierce advocate and a compassionate and loving friend.
text:
When a political giant passes, the public discourse naturally gravitates toward the resume, the titles held, legislation enacted and all of the barriers broken. 
In the wake of former Lt. Gov. Nancy Wyman’s passing, the tributes have rightfully poured in, celebrating a woman who was as famous for her sharp fiscal mind and her ability to work across party lines, as she was for her signature high heels, her love of dancing, and her ubiquitous Diet Coke… and let’s not forget the large cup of ice on the side.

Mark Ojakian

Yet as I reflect on the 38 years I spent as her close friend and political teammate, I find that her true legacy lies not just in her public service but in the profound depth of her soul —an inner compass that guided both her personal life and political convictions.
Nancy was more than a colleague and friend to me: she was a sister. While the world saw a powerhouse politician in a petite body, I saw a woman of immense kindness and compassion who consistently placed the needs of her family and of Connecticut’s citizens above her own ambitions. Her policy decisions were never mere political calculations but extensions of her personal values. Whether advocating for high-quality education for every child, affordable and accessible health care for all, dignity for seniors, support for veterans and working families, or civil rights for the LGBTQ+ community, Nancy led with her heart.
Our journey began in 1988. I was a legislative liaison and she was the co-chair of the General Assembly’s Education Committee. We spent those early days debating policy, often disagreeing, only to resolve our differences over a shared tuna melt and French fries in her office . The ability to bridge divides with humanity and a simple meal was the hallmark of her character.
Our bond deepened during a period of personal tragedy for me. After I lost my partner in a car accident, recognizing my need to find some purpose in life amidst my grief, Nancy asked me to volunteer for her long-shot campaign for State Comptroller. What began as a mere distraction evolved into a grueling but exciting tour of every corner of Connecticut. She claimed to have taught me to appreciate the essence of county fairs, introducing me to oxen pulls and cow chip bingo events. She walked in every parade imaginable as she campaigned in her stilettos and informed folks who lined the streets that if she could control her heels she would control the finances of the state of Connecticut.
I watched her defy the skeptics who thought a woman couldn’t serve as the state’s “fiscal guardian.” I stood with her at the State Democratic Convention when she refused to buckle to party bosses as her supporters chanted “No Deals Wyman.” She went on to become the first woman to hold the office of State Comptroller, serving with distinction for 16 years. I had the honor and privilege of serving as her Deputy for those 16 years. She was a mentor to me during that time and I owe much of my success in the later stages of my career to her willingness to guide me.
On the campaign trail, I learned the true measure of the woman. I learned how much family meant to her- a devotion so essential to her identity that her first TV ad proudly identified her as a “mother and grandmother,” despite the fact that female politicians are sometimes discouraged from highlighting those roles. 
We became fixtures in each other’s families, navigating the heights of joy and the depths of loss together. She taught me the nuances of the Jewish faith, from proper etiquette of a shiva call to the correct greetings on Yom Kippur. She would remind me that you wish someone an easy fast on that high holy day and not a good fast, because as she would say “ Mark, there is nothing good about a fast.” I returned the favor by introducing her to Armenian traditions and perhaps a finer grade of wine than she was used to.
As I look through the decades of photographs, I am struck by the longevity and vibrancy of our friendship and political alliance. Though there is profound sadness in her absence from my life I find myself laughing out loud at the memories of our shared adventures.
Nancy Wyman was a gift to the State of Connecticut, a trailblazer who proved that one could be both a fierce advocate and a compassionate and loving friend. I was so fortunate to have her by my side for nearly 40 years and we are all better off for the incredible mark she left on all of our lives.
Mark Ojakian is a former Deputy Comptroller, former chief of staff to Gov. Dannel Malloy, and former president of the CT State College and University System. He now lives in Rancho Mirage, Calif.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: The missing piece of CT’s affordability puzzle — food
description: While Connecticut is a leader on many policy areas, food is one area where we unfortunately lag behind our fellow Northeastern states.
text:
In Connecticut and across the country, affordability is the issue of the day. 
A national poll from December 2025 found that the “cost of living” was by far the top issue facing the country. This past session, the Connecticut General Assembly made many sweeping proposals focused on making the state more affordable.
More specifically, major proposed and enacted legislation from both parties in the General Assembly’s 2025 and 2026 sessions has focused on key components of affordability, including housing , childcare , healthcare , taxes , and more. The bills that have passed have made major strides towards addressing key components of the affordability issue, with the Early Childhood Education Endowment being one significant example. 
While there is still more work to be done on all of these issues, there is one key component of affordability that impacts all residents but is relatively overlooked at the moment: food.
Food and affordability
Food is a key part of affordability because it is one of the largest expenses every household needs to pay. The United Way of Connecticut’s ALICE Survival Budget estimates what different size households would need to make just to get by in this state. 
Among the eight example households listed on the ALICE Survival Budget web page, food is always the second or third largest expense . The only category consistently more costly than food is housing.
Food has also gotten significantly more expensive in the last several years. According to the U.S. Department of Agriculture, national food prices rose 9.9% in 2022, which was the highest food inflation rate since 1979. Those prices kept rising each following year, and as these increases happened, one national survey found that in 2025 “more than one in four working-age adults used credit cards to purchase groceries and experienced repayment challenges” with another 5% relying on payday loans. 
These challenges have driven rising food insecurity, with Feeding America stating Connecticut has the highest food insecurity rate (15.3% or ~560,000) in all of the Northeast.
Current state of food policy in Connecticut
While Connecticut is a leader on many policy areas, food is one area where we unfortunately lag behind our fellow Northeastern states. There was undeniable progress this year, with the state enacting universal free school breakfast in budget adjustments for FY27. Additionally, the governor has released a total of $76.74 million in one-time funding for food and farm-related programs from the “Federal Cuts Response Fund” created by Special Act 25-1 .
However, there are a number of factors working against the state despite this recent progress. First, $76.74 million in one-time funding can’t fully offset the estimated $182 million in federal cuts for food in Connecticut across FY26 and 27. Second, Feeding America’s 15.3% food insecurity rate for Connecticut is from 2024, before these cuts took place ( DataHaven’s 2025 estimate was an even higher 16%). Third, Connecticut is starting well behind many neighboring states on food spending. We entered 2026 spending less per capita on all 10 food security programs, 11 farm and food system, and 30 grants and earmarks in our state budget than Massachusetts, Vermont, New York, and New Jersey spent on just three of their biggest food security programs. For these reasons, significant progress on making food more affordable will likely require more comprehensive state action.

Credit: State of Food Insecurity Report / CT.gov

How food policy can improve affordability
There are a number of ways that a more comprehensive coordinated food policy framework could make it easier and cheaper for Connecticut residents to put food on the table. 
This framework would ensure dedicated annual funding from the state to both provide households with resources to afford increased prices today and invest in a robust local food system to create downward pressure on food prices (and related costs) in the long-term. 
A few examples of immediate support include universal free school lunch to remove five meals a week from at-home grocery bills and a state minimum SNAP benefit that might ensure households get enough support to reflect the true cost of food. A few examples of the long-term food systems investments include funding community food hubs that could aggregate and distribute local food at scale, local purchasing requirements on state food spending to give local producers predictable income that could allow them to invest in expanding, and a food business incubator program to ensure every neighborhood has high quality grocery stores so no one needs to drive or take the bus across town.
 These are far from the only policy options, but the goal of these examples is to illustrate that by prioritizing food policy as a whole, Connecticut can make major progress on affordability.       
 It is important to clearly state that the purpose of this article is absolutely not to suggest that the state should prioritize food policy   instead   of   childcare, housing, taxes, utilities, and more. Instead, food policy should be prioritized   along   with   these other areas to form a comprehensive affordability policy, where no basic necessity is left out. If rent goes down but grocery bills go up, households will still be facing strain. If they both go down (along with other basic needs), it would be a substantial step towards a Connecticut that is affordable for all.   
Christian Duborg is the Food & Nutrition Policy Analyst at the Commission on Women, Children, Seniors, Equity, and Opportunity (CWCSEO), a nonpartisan legislative agency of the Connecticut General Assembly.

name: Rhode Island Current
title: Electric Boat cheers move into new campus at former Crystal Mall in Waterford, Conn.
description: This article first appeared on CT Mirror and is republished here under a Creative Commons Attribution-NoDerivatives 4.0 International License. Windy skies and a steady downpour weren’t enough to dampen spirits in Waterford on Friday morning as local officials, construction workers and business leaders gathered to celebrate the groundbreaking of General Dynam[...]
text:
Speakers including, from left, Joe Toner, executive director of the Connecticut State Building Trades Council, Rep. Joe Courtney, Mark Rayha, president of General Dynamics Electric Boat, Sen. Richard Blumenthal, Rob Brule, Waterford first selectman, and Matt Pugliese, deputy commissioner of the Department of Economic and Community Development, toss dirt during a groundbreaking ceremony at Electric Boat’s Waterford Campus, the former Crystal Mall on Friday, Aug. 21, 2026. (Photo by Sarah Gordon/CT Mirror)This article first appeared on CT Mirror and is republished here under a Creative Commons Attribution-NoDerivatives 4.0 International License.
Windy skies and a steady downpour weren’t enough to dampen spirits in Waterford on Friday morning as local officials, construction workers and business leaders gathered to celebrate the groundbreaking of General Dynamics Electric Boat’s new campus.
Work on the roughly 800,000 square foot facility, which will reuse the former Crystal Mall complex, is well underway. The majority of the mall was acquired last year, and the remaining tenants moved out of the building in the spring.
When renovation work is completed, the campus will house office and software development space as well as facilities for training and workforce development. Some 4,000 to 5,000 employees are expected to work at the campus, which is expected to open in 2027.
The facility will make Electric Boat, a defense contractor responsible for supplying the military with submarines of varying sizes, the largest employer in Waterford. The company recently celebrated a $76.6 billion contract with the U.S. Navy, one of the largest shipbuilding contracts ever awarded.
The contract, which comes amid a hiring push for the company, further cements the need for Electric Boat’s expansion, speakers said Friday.
“This groundbreaking signifies our long-term commitment in Connecticut but also in  all of you and all the workforce,” said Electric Boat President Mark Rayha.
But speakers also acknowledged that the campus marks something even greater for southeastern Connecticut: a new economic opportunity, one that could usher in a wave of growth and once-in-a-generation investment in the local workforce.
It’s a new chance for revitalization and commercial activity in the region, built using a space that supported earlier waves of development. Now, as renovation work begins, supporters say that the reused mall will become the backbone of the region’s economic comeback.
“For decades, the Crystal Mall was part of the fabric of our community. We shopped here, we worked here, we brought our families here,” said Waterford First Selectman Rob Brule. “Today we aren’t here to talk about what this property used to be. We’re here to celebrate what it’s about to become.”
 Crystal Mall is trying on something new

The mall redevelopment, DECD deputy commissioner Matt Pugliese noted, is one of the largest reuses of an existing property in the state. The redevelopment work comes as DECD looks to support projects around the state that will breathe new life into old buildings, part of a larger effort.

Rob Brule, Waterford first selectman, speaks during a groundbreaking ceremony at Electric Boat’s Waterford Campus, the former Crystal Mall, on Friday, Aug. 21, 2026. (Photo by Sarah Gordon/CT Mirror)
A place like the Crystal Mall, speakers said, is a natural fit for this work.
“Malls simply cannot meet the kind of commerce that we see today in the United States of America,” said U.S. Sen. Richard Blumenthal. “Electric Boat, with typical ingenuity and innovation, is, in effect, putting new wine in old bottles.”
When completed, the Waterford campus will complement submarine production efforts by providing additional space for administrative staff, software developers and new trainees. Submarine production work will continue in nearby Groton, where Electric Boat’s shipyard is located.
As renovations continue, parts of the Waterford campus will house temporary training spaces for new employees. A more permanent location on the campus known as SAIL, or the Shipbuilding Advanced Institute for Learning, is set to open in the near future.
When fully operational, SAIL is expected to support close to 400 shipbuilders and will also include support for welding, advanced technology work and additional innovations.
“We’re really celebrating bringing this place back to life,” said Courtney Murphy, Electric Boat’s director of talent acquisition, workforce development and compensation. “Seeing this plan take shape and now become reality is truly inspiring because it is more than just a groundbreaking. It’s the start of a new chapter in how we grow, train and support the shipbuilders who carry our mission forward.”
The growth comes as the company continues a larger expansion, including hiring a projected 8,000 workers this year, more than double what it hired in 2025.
And in a region that has long struggled to find stable economic footing, the hope is that Electric Boat’s growth will have effects that will be felt across Connecticut more broadly.
“This is just going to be one of those milestones that our children and grandchildren are going to experience,” said U.S. Rep. Joe Courtney. “It’s a big deal.”
 A deeper economic shift

The hoped-for economic transformation, coming to a region that has long relied on the manufacturing industry, is expected to bring significant change, and thousands of new workers, to the area.
Local officials are gearing up to meet the demand and figuring out how to support the workers expected to flood into the region in the coming years. The region is facing a housing shortage, with low stock and rising costs squeezing the market further. The area needs thousands of new homes to support the expected workforce.
Still, the hope is that the influx will usher in a larger wave of economic activity in the region, rippling out from Electric Boat and driving increases in tourism, recreational activities and other industries.

Rep. Joe Courtney speaks during a groundbreaking ceremony at Electric Boat’s Waterford Campus, the former Crystal Mall, on Friday, Aug. 21, 2026. (Photo by Sarah Gordon/CT Mirror)
Electric Boat says that for now, its focus is on meeting its hiring and workforce goals.
Local officials, meanwhile, say they are prepared to do their part as the region looks ahead. Hundreds of new housing units are in development, with more on the way.
“We’ll support responsible housing. We’ll invest in infrastructure. We’ll continue to work closely with DECD. We’ll support our businesses and schools,” Brule said. “Growth isn’t about getting bigger; it’s about getting it right.”

name: Mississippi Today
title: Approximately 100 detainees protest inside CoreCivic-owned Natchez ICE facility after hot food and hot water are halted
description: A sign alerts drivers to the Adams County Correctional Center in rural Adams County, Miss. on March 19, 2026.
text:
Mukta Joshi is an investigative reporter at Mississippi Today. She is spending a year as a New York Times Local Investigations fellow examining immigration and criminal justice issues. She can be reached at mukta.joshi@nytimes.com.
About a hundred men held in an immigrant detention center in Natchez began a protest over the weekend against poor living conditions and spoiled, measly meals in the facility, according to those being held there. The protest began after facility staff put signs on residential unit doors saying they were conducting maintenance on the gas system, so detainees would not receive hot food or hot water until further notice. The electricity supply in the facility had also been getting interrupted at night, several detainees reported. 
A visual representation of a two-person cell containing three beds at the Adams County Correctional Center in Natchez. Credit: Bethany Atkinson
This protest in the Adams County Correctional Center comes after an unprecedented population spike and complaints of crowding in the facility, amid a national surge in arrests by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement. Three weeks prior, nearly 70 detainees had submitted a petition to the warden, demanding an end to the practice of housing three people in two-person cells and making people sleep in beds on the floor, with many having to sleep with their heads close to the toilet bowls.
Representatives for CoreCivic did not respond to a request for explanation about the availability of hot food and hot water in time for publication. This story will be updated if they respond. 
One detainee, Melvin Funez, reported Saturday evening that his fellow detainees were outside the cafeteria “striking” because of the “meager rations” that were being served. Lunch that day consisted of two flour tortillas and sliced bologna, several detainees reported.  
“The protest was organized by the people in Pod C,” said another detainee, Johan Calderon, in Spanish. “We went out to eat with them, and when we saw the garbage food they were giving us, we stood by them and joined together to protest in solidarity.” Calderon said around 80 to 100 from two housing pods were protesting. 
The protesting detainees placed their food on the floor “as a sign that it is inedible,” said another detainee. He, along with three others, spoke on the condition of anonymity because they feared retaliation. 
Some detainees then began damaging the surrounding property, such as mail boxes, said another person who spoke on the condition of anonymity, though two detainees who participated maintained that the protest remained peaceful throughout. 
Facility staff in riot gear dispersed the protest soon after. The facility’s special response team “sprayed” some detainees and threw others to the ground before entering the dorms and locking the doors, Funez said. Some said the substance that was sprayed was pepper spray, others said it was tear gas. 
Three detainees said facility staff handed them dry cookies and ramen, well past midnight, as their dinner. Funez said it was “to make up for the lackluster food.” 
“We accepted it, but that does not make up for everything we are going through here,” one detainee said. 
The Guardian reported on Aug. 14 that a “mystery gas leak” in the same facility had led to the air conditioning being switched off amid a heat wave, which sickened many detainees who were then denied medical care. On Saturday, Calderon said the source of the gas leak still hadn’t been located. 
The situation had not improved on Sunday. For breakfast, detainees received cereal and sour milk, said Eloisa Deorta, the wife of one detainee who, along with others, threw the milk in the garbage. Deorta said the last time she had come to the facility for visitation, her husband had been served “hot dogs that were green.” Andrei Zykov, a detainee from Russia, said the facility often serves food that “looks like meat,” but isn’t. 
The written notice of the gas leak maintenance didn’t have information about when it would be fixed, Zykov said. “Just says, ‘thanks for cooperation.’”

name: Nebraska Examiner
title: Nebraska Democrats vote not to fill vacancy for Senate race
description: The approved motion continues the Democratic strategy of clearing the field for nonpartisan U.S. Senate candidate Dan Osborn.
text:
Cutouts at an Omaha office of the Nebraska Democratic Party on April 3, 2026. (Juan Salinas II/ Nebraska Examiner) LINCOLN — The Nebraska Democratic Central Committee voted Sunday not to fill the vacancy caused when Cindy Burbank dropped out of the Senate race.
The committee approved a motion not to fill the party ballot line for the race – continuing the Democratic strategy of clearing the field for nonpartisan U.S. Senate candidate Dan Osborn.
There was only one objection. Crystal Rhoades tried to offer an amendment to nominate Kishla Askins, who was a candidate in the 2nd Congressional District Democratic primary, to replace Burbank, but it was ruled out of order. Rhoades, who is the Douglas County District Court clerk, was also a candidate in that primary.
The committee vote happened amid a lawsuit by William Forbes, who lost to Burbank in the Senate primary. 
A Lancaster County district judge earlier declined to grant Forbes a temporary injunction to force the party to replace Burbank. Judge Susan Strong said Forbes was unlikely to succeed in forcing the party to fill the spot. 
A court hearing is scheduled Monday morning in the case.

Party Chairwoman Jane Kleeb wrote in her court affidavit for the lawsuit that deciding not to fill the vacancy “would align with NDP’s organizational strategy and political desires to oust Republican Senator Ricketts and ensure that Nebraskans enjoy more diversified political representation in Congress.” 
Burbank was among candidates accused of being a “plant” to help either Osborn or incumbent Republican U.S. Sen. Pete Ricketts, an allegation all have denied. Burbank filed to withdraw one day after the secretary of state verified Osborn’s petition signatures to be on the fall ballot.
While the race is technically a three-person contest, Legal Marijuana NOW U.S. Senate candidate Mike Marvin suspended his campaign and endorsed Osborn last week. The race between Osborn and Ricketts has turned state politics upside down with multiple lawsuits surrounding it.
The candidate list in the Senate race isn’t set in stone because there might be two new state political parties — pending a state Supreme Court ruling. 
The general election is Nov. 3.
Examiner Reporter Zach Wendling contributed to this report.

outlet: News From The States - Fair. Fearless. Free.
title: Race cars speed through D.C. in finale of Trump-backed Freedom 250 series
text:
WASHINGTON — IndyCar took over the streets of the nation’s capital for the Freedom 250 Grand Prix, the last in a series of events coordinated and promoted by President Donald Trump to mark the 250th anniversary of the United States.Just over two dozen racers zipped through a 1.66-mile course, reaching speeds up to 190 miles per hour as they traced a course down Pennsylvania and Independence avenues, crossing the National Mall twice, for the first-ever IndyCar series event in Washington, D.C.Trump’s motorcade traveled on the course down Pennsylvania Avenue ahead of the race, and the president waved the green flag at 1:10 p.m Eastern to start the 147 laps.Several military aircraft crossed the sky shortly before the race, including flyovers featuring a B-2 bomber and Air Force One.

 







Air Force One and fighter jets flew over Pennsylvania Avenue ahead of the NTT IndyCar Series Freedom 250 Grand Prix in Washington, D.C., on Sunday, Aug. 23, 2026. (Photo by Ashley Murray/States Newsroom)

Thousands gathered along the course fencing with close-up views. Many won free tickets via drawing earlier in the summer. Scott and Jackie Cunningham paid for a VIP Champions package and traveled from Salt Lake City for the experience.“I love this street, the venue. This is phenomenal,” said Jackie, 62. “We’re so thrilled to be here, and so thankful to President Trump for getting this organized.” 

 







Team Penske mechanics worked before the Freedom 250 Grand Prix. (Photo by Ashley Murray/States Newsroom)

The couple was rooting for star driver and “soon-to-be champion” Alex Palou, Scott, 67, said as they walked around the paddock area where team crews work on the cars ahead of the race.“We are excited for him and his success, and also excited to see some of the other teams out here, like the McLaren team. One of my favorites because I'm also a big Formula One fan,” Scott said.Bryan Bystol, 25, the strength and conditioning coach for team Rahal Letterman Lanigan, sat for a quick lunch with fellow crew members outside the team tent in the paddock. The team is based in Zionsville, Indiana.An IndyCar race through Washington, D.C., was the final event in President Trump's Freedom 250 series to celebrate the 250th anniversary of the Declaration of Independence. (Video by Ashley Murray/States Newsroom)  “My responsibility when we're in the shop is to train the drivers, the pit crew guys, everybody in the shop to improve their performance,” Bystol told States Newsroom.The team trainer takes the drivers and crew through Pilates courses and other conditioning, with a main focus on core muscles.“These street races are pretty physical. Even though there is power steering, for them to be able to keep turning their car back and forth on its tight turns. It's really physically demanding,” Bystol said.

 







An IndyCar races along Pennsylvania Avenue. (Photo by Ashley Murray/States Newsroom)

The Freedom 250 Grand Prix was the last among a series of events organized by the Trump administration for the nation’s semiquincentennial. Freedom 250 is distinct from the bipartisan America250 commission created by Congress in 2016 to plan programming around the 250th anniversary of the signing of the Declaration of Independence. The Trump-backed Freedom 250 received some federal money through the Republican “big, beautiful” law in 2025, but is mostly funded through private contributions. Michigan-based Penske Corp. was the primary sponsor of Sunday’s grand prix.

 







Actors with Fox Sports Networks played Abraham Lincoln and Thomas Jefferson as race car drivers. (Photo by Ashley Murray/States Newsroom)

name: Louisiana Illuminator
title: Ruston girl, 8, dies from brain-eating amoeba infection
description: Lillian Smart, who health officials believe contracted a brain-eating amoeba from swimming in a North Louisiana lake, died Saturday at a Ruston hospital from an infection linked to the pathogen. She had turned 8 years old a day earlier. “The injuries to her brain were too severe for her little body to recover from,” the […]
text:
Lillian Smart, 8, of Ruston died Saturday, Aug. 22, 2026, after being infected with Naegleria fowleri, an amoeba that feeds on brain tissue. State health officials believe she was exposed while swimming in Lake Claiborne. (Photo courtesy Smart family)Lillian Smart, who health officials believe contracted a brain-eating amoeba from swimming in a North Louisiana lake, died Saturday at a Ruston hospital from an infection linked to the pathogen. She had turned 8 years old a day earlier.
“The injuries to her brain were too severe for her little body to recover from,” the Smart family said in a statement posted Sunday morning on Facebook. “Everyone did everything they could to keep her here. We are heartbroken and honestly do not know what to do next. How do we put one foot in front of the other without our girl?”
In a news release Wednesday morning, the Louisiana Department of Health reported a state resident had been hospitalized after becoming infected with Naegleria fowleri, an amoeba that feeds on brain tissue. State officials have yet to confirm Lillian was the infected patient, but the Smart family confirmed on social media she was in the pediatric intensive care unit of a Ruston hospital and encouraged prayers for her recovery.
The health department said the infection was likely acquired when the girl was swimming in Lake Claiborne shortly before her illness.
This is believed to be the fifth death attributed to Naegleria fowleri in Louisiana since 2011.
The most recent fatality occurred in St. Bernard Parish in 2013, when a Drake Smith Jr., 4, contracted the amoeba while playing on a slip-and-slide. Officials confirmed presence of the amoeba in the household’s water, but tests for the pathogen in the water system were negative. However, the parish did detect low levels of chlorine and immediately treated the water system.
Two years earlier, a St. Bernard Parish man died from an infection after using tap water for a sinus rinse, and a DeSoto Parish woman perished after using tap water there for similar treatment.
Naegleria fowleri causes primary amoebic meningoencephalitis, an extremely rare brain infection that can happen when water travels up the nasal canal and reaches the brain. The amoeba cannot cause an infection if it is swallowed.
Naegleria fowleri is not found in saltwater or in properly chlorinated pools. Infection symptoms typically begin with headache, fever, nausea and vomiting before progressing to a stiff neck, seizures and coma before death within about a week or two. Symptoms typically appear within about five days after an infection and are fatal in 97% of cases, according to the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and prevention.
Nationwide, the CDC reported two cases of primary amebic meningoencephalitis last year. The U.S. count has exceeded six cases just twice since 1937, according to the agency.
Of the 173 infections documented in the past 90 years, nearly 91% have occurred during the months of July and August.

name: South Dakota Searchlight
title: South Dakota’s cybersecurity program is running out of time, money as local governments face attacks
description: Pennington County residents haven’t been able to access some services since a cyberattack knocked out county computer systems in July. The water system in Rapid City, which is part of Pennington County, was among the first of dozens of utilities targeted in a nationwide wave of cyberattacks this summer. The attackers did not access its […]
text:
(Getty Images)Pennington County residents haven’t been able to access some services since a cyberattack knocked out county computer systems in July.
The water system in Rapid City, which is part of Pennington County, was among the first of dozens of utilities targeted in a nationwide wave of cyberattacks this summer. The attackers did not access its network in Rapid City, city officials said.
Mitchell, meanwhile, is recovering from its own breach, which left city staff without computer access.
The three incidents — all hitting South Dakota local governments within weeks of each other — underscore a vulnerability that state officials have spent years and millions of dollars trying to address.
Local governments hold sensitive taxpayer data, but often lack the staff, budget or expertise to protect it from cyberattacks. A 2025 report by the Multi-State Information Sharing and Analysis Center found that 68% of state, local, tribal and territorial governments lack the budget to address major cybersecurity priorities, and that small and rural communities are especially vulnerable.
A state-funded program in South Dakota is working to close that gap — but time and money are running short.
State funding in place of declined federal funding
SecureSD is a $7 million program run by the South Dakota Attorney General’s Office and Dakota State University that delivers cybersecurity tools, training and technical support to local governments.
Lawmakers launched the program with funds in 2024 in response to Gov. Kristi Noem rejecting a piece of $1 billion in cybersecurity grants to states. Noem spokesman Ian Fury told South Dakota Searchlight at the time that the grants were “wasteful spending,” adding the administrative burden of the grant “would have far exceeded the allowable administrative cost.”
That 2022 four-year federal grant program, part of the 2021 Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act, faces an uncertain future. Congress extended the program through next month, but did not provide new funding. Efforts to reauthorize the program haven’t cleared both chambers.
After Noem turns down federal cyber money, lawmaker suggests using state funds

South Dakota’s SecureSD program is led by Mike Waldner, who previously directed South Dakota’s centralized education email system.
The program reviews regular vulnerability reports from the Department of Homeland Security for local governments that sign up for the program, which flag issues like outdated software or misconfigured firewalls. It also helps transition local governments to more secure data and email, purchases equipment or contracts with information technology companies to monitor cybersecurity needs, and trains local employees. SecureSD also runs Project Boundary Fence, in which cybersecurity experts test local governments’ defenses and report back on weaknesses.
Most counties have participated in at least one aspect of the program, including Project Boundary Fence, and participation has “ramped up” in recent years, Waldner said.
“It’s like walking through a parking lot and checking doors. We’re not there to steal anything, but we’ll tell people when their doors are unlocked so they can fix it,” Waldner said.
The “hands down number one priority” of SecureSD, Waldner said, is moving local governments onto professionally managed email systems that meet federal security standards — a step up from the patchwork of local setups many counties currently rely on. 
More than half of county-level email addresses, based on a South Dakota Searchlight analysis of county auditor email addresses, are not on government domains, making them more vulnerable to attacks and impersonation. Only verified U.S.-based public sector organizations, including state and local governments, can get a .gov email address, and agencies must have advanced security protocols that make it harder for scammers to copy or fake official government messages.
“We’re working our tails off to remedy that and fix that, for a number of reasons,” Waldner said.
Mislabeled electrical wiring sparked two-day state network shutdown

Rapid City is transitioning to a government, cloud-based email system using SecureSD funding, said Jim Gilbert, the city’s director of information technology. Katy Urban, public information officer with the Pennington County State’s Attorney Office, said the county is in the process of the same transition.
The $7 million in state funding for SecureSD expires June 30, 2028. Waldner said all of it will be spent — but once it runs out, local governments will have to absorb the cost of maintaining any improvements themselves. That uncertainty is “one of the biggest reasons an entity pauses” when considering cybersecurity upgrades, he said.
Waldner has had to prioritize the secure data and email transition as the expiration date nears. He said additional funding could eventually allow the program to expand into other areas, including cybersecurity management and data backup.
“My hope is we can secure funding and not only pay for the data and email solution, but pay for additional cybersecurity functions I know are needed,” Waldner said.
Future of state help for local governments
Sen. Randy Deibert, R-Spearfish, was among the lawmakers who championed the $7 million appropriation in 2024. A former Lawrence County commissioner, he said the program’s upcoming funding deadline was a built-in inflection point for the Legislature.
“It’s probably time to take a good look at that local government cybersecurity program and get an update on it for lawmakers: what’s working, what’s not, what should work,” Deibert said. “We should have some recommendations after a couple of years.”

Sen. Randy Deibert, R-Spearfish, speaks in the Senate chamber at the South Dakota Capitol in Pierre on March 9, 2026. (Photo by Makenzie Huber/South Dakota Searchlight)

Deibert said the original vision wasn’t just funding — it was to offer state-level IT support to counties that couldn’t afford their own, similar to how the state helped school districts move onto secure email systems. He noted that Lawrence County has been fortunate to have a strong IT person on staff, but acknowledged not every county is in that position.
“I’m not certain that throwing dollars at it is the key,” Deibert said.
Lt. Gov. Tony Venhuizen leads the Governor’s Resilience and Infrastructure Task Force. That group is evaluating South Dakota’s critical infrastructure — energy, water, data networks and more — and identifying vulnerabilities to natural disasters and cyberattacks. The task force discussed SecureSD at its August meeting and plans to recommend legislative proposals next session, including how to expand and continue the program.
“We haven’t made a final decision on what to propose, but it’s clear the need is still there and is going to still be there to continue to serve local governments in this way,” Venhuizen said.
The task force is also considering how much the state should require local governments to participate in cybersecurity programs, rather than leaving it voluntary.
Gov. Larry Rhoden recently awarded $500,000 to the task force to primarily fund research by Dakota State University and South Dakota Mines. The money is meant to build a map of the state’s critical infrastructure systems to identify vulnerabilities and redundancies. The funding will also support public education on cybersecurity and how residents can prepare for disruptions.

name: VTDigger
title: The catch in Noah Kahan’s charity concert for Vermont
description:
A worthy cause comes with a ticket price that leaves ordinary fans out.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  The catch in Noah Kahan’s charity concert for Vermont.
text:
Dear Editor,
I have been a Noah Kahan fan since 2021. I heard a Vermont Public feature about him on the radio in the car with my grandma and have been hooked ever since. I got my mom into him. I cried on my bedroom floor listening to the original “Stick Season” album and again, even harder, when I heard “The Great Divide.” All of this is to say that I really love Kahan. 
As someone who grew up in Vermont and now goes to Providence College in Rhode Island, I love having Kahan as a point of reference. Before him, it was just Ben & Jerry’s ice cream and Sen. Bernie Sanders. Now there is a tangible piece of media attached to Vermont for my generation. I am proud to be from the same state as him, and Kahan has built his brand on being from Vermont. So, why does it now appear that he is ignoring the cost-of-living crisis in his home state?

READ MORE

Specifically, I am referring to the announcement of his charity event supporting The Busyhead Project: a two-day golf tournament and acoustic show at Spruce Peak. Fans had the chance to enter a ticket lottery, and if they won, even with a Vermont resident discount, they still had to pay almost $350 per ticket. Those tickets are general admission, standing room only. Not even for my favorite artist would I shell out $350 and not have a seat. This is also the only stop in Vermont that Kahan has made since the release of his third studio album in 2022. The closest that we got was a four-night run at Fenway. 
Almost $350 for a single-night ticket is a lot anywhere, let alone in a place where the average monthly cost of living is 14% above the national average. Our effective property tax rate is among the top five highest across the country. Even groceries and utilities are higher here than in other regions. This kind of money is not small potatoes to the average Vermonter.
I am not against the event at all. My family is a monthly sustainer of The Busyhead Project. Rural mental health saves lives and is a pillar of many communities. I sincerely hope that Kahan’s foundation never goes underfunded. But is this really the way to do it? In my opinion, the golf tournament should be made a true luxury. Pay hundreds of dollars to play with Kahan and support a local charity. But if you really want to reach the average Vermonter who composes your fan base, the prices have to be lower. A fair price would be $100 a ticket. Concerts are a luxury, something to look forward to, but for someone who claims to be supporting the community that raised him, I think Kahan is overlooking the struggles of the people who live here. 
Gracie Batsie
Jericho, Vt.

name: VTDigger
title: Meet three Vermonters whose histories are lesser known
description:
“The majority of people throughout history have been common people whose stories have not been highlighted,” said Angie Grove, executive director of the Ethan Allen Homestead.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Meet three Vermonters whose histories are lesser known.
text:
An illustration of a mass revival during the Second Great Awakening. The image is a depiction of what Charles Bowles’ congregation might have looked like. Image courtesy of American History Central

Kyle Neece is a reporter with the Community News Service, part of the University of Vermont’s Reporting & Documentary Storytelling program.This summer marked the 250th anniversary of the United States, and many Vermont towns and cities celebrated residents who played important roles in the fight for independence.
But there are many other notable Vermonters who lived in the late 18th and early 19th centuries. Their names may be lesser known, but their stories reveal the realities of life at the time.  
Charles Bowles, founder of the first Baptist Church in Huntington 
Charles Bowles was born in Boston in 1761. His father was “an African, In the humble capacity of a servant,” and his mother was the daughter of a Revolutionary War hero named Col. Morgan, according to a biography by John W. Lewis. At the age of 12, Bowles became a servant in a Loyalist household.
When the Revolutionary War kicked off, Bowles joined the Colonial army as a waiter. In 1776, Bowles served in a New Hampshire regiment as a private. After the war, in 1779, Bowles was honorably discharged in Newburgh, New York. Shortly after, he moved to Warren, New Hampshire, and began preaching in nearby communities. 
A few years later, Bowles moved to Vermont, where he continued preaching.
Author and historian Elise Guyette researched and wrote about Bowles for her book “Discovering Black Vermont.” 
“This was during the Second Great Awakening, which is a very important movement in our country,” said Guyette, referring to a major religious revival around the start of the 19th century. “But usually you don’t read about people like Charles Bowles, even though he was a very important part of it.”
Bowles lived in Huntington, where he was a successful preacher with a congregation of about 60 people, according to Guyette’s research. He also preached across central and northern Vermont and upstate New York. He founded Free Will Baptist churches in Huntington, Hinesburg, Shelburne and Duxbury. 
“He held huge revivals all over the state, and hardly anybody remembers this man,” Guyette said. 
Bowles eventually moved to Malone, New York, where he purchased small farmland and settled down with his daughter, Eunice. He died March 16, 1843, at age 81. 
The church Bowles built in Huntington still stands today. The building became the town hall, then the first volunteer fire department. According to Guyette, the town has been working to preserve the building.
Joseph Susap, Indigenous Revolutionary War veteran 

Two handmade dolls of Joe and Molly, made by a woman in Morristown, were sent to President Eisenhower. Photo by Kyle Neece/Community News Service

Joseph Susap was born circa 1739 in Louisbourg on Cape Breton Island in Nova Scotia, a member of the Mi’kmaq people. When he was only 6 years old, the British set siege to Louisbourg and killed his family, according to Jill Mudgett, an independent historian who has researched Susap’s life.
Susap, along with other Indigenous people, fled to Odanak, Quebec, where he was taken in by a group of Abenaki. This is where Susap grew up and met Molly, an Abenaki woman with two sons, whom he would eventually marry.
However, trouble followed Susap as he escaped death a second time. In 1759, British Army Officer Robert Rogers and his rangers attacked the Odanak village. Susap and Molly fled south and lived in a variety of places ranging from Derby at the northern Vermont border down to Cabot, Morristown and as far south as Newbury. 
When the Revolutionary War started in 1775, Susap enlisted to fight for the Colonies.
“He had strong opinions about the British,” Mudgett said. 
Susap served as a scout for Gen. Jacob Bayley and helped map out the Bayley-Hazen Road, which was ordered by George Washington to connect the Connecticut River Valley with Canada. 
After the war, Susap traveled far and wide within northern Vermont. He had a reputation for being kind to settlers and was known as “Indian Joe.” 
In one story, Susap shared moose meat with a family before feeding himself. In another, he killed a catamount to protect a group of settlers. Mudgett said Susap’s friendly actions left a complex legacy. 
“He unintentionally and culturally gave the sense that (settlers) have the go-ahead to colonize due to his friendly nature,” Mudgett said. “It’s not so much that he is literally doing that, but he is symbolically used to do this. The settlers used his actions as one guy as a stand-in for Indigenous people.” 
As he grew older, Susap was taken care of by a group of Vermonters. He died in 1819 and is buried in Oxbow Cemetery in Newbury. 
Joe’s Pond, which straddles Caledonia and Washington counties, is named after Susap.
According to Mudgett, Susap’s story has persisted with Vermonters because of his “friendly” attitude toward white settlers. But she said Susap’s tale is a reminder that other Indigenous peoples’ stories are not as popular. 
“The communities that claim him as their own have always historically embraced him because he’s Joe the ‘friendly Indian,’” Mudgett said. “And if it’s more complicated than that, then these stories get erased.” 
Martha Powell, a woman on the frontier 

A map of early land lots of Burlington, where the Powells would eventually settle. Photo by Kyle Neece/Community News Service

Martha Winslow Powell was born in 1724 in Gloucester, Massachusetts. In 1748, at age 24, she married John Felix Powell. Shortly after their marriage, they had their first child, who died as an infant. In 1761, she gave birth to a son, Felix Powell Jr.
In 1768, the family moved to Dorset, Vermont, where Felix Powell is credited as the first settler; Martha Powell was left unmentioned in the land deeds, according to Angie Grove, executive director of the Ethan Allen Homestead, who has researched Martha Powell’s life. 
In 1770, the Powells moved to Pittsford, where Martha Powell gave birth to a second daughter, only for her to die as an infant as well. 
Martha Powell’s life “reflects the hardships, displacement and active contributions of working-class women who helped settle the frontier and establish the state of Vermont during the Revolutionary period,” Grove said during a panel discussion in April.  
The Powells eventually settled in Burlington, where the family purchased property in 1774. 
Martha Powell helped with her husband’s trade activities, managed household financial accounts and spending, and performed various tasks like cleaning, cooking and maintaining gardens. 
When the American Revolution began, both Felix Powell Sr. and Felix Powell Jr. left to serve in the war. In September 1777, forces aligned with the British attacked and burned down the Powells’ home during a raid. 
“The American Revolution was experienced by everybody. It was not just soldiers on battlefields; the chaos, fear, and drama were experienced by everyone on every piece of land. 
People’s experiences differed vastly and were heavily influenced by their demographics and personal relationships,” Grove said. 
According to Grove, Martha Powell, who was pregnant at the time, escaped into the surrounding woods. While hiding from the raid, she went into labor and delivered her baby alone in the forest. This baby, too, didn’t survive. 
Martha Powell did not live to see the conclusion of the war, as she died sometime between 1777 and 1780 in her early to mid 50s. In October 1780, her father wrote a revised will leaving portions of his estate to his surviving daughters and “to my grandchildren born of Martha Powell, deceased.” 
Grove said that researching stories like Powell’s takes a lot of time and resources but that the histories of everyday people are essential. 
“The majority of people throughout history have been common people whose stories have not been highlighted,” she said. “Most people today would relate more to these untold stories than to the political leaders whose stories are commonly told.”

title: Vermont Secretary of State urges voters to update state records before ballots get mailed out
description:
Despite rampant national claims to the contrary, mail-in ballots are a safe and secure way to vote, Secretary Sarah Copeland Hanzas said.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Vermont Secretary of State urges voters to update state records before ballots get mailed out.
text:
A ballot drop box outside the Randolph Town Clerk’s office in October 2024. File photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger

The Vermont Secretary of State’s office is urging voters to make sure they have a current address on file with the state before ballots get mailed out for this fall’s general election.
After Sept. 1 — which is in less than two weeks — whatever voter addresses the secretary’s office has listed will be used to mail ballots. The state will start sending out ballots late next month ahead of the election on Tuesday, Nov. 3, said Sarah Copeland Hanzas, the secretary of state.
Despite rampant national claims to the contrary, mail-in ballots are a safe and secure way to vote, she said. Recent state data shows they are widely used in Vermont. In the 2024 election, nearly two-thirds of people who voted did so by mail, also known as voting absentee.
Checking addresses
In Vermont, state law requires that every registered voter be mailed a ballot for the biennial general election. Voters can fill out their ballot at home and return it by mail or at a drop-off location. They can also disregard the mail ballot entirely and vote in person on election day.
The state does not mail out ballots for primary elections, like the one held earlier this month. If a voter has moved since the 2024 election, though, they should update their address with the state as soon as possible, Copeland Hanzas said.
“We want to make sure that ballots are going exactly where the voter lives,” she said. 
Voters who will be away from home this fall should submit an absentee ballot request, which will direct their ballot to the address they’ll be at instead. That’s a good option for college students and members of the military who will be overseas, she said. 
Voters can verify or change the address that’s on file — or request an absentee ballot — at the online Vermont Voter Portal, which is vote.vermont.gov. They can also contact their local town or city clerk.
Voter rolls, mail delays
Copeland Hanzas said Vermont puts multiple sets of eyes on every stage in the vote-by-mail process to make sure it’s as accurate and secure as possible.
She explained that since last fall, officials in every city and town have completed a legally-mandated review of their local voter checklists to identify anyone who they believe has moved, passed away or otherwise cannot vote there. That review is done by each town’s Board of Civil Authority.
Any people who are flagged by the board will not be automatically mailed a ballot this fall unless that person clarifies with local officials that they are listed correctly, Copeland Hanzas said. That means it’s highly unlikely that someone would be mailed a ballot who was not registered to vote in a given city or town.
At the national level, President Donald Trump is trying to limit access to mail voting, in part with an executive order in March directing the U.S. Postal Service to only deliver ballots from people who are on a federally-approved list. That followed another order last year attempting to prohibit counting of mail ballots that are postmarked by Election Day but arrive afterward, among other changes. (In Vermont, election officials must get mail-in ballots back before polls close on Election Day in order to count them.)
Federal courts have so far blocked implementation of both orders in response to legal challenges from states, including Vermont, and national voting rights groups. The president continues to disparage mail-in voting, though he has voted by mail himself, including in Florida’s Republican primary earlier this month.
Even if Vermonters aren’t concerned about the security of mail-in voting, they may be worried about the timeliness with which their ballot will be delivered. Mail delivery delays are well-documented, especially in the state’s most rural communities. 
More than 2,000 people have made complaints to the three members of Vermont’s congressional delegation about mail service so far this year, according to a letter the lawmakers sent Friday to U.S. Postmaster General David Steiner.
Copeland Hanzas said that voters should feel confident they will receive a ballot in the mail this year. If they’re concerned about it getting back in time, they can use a ballot dropbox, locations of which are listed online. They can also turn in a filled-out ballot up until polls close on Election Day.

title: What’s next for Vermont? Meet the reporters covering politics, elections and health care
description:
Join VTDigger at the Manchester Community Library for a free, public conversation with the journalists following some of the biggest decisions facing Vermont this fall.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  What’s next for Vermont? Meet the reporters covering politics, elections and health care.
text:
VTDigger’s Shaun Robinson and Ethan Weinstein at an event with historian Jill Lepore at the Manchester Community Library on Thursday, September 5, 2024. Photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger
State government can be difficult to follow. Major policy decisions take shape through legislative debates, agency actions, elections and negotiations that often happen far from public view.
On Thursday, September 10, VTDigger is bringing the journalists who follow those decisions to Manchester for a candid conversation about what they’re seeing, what they’ll be watching this fall and how their reporting helps Vermonters understand how consequential decisions are made.
The panel will be moderated by Editor-in-Chief Sue Allen and feature Senior Editor Ethan Weinstein, Health Care Reporter Olivia Gieger and State Government & Politics Reporter Shaun Robinson.




Ethan Weinstein, senior editor




Olivia Gieger, health care reporter




Shaun Robinson, government & politics reporter


The reporters will discuss the November election, state politics and the forces shaping Vermont’s health care system. They’ll also pull back the curtain on their work: how they develop sources, scrutinize public officials’ claims, navigate complex policy debates and uncover information the public needs to know.
Attendees will leave with a clearer understanding of the issues and decisions VTDigger’s reporters are following, how those decisions could affect Vermont communities and what it takes to bring readers accurate, independent reporting from the Statehouse and beyond.
VTDigger’s new CEO, Brendan Kinney, will open the evening, share how the organization is working to bring more reporting to more Vermont communities and offer a look at what’s ahead for the newsroom. 
Event details
When: Thursday, September 10, 2026, from 5–7 p.m.Where: Manchester Community Library, 138 Cemetery Ave., Manchester CenterAdmission: Free and open to the public; registration is required.
Doors open at 5 p.m. The program will begin at 5:30 p.m. Hors d’oeuvres will be provided, with beverages available by donation. The venue is wheelchair accessible, and onsite parking is available.

Reserve your seat

What do you want VTDigger’s reporters to address?
Readers are invited to help shape the conversation by submitting a question in advance:
What question do you have about Vermont government, the upcoming election or another issue affecting your community?
While we may not be able to address every submission during the event, our team will read them all and use them to guide the discussion.

Submit a question

Space is limited. Register today to join VTDigger’s journalists and your neighbors for a closer look at the decisions shaping Vermont — and the reporting that helps bring those decisions into public view.
Events like this are made possible through community support. When you register, please consider making a donation to sustain VTDigger’s mission of providing trusted daily news for Vermont.
