name: Connecticut Mirror
title: UConn’s puppetry program is famous. John Bell played a big part in that
description: For nearly two decades, the professor and museum director has introduced students and visitors to the idea that anything can be a puppet.
text:
An occasional look at Connecticut’s remarkable people, places and things

John Bell sees puppets everywhere.
Props at political protests, college sports mascots, Thanksgiving parade balloons, video game characters, Yoda — the list goes on.
As director of the University of Connecticut’s puppetry museum and associate professor of puppetry, Bell has imparted this way of seeing the world to scores of students and museum visitors since he arrived on campus in 2007. 
“My definition of puppetry is performing with elements of the material world,” Bell said. “There are many different ways that people communicate, tell stories, celebrate with things that they make out of different materials.”

The Ballard Institute and Museum of Puppetry showed Becoming Modern, an exhibit curated by John Bell, in Storrs on August 6, 2026.  Credit: Julia Levine / CT Mirror

To Bell, puppetry isn’t strictly for kids. It isn’t all that niche, either. It’s deeply embedded in everyday life, “invisible and ubiquitous,” he said. 
Next month, after nearly two decades as the resident expert in puppetry history and traditions at UConn’s Ballard Institute and Museum of Puppetry, Bell plans to retire and turn his attention back to puppetry performance, where his interest in the art form started. Bell’s tenure leading the institute included the museum’s 2014 expansion and relocation to UConn’s main campus in Storrs — and its increasing renown within and beyond the professional theater world.

UConn mascot Jonathan The Husky in the second half of an NCAA college basketball game against Xavier, Tuesday, Feb. 3, 2026, in Hartford, Conn. Credit: Jessica Hill / AP Photo

The museum now houses more than 4,500 puppets from around the world. Each year, it welcomes about 8,000 visitors and hosts more than a dozen performances, along with puppet forums and exhibitions. 
UConn offers the country’s only degree-granting program in puppetry of its kind, earning a reputation in the puppetry world akin to UConn’s legendary college basketball pedigree. The programs are aligned in another way, Bell likes to point out: Jonathan the Husky — the mascot, not the actual dog — is a puppet.
Emily Wicks, manager of operations and collections at the Ballard Institute, said Bell made a big impression on her when she interviewed to work at the institute 14 years ago. 
“He told me during that interview that anything can be a puppet, and that literally has stuck with me since,” Wicks said.
Focusing outside the self
Growing up in the 1950s, Bell first saw puppets on television shows geared toward children. 
However, it was a live performance by the Bread and Puppet Theater in Vermont in 1972 that would ultimately change the course of his life. The performance group was known for using puppetry to address political and social issues — and for baking fresh bread that was served during performances. 
One particular show about the Vietnam War resonated with Bell, then a young college student.
Through it, Bell saw the ability of puppets to say things that might otherwise be difficult for a human performer to say directly. “It opens up what’s possible with politics,” Bell said. 
John Bell leads flying lessons for a Bread and Puppet Theater performance in Istanbul in 2024. Credit: Photo Courtesy of John Bell
As a student, Bell said, he was interested in acting, but he felt uneasy on stage. 
“Acting is an amazing art form, but it requires you to focus on your body,” Bell said. “With puppetry, you focus just outside of yourself.”
That distinction opened a new door. After graduating from Middlebury College, Bell joined the Bread and Puppet Theater troupe, touring throughout the United States and Europe. 
He remembers one performance in Poland in particular. The piece was about the challenges of modern life in the communist country. During the performance, the audience rose from their seats, moved by the story. Bell had never seen anything like that before, and it helped him see the power of puppetry in connecting with audiences.
Bell and his wife, Trudi Cohen, met while they were both members of the Bread and Puppet company, and they built a life around puppetry, eventually becoming founding members of a Brooklyn-based puppet company called Great Small Works.
“We share this pleasure and faith in the power of puppetry to tell important stories, to change the world even,” she said.

John Bell and Trudi Cohen perform a Living Newspaper toy theater show in Cambridge, Massachusetts in the early 2020s. Credit: Courtesy of John Bell

After studying theater history at Columbia University and teaching puppetry at several schools including New York University, Emerson College and Rhode Island School of Design, Bell eventually found a home at UConn. He joined first as director of the Ballard Institute, named for the founder of UConn’s Puppet Arts Program, Frank Ballard, who started teaching puppetry to Connecticut students in the early 1960s. 
Bell joined the faculty of UConn’s Dramatic Arts Program and began teaching classes in 2014.
The following year, Bell teamed up with Bart Roccoburton, head of UConn’s Puppet Arts Program, to host the National Puppeteers of America Festival, which brought hundreds of puppeteers from 40 states and five continents to Storrs for performances.
Bell continued to find ways to bring puppetry to campus. In 2022, Bread and Puppet Theater’s “The Persians” performed on UConn’s South Campus Lawn. More than 20 community volunteers performed alongside the company, giving students a chance to experience the company’s large-scale political puppetry firsthand. 
“Anytime John is part of anything that we are doing, we all get richer for it. His energy, his creativity, his knowledge always play into anything that we do,” Roccoburton said.

Bell has curated more than 30 puppet exhibitions at the museum, including “Living Objects: African American Puppetry” and “Somos Uno: Mexican and Mexican American Puppetry.” 
In the classroom, he taught courses such as “History of World Puppetry,” introducing hundreds of students to the art form over the years. 
Bell is also the author of several books and articles on puppetry, among them “American Puppet Modernism,” which won Iran’s Jalari Itari award and France’s Prix de la Recherche in 2011. 
Many of Bell’s students have gone on to build careers of their own in puppetry. 
Mel Carter, a recent MFA graduate in Puppet Arts at UConn, has taken her MFA project “B*tch Eat Dog” across the country and this month to the Edinburgh Festival Fringe in Scotland, one of the world’s largest arts festivals. 
Joe Therrien, a former graduate assistant of Bell’s, has gone on to work as a teaching artist and core member of Brooklyn-based BoxCutter Collective while producing his own puppet shows in New York City. 
Sarah Nolen, another former student of Bell’s, became the third-ever resident artist at the Puppet Show Place in Brookline, Mass.
For these students, Bell left a lasting impression.
Carter described Bell as humble and generous with his knowledge. 
“John Bell kind of touches everyone that he meets just by showing that to be an intellect and to be respected, you don’t need to sit on a high horse and demand respect,” she said. 
And while Bell spent plenty of time at the front of the classroom giving lectures, he also watched his students from the sidelines as they performed, offering notes and guidance. 
Allison Free, a rising senior in the Puppet Arts Program, said, “He just teaches me new things all the time, and it’s like, ‘Wow.’ It’s such a wide world that you’re just constantly learning.”
Therrien said that Bell and Cohen are such pillars of the puppetry community that their home in Cambridge, Mass., has become something of an “international puppet way station,” where performers from around the world can stay while passing through Boston. 
Even while teaching, curating and writing about puppetry, Bell never stopped performing. 
Bell takes part in UConn’s Puppet Slams, a showcase held each semester, where students and professional performers can put on new and experimental short works. 
And throughout his time at UConn, Bell has continued performing with the Bread and Puppet Theater at its farm in Glover, Vt., during the summer. This summer, Bell performed in the “Upside Down World Circus,” a political spectacle that uses giant puppets, stilt dancers and a brass band to respond to the political turmoil of the present day. 
As Bell put it, “Puppeteers love to perform.”

Puppets in the exhibit Becoming Modern include recognizable characters like Mickey Mouse, alongside works from Yiddish puppet theaters in the early 1900s at the the Ballard Institute and Museum of Puppetry in Storrs on August 6, 2026. Credit: Julia Levine / CT Mirror

Bringing life to the material world
Bell sees puppetry as a fluid art form in the way it takes different shapes across cultures. 
For example, the traditions of puppetry in Europe can look very different from those found in Native American, African and Asian cultures. But the foundational ideas are similar. 
Puppetry also embodies something uncanny and mysterious, he said, in how it incorporates life and death. Humans are living beings who eventually return to the material world when they die, he explained. But puppets begin as part of that material world — wood, leather and paper — and are brought to life through humans’ movements. 
Many of these big ideas permeate Bell’s final exhibition, “Becoming Modern: U.S. Puppetry in the 20th Century,” on display at the Ballard Institute through October.
The exhibition traces five decades of American puppetry, featuring artists and objects that have shaped Bell’s own career. The collections explore themes such as immigration and feminism while showcasing the many forms puppetry can take, from marionettes and hand puppets to shadow theater. 
For Bell, retirement from UConn doesn’t mean stepping away from puppetry. 
“It’s really unusual. I mean, you’re giving up something you’ve done for a really long time,” Bell said. “What I want to do is to make more puppet shows and figure out ways to do that and other things — maybe write about puppetry and continue to be involved in puppetry in different ways and see what happens.”
Next month, Bell and Cohen are headed to the Minneapolis Cranky Festival, where they will perform puppetry through scroll pictures. Bell also looks forward to working with his Bread and Puppet Theater colleagues on a project in Turkey about an environmental conference. 
“I’ve told him he’s graduating,” Cohen said. “It’s not just ending but opening some doors.”
John Bell performs a Dancing Bear act with the Bread and Puppet Theater’s Upside Down Circus in Brattleboro, Vt., in summer 2026. Credit: Photo Courtesy of Matthew Cohen

name: Kansas Reflector
title: The art of protest is alive and well in Kansas. It is the color of democracy.
description: As protest art goes, we’re experiencing an American revival. Not since the turbulent protests of the Vietnam War era have so many taken paint and poster board in hand to express their displeasure. The current wave started six years ago with the summer of George Floyd, during which demonstrations erupted nationwide after the killing of […]
text:
Protestors march at the No Kings event on Oct. 18, 2025, crossing Sixth and Commercial streets in downtown Emporia.  (Photo by Max McCoy/Kansas Reflector)As protest art goes, we’re experiencing an American revival.
Not since the turbulent protests of the Vietnam War era have so many taken paint and poster board in hand to express their displeasure. The current wave started six years ago with the summer of George Floyd, during which demonstrations erupted nationwide after the killing of a Black man by a white police officer in Minneapolis.
Protest signs are common to just about every cause that brings people together in a public space, as they have been since before any of us were born. Photographs of the hand-lettered banners carried by women in the suffrage movement of a century ago look surprisingly modern, if a bit neater.
Historically, resistance movements have harnessed the power of human expression — paintings, poetry, paper cranes — as paths toward progressive goals. One now recognizes Picasso’s “Guernica,” produced in the wake of the 1937 bombing of a Basque village by the fascists, as an important ant-fascist work that transcends its specific subject matter. The same goes for Randall Jarrell’s “The Death of the Ball Turret Gunner,” written in 1945 and possibly the shortest poem about the violence of war, and perhaps the most effective. The novels typically come a decade or two later, such as Erich Maria Remarque’s “All Quiet on the Western Front.”
Not a painter, poet or novelist?
Not to worry, because posters are the folk art of contemporary politics.
Just because they were produced by those untrained in graphics and design doesn’t disqualify them as art. Some might say it adds to the power of the message, because anything produced with the too-finished and generic look of artificial intelligence lacks authenticity. Someday, if museums survive the current moment, a sign carried in Minneapolis or Portland or Emporia may be on permanent display with a card reading, “Melt ICE,” circa 2026. Artist unknown.
The modern DIY protest art movement may have reached a zenith with the three No Kings protests opposing the second administration of Donald Trump, held in June and October of 2025 and March of this year. Kansans participated in the thousands during all of those events, including in my home city of Emporia.
In March, protestors chanted and waved their handmade signs as they gathered at the intersection of Sixth and Commercial, the center of town. One of those protestors was my wife, Kim. She approached the making of her homemade sign with all the deliberation of an important homework assignment. What color of poster board to use? What about the letters? What should it say? She settled on a brilliant yellow background with “No Kings!” in blue and an x-ed out pink crown.
Looking over photographs of the event, the sign was easy to spot. It may not have been the best sign, or the most creative, but it was authentic. There were dozens, if not hundreds, of other handmade signs, and a few stood out: “Love America, Hate Orange Swine” with a caricature of Trump as a pig, another that warned “Hands Off Our Democracy,” and a simple one in bold type that proclaimed: “ENOUGH ENOUGH.”
The No Kings protestors have a sharply partisan viewpoint, but during the past two months I’ve seen the rise of another group that relies largely on handmade signs to get their point across. While anti-data center groups use the same strategy for their signs, the protestors represent an unexpected coalition. In Emporia, I’ve seen people holding signs against a proposed data center here that come from all points on the political and cultural spectrum. Grassroots is an overused word, but in this case it fits.
If the protestors, led by Emporia Neighbors United, have anything in common, it’s that they feel betrayed by city officials who, since June 3, have rushed to adopt the municipal framework necessary to establish a 1,000-acre hyperscale data center. That betrayal has resulted in a petition drive to force the issue on the ballot, a move the city is attempting to block in district court with a declaratory judgment. It has also spawned other petitions, aiming to recall city commissioners and change the form of city government to a council.
Data center protestor Sherrie Kennison waves a sign at passing traffic on June 23, 2026, outside the Emporia city offices. (Photo by Max McCoy/Kansas Reflector)
There’s also a group recently formed to support local government, “Emporians for Progress,” but they are far outnumbered by the dissenters, who have turned out in the dozens. On Aug. 19, seven neatly dressed individuals held carefully lettered signs across the street from City Hall, with many saying they “back city officials.” The signs were duller than those carried by Emporia Neighbors United. They were carefully lettered and bore no caricatures. One of the seven supporters at the pro-city rally was the interim president of the local chamber of commerce. Perhaps I’m being too hard on Emporians for Progress. But then, I think the definition of progress is that which improves the human condition for everybody.
On Aug. 20, a district judge ruled the data center ban would go to a public vote on the November ballot, according to local reporting. But Glenn R. Braun, the Hays judge assigned to hear the case, also said the question of whether the petition’s aim was administrative or legislative in nature remained unresolved. If deemed administrative, the ban would be voided even if approved by public vote.
The quick rise of the data center resistance has caught a lot of people off guard, including some of my friends who are educators and journalists. The movement is so new that nobody knows in which direction it will eventually lead, but what seems certain is that it will play a significant role in politics at all levels of government in the coming months. Personally, I think we must resist the proliferation of data centers with the same zeal that one would campaign against the proliferation of nuclear weapons, because both involve existential threats to humanity.
Somewhere, right now, a self-taught artist may be creating the symbol of the data center resistance, intentionally or by chance. It will be something that is at once simple in design but powerful in message. I don’t know what the symbol might be, but the movement will embrace it when it sees it.
There are examples we can take from history.
Paper cranes have become a near-universal symbol for world peace, but the symbol began with a dying girl’s wish. Sadako Sasaki was 2 years old when her home town of Hiroshima was destroyed by the atomic bomb in 1945. She later was diagnosed with leukemia, an ailment linked to radiation that plagued many victims. While in the hospital, she was inspired by folklore that one’s wish would be granted by producing a thousand origami cranes. Sadako’s wish was to recover and join her school’s running team. She completed the task of 1,000 cranes, but did not get her wish. She died in 1955, at age 12.
Sadako’s story was made famous by a 1977 children’s book, “Sadako and the Thousand Paper Cranes,” by Eleanor Coerr. Many thousands of paper cranes are sent each year to Hiroshima, along with wishes for world peace.
Another symbol that has global recognition is the peace sign, created by Gerald Holtom in 1958 for the British Campaign for Nuclear Disarmament. Holtom, a pacifist, was inspired by the letters N and D in the semaphore alphabet, standing for “nuclear disarmament.” It has since transcended its original meaning to mean peace in general, on countless bandanas and tee shirts worn from the summer of love to the present day. I have a peace sign on my acoustic guitar case. When I was in junior high school, one of my teachers told me the peace sign was an anti-Christian symbol, a Satanic icon, representing the “broken cross.”
That was my introduction to the cultural divide in which those values that are normally thought of as being politically “left” — you know, radical notions of world peace and universal healthcare and social equality — are demonized. The hippies and their peace signs were an outsider threat to traditional values, a nest of Communists in tie-dye, Mao-quoting atheists who could either love America or leave it.
It was hogwash then, and it is hogwash now.
But many would have you believe that contemporary American resistance — whether to draconian immigration enforcement or data centers that would make our tech oligarchs even richer — is part of a radical leftist conspiracy to weaken America. Few things could be further from the truth. In the first place, there is no conspiracy, no anti-“Project 2025” playbook. In the second, those in the resistance are embracing traditional American values of empathy, equality, and a love for the earth and those who inhabit it. Those who claim such conspiracies are trying to sell you a notion as tired and untrue as Joseph McCarthy’s Red Scare.
Just because I have a peace sign on my guitar case doesn’t mean that I’m a Satan-worshipping hippie with a poster of Fidel Castro on my wall. The poster in our living room is of the Americana singer-songwriter Gillian Welch. I’m not even sure I’m all that politically left, because at some point in the past decade the middle shifted suddenly beneath my feet. I regard the First Amendment as the basic tenet of civic religion, as readers of this column will know, but I also support the Second Amendment. I’ve had guns all of my life, both for hunting and for target practice. I believe all nuclear weapons should be abolished, but I’m not a pacifist. My three favorite presidents are Abraham Lincoln, Teddy Roosevelt and John F. Kennedy. My personal philosophy isn’t so much a political one but an aesthetic and ethical one. It was honed by Mark Twain and Edward Abbey, Susan Sontag and Virginia Woolf, Robert Altman and Stephen Spielberg. I don’t fit into any neatly labeled categories, and I don’t think many other Kansans do, either.
We are in a moment when traditional party labels have lost their meaning. At the same time, class distinctions — the ever-widening gulf between those in power and those who feel powerless, the chasm between the rich and the rest of us — have become sharper. A free-floating discontent has plagued America, and part of it has been expressed in frustration and anger since the summer of Floyd. It was also expressed during the No Kings rallies. Nearly three out of four Americans think the country is headed in the wrong direction, according to recent Associated Press-NORC polling.
We stand on the edge of tomorrow but are unsure of our footing.
It’s easy to feel crushed when confronted by today’s challenges. But this is just the moment to use our creativity to share something powerful with the world. What you share might even be beautiful and hopeful. But if it is to succeed, it must be authentic, the product of your own mind and your own hands.
The other day, I found just that kind of art when I visited the tent where Emporia Neighbors United were circulating one of their many petitions. It was nearly 100 degrees out, but members of the group were still at it, gathering signatures in an attempt to change a local government they saw as deaf to their wishes.
I wasn’t there to sign a petition but to ask how things were going.
Activity was steady, I was told.
The hot wind was whipping out of the southwest, rattling the canopy and ruffling the pages of the petitions on the plastic folding table. That’s when I noticed the rocks. Several grapefruit-sized rocks were being used as paperweights. Each of the rocks was painted. Some had slogans while others featured landscapes. One showed a prairie scene with sunflowers, and in the blue sky above was, “Keep Kansas Beautiful.”
The rocks were the work of Judith Bilyea.
She told me she had the rocks at her house and just decided to paint them.
The rocks carried messages of hope, authenticity and activism.
A fist-sized rock is likely the earliest of weapons. You can use it to kill your brother or smash your neighbor’s window. But Bilyea chose to use her rocks as peaceful messages with which to hold down documents literally representing the people’s First Amendment right to petition government for a redress of grievances.
Bilyea has a master’s degree in biology with a concentration in ecology and biodiversity. She could have given a lecture on all the environmental reasons she had become an activist. But I’m glad she let the rocks do her talking.
A rock painted by Judith Bilyea was used as a paperweight for a petition seeking to change Emporia’s form of government, as seen Aug. 9, 2026. (Photo by Max McCoy/Kansas Reflector)
Max McCoy is an award-winning author and journalist. Through its opinion section, the Kansas Reflector works to amplify the voices of people who are affected by public policies or excluded from public debate. Find information, including how to submit your own commentary, here.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: The traffic calming illusion
description: You've seen the bumper stickers: Slow down in town. They're a nice thought. Completely useless, but nice.
text:
While Jim enjoys a “train spotting” vacation, let’s revisit this column from a while back…
You’ve seen the bumper stickers: Slow down in town. They’re a nice thought. Completely useless, but nice.  
Apparently, the theory is that shame, printed on vinyl, will penetrate the skull of someone doing 45 mph in a 25 zone while texting.



I wouldn’t exactly call it road rage, but why is it that when we’re behind the wheel our goal is to get on down the road as fast as traffic will allow, the speed limit be damned?  But, once in our own neighborhood, we transform into traffic calming zealots.  It’s remarkable how quickly self-interest masquerades as public safety.
Increasingly, local neighborhoods are serving as shortcuts for GPS apps like WAZE, offering drivers routes around clogged arterial streets, spreading out the traffic into our gated suburbs of the mind.  But there is a way to enforce the speed limit without radar traps.  It’s what traffic engineers call “traffic calming.”
More than just “speed bumps”, engineers now have a slew of street re-designs in their repertoire that can force us to reduce our speed.  Among them…
Speed tables: Think of these as extended speed bumps with a six-foot long ramp up, a ten-foot long flat table and a six-foot long ramp down.  Slow down or lose your muffler.
Roundabouts: Small traffic circles with landscaping in the center make us slow down as we go around, eventually taking a right turn to continue our journey… assuming our fellow motorists know how to maneuver these rounded roadways without circling endlessly.

A roundabout connecting Routes 82 and 85 in Salem. Credit: Courtesy / CT Department of Transportation

Chicanes: A traffic chicane is a series of alternating curves or S-shaped shifts built into a roadway.  It forces drivers to steer back and forth instead of driving in a straight line. This design interrupts sight lines, narrows the travel path, and naturally forces motorists to slow down.
Bulb-outs or neck-downs: These are extensions of the sidewalk into car parking areas at corner crossings. Again, you got to slow down… or else.
Sidewalks: It’s amazing how many of our communities lack these pedestrian amenities, forcing hoofers to compete for space on the asphalt with cars. Sidewalks get pedestrians out of the traffic and encourage us to walk and leave the car at home.  And PS: sidewalks are NOT for bikes.
Crosswalks: What a concept!  A place where pedestrians have the right of way over cars, sometimes even mid-block and without the need for stop signs or red lights.  Good concept, if it’s observed by motorists.  Otherwise, pedestrians beware!
Roadblocks and mazes: These were inspired by anti-crime efforts in drug dealing neighborhoods (“crime calming”), making it hard for drive-through drug buyers to find their way in and out of a neighborhood.  Local residents know how to maneuver the maze, but casual short-cutters won’t try it again.
Of course, all of these traffic calming techniques assume that the major traffic arterials, where the cars belong, can be kept flowing with their own traffic tricks.
Otherwise, we’re just playing whack-a-mole with traffic. We beat it back from the arterials into the neighborhoods, feel virtuous, then act shocked when the neighborhoods become cut-through nightmares. Turns out you can’t engineer your way out of bad urban planning.  You can only shuffle the misery around.

title: Harmful algal bloom advisory issued at southwest Idaho reservoirs
description: The Idaho Department of Health and Welfare issued a health advisory for harmful algal blooms for the Grasmere Reservoir and the CJ Strike Reservoir’s Bruneau Arm. Recent reservoir samples showed high levels of cyanobacteria that produce cyanotoxins that can harm people, pets and livestock, the state agency announced in a news release Friday. During the […]
text:
An algae bloom is pictured on the Big Hole River on Friday, Sept. 26, 2025. (Jordan Hansen / Daily Montanan)The Idaho Department of Health and Welfare issued a health advisory for harmful algal blooms for the Grasmere Reservoir and the CJ Strike Reservoir’s Bruneau Arm.
Recent reservoir samples showed high levels of cyanobacteria that produce cyanotoxins that can harm people, pets and livestock, the state agency announced in a news release Friday.
During the advisory, the Idaho Department of Health and Welfare advises people to be cautious while recreating near or in water — such as avoiding swimming, wading or contact with the water — in the two reservoirs located in southwest Idaho.
The Grasmere Reservoir is about is about 35 miles south of Bruneau on State Highway 51. The Bruneau Arm of CJ Strike Reservoir is northwest of the town of Bruneau. 
Under Health and Welfare’s advisory: 

Children should not drink or contact reservoir water, and others should avoid it. 
Pets and livestock shouldn’t drink the water, or go in it. If pets and livestock contact the water, immediately clean their skin, hide or fur with clean water. 
Do not cook with or drink the water. Toxins aren’t removed by boiling or filtering the water, which can raise the risk of illness.
After handling fish or objects from the water, thoroughly wash hands in clean water. If you eat fish from the water, clean and wash it thoroughly in clean water. Before cooking, filet the fish and remove all internal organs, fat and skin. Cyanotoxins can build up in fish, Health and Welfare says, and human risk is unknown.

And watch for symptoms: 

People who touch or swim in the water, or breathe water droplets, might have a rash, hives, red eyes, wheezing, coughing or shortness of breath. People who swallow the water might have stomach pain, diarrhea or vomiting. People whose liver becomes damaged might have yellow skin and dark urine.
If you think you’re sick from cyanotoxin, contact your health care provider or call the poison center at 1-800-222-1222. You can also notify algae@deq.idaho.gov.
Within minutes to days after exposure to cyanotoxin, pets, livestock and wildlife can become sick or die. Dogs might get sick before humans, since they are more likely to swim in, drink or lick contaminated water or bloom material off their fur. If your pet or livestock seem sick after entering or drinking the water, immediately seek veterinary care.

Cyanobacteria are natural to Idaho’s recreational water bodies. Rising temperatures can lead to blooms that release toxins into the water.
Blooms can look different — like mats, foam, spilled paint, or surface scum with a foul odor. And they might not always be visible, such as mats on the bottom of water.



 How to find out more about harmful algal blooms?

Idaho state agencies list other harmful algal blooms health advisories online.
Report a potential harmful algal bloom using the Department of Environmental Quality’s online form, by phone at 866-671-5385 or email algae@deq.idaho.gov.

name: Florida Phoenix
title: Uthmeier’s found another windmill to tilt at
description: Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier is a busy, busy bee, darting from human trafficking prosecutions to going after shoplifting gangs to trying to outlaw drag queen Christmas shows to accusing Microsoft of anti-Christian bias to cheerleading book bans. Incensed by a recent hard foul the Chicago Sky’s DiJonai Cunningham landed on the Indiana Fever’s Sophi[...]
text:
Palestinian emergency services and local citizens search for victims in buildings destroyed during Israeli raids in the southern Gaza Strip on Oct. 17, 2023, in Khan Yunis, Gaza. (Photo by Ahmad Hasaballah/Getty Images)Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier is a busy, busy bee, darting from human trafficking prosecutions to going after shoplifting gangs to trying to outlaw drag queen Christmas shows to accusing Microsoft of anti-Christian bias to cheerleading book bans.
Incensed by a recent hard foul the Chicago Sky’s DiJonai Cunningham landed on the Indiana Fever’s Sophie Cunningham, he’s even threatening charges of assault and battery.
Never mind Carrington was ejected from the game (the appropriate penalty); never mind the WNBA doesn’t play in Florida.
If athletic violence is a concern, perhaps we can look forward to the AG policing vicious hits in college football?
Here’s an idea: Uthmeier gets himself a whistle, enlists a couple of cops, and pre-prints a stack of charge sheets.
All he has to do is stand on the sidelines of the FSU-Miami game for a quarter, and he could score a bunch of arrests.
It could be since closure of his pet detention camp, Alligator Alcatraz, Uthmeier feels he doesn’t have enough to do, even though there are still pending lawsuits over the environmental damage done to the Everglades to deal with.
His current obsession is The New York Times. The AG has sent the paper’s parent company a 28-page letter outlining what he sees as its manifold transgressions and demanding six years-worth of board documents, information on editorial decisions, and internal communication records.
He’s ordered the Times Co. to respond by Aug. 25.
The ostensible reason? The State Board of Administration, which manages Florida’s pension funds, holds 147,831 shares of Times Co. stock.
Bias?
What Uthmeier sees as the paper’s “editorial malpractice” could, he claims, cause the Times’ value to tank and blameless Floridians to suffer financial losses.
He says, “The Times tells investors that its brand and reputation are its most important asset,” but “if people see its journalism as unreliable or biased, the company can be hurt.”
His beef is over the Times’ coverage, some in its news sections, more in its editorial pages, of Hamas’ terrorist attack on Israel in October 2023 and Israel’s prosecution of the war in Gaza.
Uthmeier’s particularly upset about two-time Pulitzer winner Nicholas Kristof’s May 2026 column on Israeli sexual violence against Palestinians.
Palestinian prisoners say they were raped and abused by Israeli soldiers, West Bank settlers, and members of Shin Bet, Israel’s domestic security force.
Kristof’s piece was carefully reported, based on evidence gathered from human rights organizations, interviews with Palestinian detainees, Israeli lawyers, other journalists, and eyewitnesses.
In other words, it was vetted and fact-checked to a fare-thee-well, and Times editors stand by it.
It should be noted the newspaper has also published numerous stories (I counted at least 10) on how Hamas raped, mutilated, and murdered Israeli women during its Oct. 7, 2023, attack.
In his letter, Uthmeier blasts the Times for what he sees as bias — an article of faith on the right — and cites the case of Graham Platner, Maine’s one-time Democratic U.S. Senate candidate.
Platner’s campaign imploded after multiple women accused him of sexual assault, including rape. The Times, according to Uthmeier, would not “report self-evidently newsworthy information” about Platner, and was clearly “downplaying or outright ignoring information, such as his Nazi tattoo.”
Try research
Now, I’m pretty sure somebody in the AG’s office knows how to deploy that useful tool we call “Google,” and might, with the tiniest expenditure of energy, have discovered the Times was, in fact, among the first news outlets to report on the “Nazi tattoo” in October 2025.
Now, come on, Mister Attorney General. You’re a Georgetown Law J.D. You know better than to make stupid assertions that don’t stand up to minimal scrutiny.
But that’s not all: Uthmeier trots out what he thinks is damning evidence of malfeasance: “between October 7th 2023 and June 2024, the Times admitted 72 errors in its coverage of the Israel-Hamas war that had to be corrected.”
He insists the majority of those errors were somehow “favorable” to Hamas.
Perhaps the AG needs to learn how responsible journalists work. If you make a mistake, you own it, fix it, and run the correction in a prominent place.
Which is what the Times does — mostly. No newspaper gets it right 100% of the time.
The Times has indeed struggled with some notable scandals and screw-ups: Judith Miller, the reporter who swallowed the Bush administration’s nonsense about Iraq’s Weapons of Mass Destruction, helped push the nation into a stupid, destructive and wholly unnecessary war.
Then there was Jayson Blair, the serial plagiarist who faked his reporting and was forced out in 2003.
The Times wrote a 7,000-word story detailing Blair’s — and its own — sins against journalism.
On Oct. 23, 2023, the Times, along with the AP, Reuters, Politico and others, initially blamed Israel for a rocket blast that killed hundreds at a Gaza hospital.
Honest errors
You can see why they might have thought that: The IDF has never hesitated to kill Palestinian civilians, including aid workers, reporters, and a 5-year old girl called Hind Rajab.
But the story was wrong. It wasn’t the Israelis. The various news outlets, including the Times, admitted their mistake.
Finding the facts in violent, chaotic conditions — terrorist attacks, wars, humanitarian crises — is difficult. Reporters get it wrong sometimes and then, when better information comes along, strive to get it right.
Contrast this with Uthmeier’s selective outrage over Kristof’s column, huffing puffing and gotcha-ing in his letter, pouncing on Times Executive Editor Joe Kahn’s statement that the paper would not have run “that exact piece” in its news pages
Of course it wouldn’t. It’s an opinion piece, not a news story.
Uthmeier again demonstrates his ignorance of journalism, declaring the Kristof column wasn’t actually opinion because it “did not express a view. It asserted events.”
He says Kristof “asserted that Israeli prison guards committed sexual violence against Palestinian detainees,” claims Uthmeier insists must be either true or false.
He adds, “They are not opinions in any sense the law recognizes, and the [Times] Company did not defend them as opinions. Its spokesperson defended them as reporting.”
Note to the AG: In a newspaper, “opinion” isn’t confined to somebody ranting about how “The Odyssey” movie didn’t do justice to the poem or speculating that Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez freezing her eggs means she’s running for president in 2028. Many pieces published on the Opinion Page rely on in-depth, often difficult, often controversial reporting to tell a story in a personal, engaged, morally urgent voice that conveys the writer’s feelings.
You don’t do that in a news story.
Define ‘opinion’
What Uthmeier’s doing is constructing a legal framework based on a definition of “opinion” he thinks can inflict damage on the newspaper he sees as MAGA’s chief antagonist.
So, what’s this really about?
Uthmeier insists he simply wants to protect shareholder value on behalf of Florida’s retirees.
OK, I’ll bite. Is the New York Times Co. financially shaky, then?
Doesn’t look like it: The paper’s been adding subscribers and shows an 11% increase in revenues this year.
That’s a pretty good return.
Florida’s portfolio isn’t wall-to-wall winners, anyway. The state also invests in Meta, which has lately lost 10% of its stock price, and Oracle, which has seen its stock downgraded to one rung above junk.
In his letter, the AG raises the defamation suit Dominion Voting Systems brought against Fox “News,” which claimed Dominion was part of a vast conspiracy to steal the 2020 election and was somehow controlled by Venezuelan strong man Hugo Chavez (who died in 2013) and aided by George Soros.
Fox’s factchecking “Brain Room” told the network it was all nonsense. Fox talking heads didn’t care: They kept throwing gasoline on the flames.
Dominion sued the notoriously truth-challenged Fox and settled for $800 million.
I expect you can see there’s a big difference between what Fox did and what he alleges the Times did.
(To be fair, Uthmeier could have pointed to how the Times reported an Alabama basketball player was present at a murder. He wasn’t.
The paper corrected its error, but lost a recent defamation suit.)
The AG’s letter also notes the Israeli government has vowed to sue the Times over the Kristof story. If the Times loses, it might have to shell out millions.
Ulterior motive?
To date, however, no suit has been filed.
And it won’t be. The discovery in such a case (prison records, medical records, witness statements) would be ugly.
Again, what is this really about?
Could it simply be another ultra-conservative attack on freedom of the press? Even if Uthmeier’s high-handed letter produces exactly nothing, he might hope it has a chilling effect on a newspaper he views as antithetical to his values.
Or is it a publicity grab by an ambitious guy running for a high-profile gig as attorney general of the third largest state in the nation?
Uthmeier knows he’s likely to win his race. I suspect he’s looking beyond AG to, maybe, governor? U.S. senator? An even higher office?
The current occupant of the White House will not, despite the fervent hopes of his disciples, live forever.
Somebody has to wrap himself in the MAGA flag and raise the sword of Trumpism in the battle against the 21st century.
Why not James Uthmeier, Esq.?

name: Florida Phoenix
title: Florida abandoned transparency in gift to Trump library
description: “Secrecy breeds corruption, and transparency protects liberty.” – Connor Boyack When Marvin Dunn learned about a clandestine deal through which Gov. Ron DeSantis, Attorney General James Uthmeier, and company bestowed President Donald Trump with 2.63 acres of prime real estate in downtown Miami, he was so incensed he filed suit. Dunn’s lawsuit alleges that wh[...]
text:
In an aerial view, a parking lot adjacent to the Freedom Tower was voted by Florida officials to be donated as the potential site for President Donald Trump's future presidential library on Sept. 30, 2025, in Miami. Republican Gov. Ron DeSantis and the Florida Cabinet voted to give the 2.63-acre parcel, appraised at more than $66 million, to the foundation planning the president's library.  (Photo by Joe Raedle/Getty Images)“Secrecy breeds corruption, and transparency protects liberty.” – Connor Boyack
When Marvin Dunn learned about a clandestine deal through which Gov. Ron DeSantis, Attorney General James Uthmeier, and company bestowed President Donald Trump with 2.63 acres of prime real estate in downtown Miami, he was so incensed he filed suit.
Dunn’s lawsuit alleges that when Miami-Dade College and Florida officials orchestrated the land transfer, ostensibly for a Trump presidential library, they violated Florida’s open government law because there was no transparency or opportunity for public comment.
“According to the state emoluments law, the state cannot give the president gifts. It’s against the Constitution,” Dunn told the Phoenix in an Aug. 13 interview. “Oh yes, it was land grab, almost a land steal.”
In a separate interview with South Florida public radio, Dunn explained further.
“It hit me immediately as a theft of land that belongs to children unborn in Miami-Dade County,” he said. “You’re stealing land from children who are not even born yet, and any politician who would stoop to that … is entitled to my sense of anger and repulsion.”
Dunn and people familiar with the situation say the board held an emergency meeting and unanimously voted to seal the deal. Shortly after the meeting, Uthmeier announced plans for the Trump library on that site.
“This was underhanded, behind-the-scenes scheming by Ron DeSantis, the governor. The governor orchestrated this whole thing,” Dunn said. “People were following his orders, and I take this straight to his doorstep. Ron DeSantis orchestrated to steal land that belongs to our kids for Donald Trump, the person he apparently idolizes.”
Dunn, an historian and civil rights advocate, said his lawsuit seeks to halt the transfer and force the board to comply with public transparency requirements under state law.
DeSantis has not commented on the lawsuit but insists having the Trump library in Miami would be “good for Florida.”
 Prime real estate
The prime piece of real estate — one of the last undeveloped parcels on Biscayne Boulevard — is valued by Miami Dade real estate appraisers at $67 million and possibly could fetch as much as $300 million.
The property was transferred to a state fund overseen by DeSantis and then deeded to the Donald J. Trump Presidential Library Foundation. The land is located near the waterfront, across from the Miami Heat arena, and had previously been used as a college parking lot.
Miami-Dade paid $24 million for the plot in 2004. The college received no money in return for signing over its land to the state, while it could cost the college up to $300,000 in legal fees, Javier Ley-Soto, general counsel for the college, testified in a court hearing last month.
Dunn has held “teach ins” and rallies to educate the public while trying to organize community opposition from those teed-off by Florida officials’ actions. The only beneficiaries are politicians in high places seeking to placate Trump, he said.
“Miami Dade College is a public institution that serves primarily Black and brown students,” Dunn told WLRN. “They’re struggling for scholarship money. They’re struggling to keep faculty and staff on board, and then to have this giveaway is just an insult to the community.”
According to WLRN, a poll conducted in October by the public research firm Bendixen & Amandi showed 74% of respondents believed that Miami Dade College should keep the land. Opposition to the transfer included 59% of Republicans.
“We want to have students out there,” said Dunn. “We want to have faculty members, community members, anyone who cares about the future of Miami Dade College, who wants to come out on the same day that the president is speaking to say, ‘Don’t take this land from our kids.’”
 Litigation

Bob Norman, an investigative reporter with the Florida Trident, wrote a scathing piece titled, “The Staggering Cost of James Uthmeier,” which presents in detail Uthmeier’s cavalier attitude towards Floridians’ hard-earned tax dollars. Norman estimates that the AG’s partisan political shenanigans has cost Florida more than $1 billion.


“It was a dumb move,” Dunn said of Uthmeier’s Trump Library announcement. “It showed that there had to have been previous discussions among people at the state level and even at the level of the White House for that library to be placed on the site.”

Dunn said his lawsuit is moving forward.
“It has been assigned to a judge in federal court. Oct. 1 is the date when he will announce whether the case will continue or be dismissed,” he told the Phoenix.
Will he win? Dunn was asked. “Of course, I expect to win. If the Constitution is followed, we will prevail.”
The case survived Miami-Dade Circuit Judge Mavel Ruiz tossing out a temporary injunction she’d imposed to block the planned land transfer.
“This is not an easy decision,” Ruiz said in explaining her ruling from the bench, finding that the college hadn’t given the public reasonable notice ahead of the vote last month but staged a second vote following a public hearing. “This is not a case, at least for this court, rooted in politics,” she said.
In response to the Dunn legal filing, Uthmeier pulled together a band of state-funded lawyers to defend Miami-Dade College.
“Under my authority as Florida’s Chief Legal Officer, our office stepped in Wednesday) to represent Miami-Dade College in this bogus lawsuit,” Uthmeier posted on his X account.
Uthmeier, 38, running for election in November after being placed in the job by DeSantis, was hunting for Trump’s endorsement and got it after the land transfer powerplay, Norman says.
“And just a week after Uthmeier voted for the land transfer, Trump gave him a rousing all-caps-strewn endorsement,” Norman writes.
 Bait and switch?
“James is an America First Warrior, who is a true champion for ‘MAGA,’” Trump wrote online. “He is THE MAN behind ALLIGATOR ALCATRAZ … James Uthmeier is a Strong Conservative Fighter and Prosecutor, and has my Complete and Total Endorsement — HE WILL NOT LET YOU DOWN!”
Ben Wilcox, research director for the nonprofit watchdog group Integrity Florida, says the endorsement smacks of a political quid pro quo, Norman noted.
“It does give the appearance that the endorsement of Uthmeier by Trump was transactional,” Wilcox told the reporter. “It’s just ugly.”
Dunn points to evidence Trump plans a bait and switch. The Trump Organization has released plans for a towering skyscraper complete with a giant golden statue of Trump and the $400 million Boeing 747 gifted to him by Qatar displayed in the lobby.
“President Trump said the quiet part out loud: ‘I don’t believe in building libraries or museums,’ adding, ‘It’s going to be most likely a hotel,’” Norman notes.
That inspired another lawsuit, this one by the Constitutional Accountability Center in Washington, D.C.
CAC’s attorney wrote in the still-active federal complaint, “Due to the President’s influence on so many aspects of federal policy … every state has an incentive to enrich the President should such private rewards be permitted. To avoid even the possibility that conflicts of interest like these would harm the American people by compromising their leaders’ judgment, the Founders enshrined the prohibitions of the Domestic Emoluments Clause in our national charter.”
Dunn says the president’s admission it would be a hotel helped make the case a “very powerful” one, Norman said.
 ‘Big foot’
“It’s a big foot and it’s hard to extract it from his mouth,” Dunn told Norman of Trump’s admission. “He gave truth to the central element of our lawsuit, that the president took a personal gift from the State of Florida with a commercial benefit. A hotel is a leap into another universe. It has no relationship to the mission of a presidential library.”
Dunn said he’s prepared to take his case all the way to the U.S. Supreme Court, but in the Phoenix interview worried that Trump “will delay and delay.”
“My concern is that the president will stretch it out until he leaves office,” he said.
Dunn castigated Uthmeier, saying he has done a disservice to Floridians.
“He has represented himself and has not represented the public well. I am extremely outraged with his University of Florida “job.” He is making eight times the regular adjunct’s pay. It’s a scam job,” Dunn said. “He may not be required to be on campus at all but if he is, is he using the state airplane and state security on his $100,000 a year scam job? I doubt that he drives from Tallahassee to Gainesville twice a week. I’m also wondering, does he have a new contract this fall?”
When asked whether the bad press that has dogged Uthmeier — “Alligator Alcatraz,” the Hope Florida Foundation debacle, and the land grab — will damage him enough to cause him to lose, Dunn said he’s not sure.
“That’s a good question. I think so, but only if the public becomes aware of the egregious behavior of this man in office. It will help him because his is a down-ballot race. I hope he is defeated in November, because Florida can’t afford to have him in office for another term.”

name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: State paying $625K to settle lawsuit over Braun firing utility commission member
description: The state is paying $625,000 to settle a lawsuit in which a former member of the Indiana Utility Regulatory Commission claimed he was illegally fired by Gov. Mike Braun.
text:
Andy Zay, then the chair of the Indiana Utility Regulatory Commission, leads a daylong utility affordability hearing on March 24, 2026, at the IURC's downtown Indianapolis headquarters. (Photo by Leslie Bonilla Muñiz/Indiana Capital Chronicle)The state is paying $625,000 to settle a lawsuit in which a former member of the Indiana Utility Regulatory Commission claimed he was illegally fired by Gov. Mike Braun.
The governor’s office announced the deal Saturday with former utility commission member Andy Zay, calling it a “mutually agreeable settlement.”
Zay argued in his suit filed Aug. 10 that Braun lacked sufficient reason to replace him on the commission and described a pattern of the governor’s office infringing on the commission’s statutory duty as an “impartial fact-finding body.” 
Braun’s attorneys had responded to Zay’s lawsuit with claims that Zay, a former state senator, had improperly spent thousands of dollars in campaign funds on gifts to commission staffers and improperly awarded bonuses to IURC employees.
Deal covers Zay’s salary and legal costs
Neither side admitted any wrongdoing under the settlement terms that were released by the governor’s office.
“This Agreement does not constitute an admission by any Party that any of them have violated any law, and each specifically denies having done so,” the terms said.
The settlement includes $485,000 in payments to Zay that were described as “the reasonable net present value of the remaining salary and benefits if Zay had served through March 31, 2030.”
That date is when Zay’s term as one of the five IURC commissioners was to expire.
IURC head, governor talk Zay firing and AES hike reconsideration

The remaining $140,000 will be paid to Zay and the Indianapolis law firm Betz + Blevins to cover his legal expenses. The law firm Kroger, Gardis & Regas was representing the governor’s office in the case.
Braun announced in December he was appointing Zay as the new chair of the commission that determines what residents and businesses in most of the state pay for electricity, natural gas, water and other utility services.
Zay, a Republican from Huntington, resigned from the state Senate seat he had held since 2016 on Jan. 8 and began work at the IURC on Jan. 12.
But Braun demoted Zay from the chair position in June, days after he was part of a 3-1 commission majority that  approved a contentious $71 million rate hike for AES Indiana electricity customers.
Braun denounced that rate hike and said “affordability is my top priority” in announcing he was removing Zay as commission chair.
The governor went further on Aug. 3 in firing Zay from the commission entirely. Braun soon replaced him with former Indianapolis City-County Councilor Joshua Bain.
The Indiana Office of Utility Consumer Counselor and Citizens Action Coalition have asked the commission to reconsider the AES rate increase decision.
Braun, Zay amicable in statements
Zay said in a statement released by the governor’s office that he was proud of his work with the IURC “balancing the affordability of services needed by all citizens …  against the costs for maintaining and supplying those services.”
“I am disappointed that I will no longer be directly involved in this important work, but I believe resolution with the State is in everyone’s best interest at this time,” Zay’s statement said. “I appreciate Governor Braun’s willingness to reach satisfactory terms so that we can all move forward in a positive direction.”
Gov. Mike Braun speaks with reporters on July 15, 2026. (Photo by Tom Davies/Indiana Capital Chronicle)
Zay’s lawsuit described meetings and phone calls involving Braun and top administration officials seeking to discuss the AES rate case. Zay claimed those crossed into banned “ex parte” communications — seeking to sway a decision-maker in a case without the other parties to the case present.
A Marion County judge had scheduled a court hearing for Thursday on Zay’s request for an order reinstating him to the commission.
Braun said in the governor’s office statement that he was pleased with the resolution.
“This agreement allows all involved to move forward constructively in the best interest of Hoosiers,” Braun said. “I want to recognize Andy for his service to the state. Public service is demanding work, and I appreciate his contributions over the course of a decade on behalf of Hoosiers.”

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Ag secretary candidate Chris Jones touts systemic changes to Iowa agriculture
description: The Democratic candidate for Iowa secretary of agriculture told Iowa State Fair attendees Saturday that “the outrage has finally arrived” for the state of Iowa’s water, and said systemic change rather than incremental fixes is the way to clear up waterways and improve other areas of Iowans’ lives. Chris Jones criticized “Band-Aid approaches” to fixing […]
text:
Iowa Secretary of Agriculture candidate Chris Jones speaks to Iowa State Fair attendees on Aug. 22, 2026. (Photo by Brooklyn Draisey/Iowa Capital Dispatch)The Democratic candidate for Iowa secretary of agriculture told Iowa State Fair attendees Saturday that “the outrage has finally arrived” for the state of Iowa’s water, and said systemic change rather than incremental fixes is the way to clear up waterways and improve other areas of Iowans’ lives.
Chris Jones criticized “Band-Aid approaches” to fixing Iowa’s environment and rural economy during his Des Moines Register Political Soapbox speech, including President Donald Trump’s decision to import more ground beef and infusions of money by the state into initiatives that haven’t fixed things.
Jones joined Iowa cattle farmers in expressing disappointment at Trump’s Friday announcement that he is suspending tariffs on 300,000 metric tons of imported ground beef, saying the move isn’t helpful to farmers in and outside of Iowa.
“High demand creates better profitability for cattle production, so why is the president, you know, kicking farmers in the gut with this 660 million pounds of hamburger that’s only going to be around for 90 days,” Jones said.
Jones is running against incumbent Republican Mike Naig, who spoke on the soapbox Aug. 17.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Iowa has been taking an incremental approach to trying to fix Iowa’s water quality and other problems, Jones said, like encouraging voluntary adoption of conservation policies and spending $1 million at a time in different areas of “the corn-soy system and the CAFO system,” and these efforts have not worked.
The “most important thing” Jones said he shares with people about creating a more resilient and thriving agriculture industry in Iowa, as well as Iowa’s water quality, is to diversify farm operations. Some have told Jones this practice would send Iowa agriculture backward, to which he responded that going forward the way things are “looks pretty bad” to him.
Farmers need to grow more than just corn and soybeans but expand into fruits and vegetables, Jones said, as well as create more pastures for cattle in order to rebuild Iowa’s cattle industry. These practices would help with sustainability as well as diversify the agriculture economy in the state, he said.
“We need systematic change in this farming system if we’re going to get the environmental outcomes that we want,” Jones said. “At the same time, we need to do that in a way that preserves farmer incomes, preserves their livelihoods, preserves their way of life, but also help(s) us.”
“Common sense regulations” on concentrated animal feeding operations and corn and soy production would help clean up Iowa waterways, Jones said, alongside taxpayer-supported off ramps to help farmers transition into better practices.
Jones said he also wants to support small-scale livestock production as well as in-state meat and grain processing to keep those economic benefits in Iowa rather than sending them to another state. If Iowans diversify their crops and begin growing more fruits and vegetables, Jones added that Iowa could grow its own food for its own residents rather than import the majority of what Iowans eat. He said he would commit $10 million annually to growing food in Iowa for Iowans to eat.
Diversifying crops comes with additional labor needs, Jones said, and farmers would need “certainty on labor” if they were to make this kind of transition. He said the “big effort to send people back to their home countries” from the federal government is harming the potential workforce in this area.
“These are people that could help repopulate rural Iowa, they can provide labor for fruit and vegetable farmers. They want to do these jobs, right? A lot of these people that come from other countries, they have agricultural backgrounds,” Jones said. “This is the work that they want to do, and so we need policy that’s going to make labor available to these sorts of farmers.”
Jones said he’d like to see practices like fall tillage and fall anhydrous ammonia application reduced or done away with through restrictions or taxes on the practices, as they aren’t necessary and can cause problems like increased soil erosion and nutrient loss.
Another topic impacting Iowa’s water and land is data centers, which Jones responded to an audience question about by saying he wants to see at least a one-year moratorium on data center construction in the state.
Iowa land should be used for its “highest use,” he said, which he identified as growing food. He said restoring small livestock production and meat processing in rural Iowa would be a better way to bring in jobs than building data centers.
“If we want more farmers, if we want more young farmers, if we want these vegetable crops and these other diverse crops, if we want cattle on pasture, we can’t have data centers, you know, gobbling up all this land,” Jones said.

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Libertarian Jacob Heard committed to fight for party’s ballot access
description: The Libertarian Party’s new nominee for the 3rd Congressional District race in Iowa gave two reasons to Iowa State Fair attendees for why he shouldn’t have the chance to speak with them on the Des Moines Register Political Soapbox stage. The first was that Marco Battaglia, the initial Libertarian candidate in the congressional race, was […]
text:
Iowa 3rd Congressional District candidate Jacob Heard speaks to Iowa State Fair attendees on Aug. 22, 2026. (Photo by Brooklyn Draisey/Iowa Capital Dispatch)The Libertarian Party’s new nominee for the 3rd Congressional District race in Iowa gave two reasons to Iowa State Fair attendees for why he shouldn’t have the chance to speak with them on the Des Moines Register Political Soapbox stage.
The first was that Marco Battaglia, the initial Libertarian candidate in the congressional race, was supposed to be up there but didn’t qualify to be placed on the election ballot, as ruled by the State Objections Panel and upheld by a Polk County District Court judge. The second was that Heard himself has not been deemed qualified to run, either.
“The Libertarian State Committee voted about two weeks ago to replace Marco, as well as Nick Gluba and Jules Cutler for the governor and lieutenant governor seats,” Heard said. “When we turned in our nomination papers this last Monday, two days later, the Secretary of State’s Office said that the proper procedure wasn’t filed with their office in time, and therefore he’s not accepting … my candidacy as well as the governor and lieutenant governor’s candidacy to appear on the Nov. 3 general election ballot.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Like Libertarian gubernatorial candidate Nicholas Gluba said after his own soapbox speech, Heard told reporters he is confident the “petition for writ of mandamus” filed by the candidates will force Iowa Secretary of State Paul Pate to allow their names to be placed on election ballots. He believes the Secretary of State’s Office is using a “novel interpretation” of Iowa code detailing processes for non-party political organizations to fill vacancies in candidacies.
A ruling on the petition is expected to come on Aug. 27, Heard said. If the case goes up to the Iowa Supreme Court, Heard will argue for the Libertarians.
Heard focused his speech to fairgoers on the risks he sees to having a two-party system in Iowa, but told reporters he’s focusing on constitutional amendments in this campaign “that will try to fix Congress.”
These amendments would include requirements for single-subject bills rather than omnibus bills like those seen at the federal level, repealing the 18th Amendment relating to the direct election of senators and adding an amendment to “force Congress to spend within their means.”
“Congress is, in my opinion, our most dysfunctional branch of government, both federal and state level,” Heard said.
Pulling back the War Powers Resolution to limit presidential powers in engaging in acts of war without congressional authority are other priorities Heard shared.
In his time working as a legislative analyst for Iowa Senate Republicans and as chief of staff to then-Iowa Senate President Jake Chapman, Heard said he learned that Iowa Republicans and Democrats agree on one thing — they will remain the only two political parties in Iowa if they can help it. This was clear in 2024 when Libertarian candidates were taken off ballots, he said, and it’s clear now.
Two-party systems like the one in Iowa cause problems whether the parties have split control over state government or if one has the majority, he said, like nothing getting done if a policy issue keeps the parties at odds or the pendulum effect of the majority party passing its preferred policies then policies swinging the other way when control shifts.
In Iowa’s current case of Republicans being in charge of state government, Heard said the checks that are supposed to be in place go away “because that party isn’t going to want to embarrass or reduce the power of their governor, so to speak.” An example of this he said was during the COVID-19 pandemic when Gov. Kim Reynolds passed executive orders banning certain gatherings.
Iowans are also given a “false choice” at the ballot box that makes them believe they’re wasting their vote if they cast their ballot for a Libertarian or other non-major party candidate, he said.
“Every Iowan can have a good idea, have a good policy solution, but when you limit it to just Democrats and Republicans, it gives you a false choice and a false idea or premise that there’s only two solutions,” Heard said.

title: Auditor candidate Taylor Wettach says he’ll work to reverse law limiting audits
description: The Democratic candidate for state auditor told Iowa State Fair attendees Saturday he wants to build on the good work Rob Sand has completed in the office — hopefully with Sand as a partner in the governor’s office. Taylor Wettach spoke at the Des Moines Register Political Soapbox to detail his bid for the state […]
text:
Taylor Wettach spoke to Iowa State Fair attendees and reporters during the Des Moines Register Political Soapbox on Aug. 22, 2026. (Photo by Brooklyn Draisey/Iowa Capital Dispatch)The Democratic candidate for state auditor told Iowa State Fair attendees Saturday he wants to build on the good work Rob Sand has completed in the office — hopefully with Sand as a partner in the governor’s office.
Taylor Wettach spoke at the Des Moines Register Political Soapbox to detail his bid for the state regulatory position, saying his career as a lawyer will aid him in holding people and institutions accountable even with limitations that have been placed on the auditor’s office.
“I have experience and understanding to look into those financials, and then as a lawyer, I have experience and understanding to make sure that where there are problems that we do find, we can do something about it,” Wettach said. “So I’m excited to take that background and leverage it.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.

Candidates speak at Register Soapbox
Saturday is the final day of candidate speeches at The Des Moines Register Political Soapbox at the state fair.  Here’s the schedule.
Republican U.S. Senate candidate: Ashley Hinson
Democratic U.S. Senate candidate: Josh Turek
Libertarian U.S. Senate candidate: Thomas Laehn
Republican gubernatorial candidate: Zach Lahn
Democratic gubernatorial candidate: Rob Sand
Libertarian gubernatorial candidate: Nicholas Gluba
Republican secretary of agriculture candidate: Mike Naig
Democratic attorney general candidate:  Nate Willems
Republican attorney general candidate: Brenna Bird
Democratic secretary of state candidate: Ryan Peterman
Republican secretary of state candidate: Paul Pate
Democratic state treasurer candidate: John Norwood
Independent 1st Congressional District candidate: Michael Bridgford
Republican 2nd Congressional District candidate: Joe Mitchell
Democratic 2nd Congressional District candidate: Lindsay James
Independent 2nd District Congressional District candidate:  Dave Bushaw
Libertarian 2nd District Congressional candidate: Rick Stewart
Republican 3rd Congressional District candidate: Zach Nunn
Democratic 3rd Congressional District candidate: Sarah Trone Garriott
Republican 4th Congressional District candidate:  Chris McGowan


In his work as an attorney, Wettach said he’s negotiated complex financial matters involving millions of dollars and “working with some of the best auditors in the country.” He told fairgoers he resigned from Simpson Thacher & Bartlett LLP, his former firm, in protest of pressure on the firm from President Donald Trump’s administration “to cut a deal to do $125 million worth of free work in support of their priorities.”
The state auditor’s office is supposed to be an “independent watchdog” in service of Iowans and their tax dollars, Wettach said, a role he added Sand has filled successfully despite efforts from the state to restrict access the office has to information. The Iowa Legislature in 2023 passed a bill, later signed into law by Gov. Kim Reynolds, that limits the auditor’s office’s ability to access personal information when investigating matters.
Lt. Gov. Chris Cournoyer, Wettach’s Republican opponent in the state auditor race, did not participate in the Des Moines Register Political Soapbox.
One of Wettach’s focuses will be trying to get rid of that law, he said, as well as continuing Sand’s work, including the operation of the Public Innovation Efficiencies program and maintaining the office’s independence.
“With the school voucher program, Rob was still able to pursue an audit of what was going on there,” Wettach said. “Now, did he get all the information he needed to do it in a really fulsome way? No, he didn’t. But he was able to dig in, look at the challenges, and put that forward. So, I think it’s important to note that while we talk about threats to that office in that sort of way, this office can continue to do a lot of good.”
In response to an audience question about the first thing he’ll focus on if he is elected to the auditor position, Wettach said he would turn the office’s eye once again to Education Savings Accounts for non-public schools. He also wants to further expand support from the auditor’s office to rural areas in order to provide resources and services for local citizens trying to fight corruption.
“It’s kind of like primary care versus, you know, expensive treatment … when you already are sick, right,” Wettach said. “If you can provide more support up front for these areas, we’re not going to have all the pain of playing whack-a-mole in the back end, trying to find the problems and fix things when they are already problems.”
If Sand is elected as governor alongside Wettach as auditor, Wettach said he hopes to have a partner in Sand as someone who understands the work of the office and Wettach’s drive to combat fraud, abuse and misuse of Iowa tax funds. However, if Republican Zach Lahn wins the seat rather than Sand, Wettach said that doesn’t mean the auditor’s office won’t be able to get anything done.
It will still be just as important to serve the state as an independent watchdog, he said, and to reverse the law that has somewhat tied the auditor’s hands.
“It shouldn’t matter if the governor is a Democrat or if the governor is a Republican, if I’m elected, I’m going to work to undo that law because that’s how it’s supposed to be done,” Wettach said. “Because the folks in that office deserve to be able to get the information they need to fight for the taxpayer, and that doesn’t matter who’s in charge.”
